#5633. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? #5632. Attached Housing Stands Out in Baltimore’s Housing Market

Annualized new-home sales declined 5.2% in September to 2,613 units. Attached housing accounted for 1,951 sales versus 662 detached sales during the period. However, the Baltimore market is sending mixed signals as 2026 winds down. By comparison, the market’s average new-home sales rate of 2.4 homes per project matched Maryland and remained above the national rate of 2.0.

That aforementioned product split is one of Baltimore’s defining characteristics. Annualized attached sales fell just 0.9% year over year compared with a 16% decline for detached homes as of September data. The strongest sales activity also sits toward the more attainable end of the new home market, with attached homes priced from $350,000 to $450,000 experiencing the most closing activity over the past year.

Related, affordability remains a constraint. As of July, the median new-home closing price stood at $555,337, down 2.9% year over year, compared with $420,000 for existing homes.

The economic backdrop adds another layer. Total nonfarm employment in the Baltimore metro declined 0.6% year over year in August, while the unemployment rate was 4.1%. Households are estimated to decline 0.1% in 2026 and post flat annual growth through 2028.

One potential longer-term catalyst comes from defense manufacturing. Anduril Industries announced a $3.7 billion investment in a high-tech shipyard at Baltimore County’s Tradepoint Atlantic industrial center. The project is expected to create 3,100 direct jobs and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs, while generating more than $2 billion in annual economic output.

Baltimore’s opportunity is therefore less about broad based growth and more about positioning. Ideal locations, attainable price points, and disciplined starts stand out in a market where buyers are still active but increasingly selective.

#5631. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. #5630. Social Security Could Have Paid Full Benefits Until 2059. What Went Wrong?

Social Security could have paid full benefits until 2059—25 years longer than currently projected—if the share of the U.S. economy subject to payroll taxes had remained at its 1983 level, according to a new analysis.

Under that scenario, the program would have collected an additional $10.8 trillion in payroll tax revenue and interest between 1984 and 2034.

The findings, from AARP's Public Policy Institute, come as Social Security's combined trust funds are projected to run dry in 2034. Without congressional intervention, incoming revenue would cover only about 83% of scheduled benefits that year.

And while much of the debate over Social Security's financial troubles has centered on declining birthrates and a growing number of retirees supported by fewer workers, the new analysis points to another major factor.

As more of the nation's income flows to high earners and investors, a shrinking share of the economy is subject to the payroll taxes that finance Social Security.

In 1983, wages subject to those taxes accounted for 41% of the nation's gross domestic product. By 2025, that share had fallen to just 34%.

To understand what changed for the trust fund, it helps to take a trip back to 1984: when "Ghostbusters" dominated the box office, Madonna broke out with "Like a Virgin," and the median household income was $61,910, compared with an average of $75,850, according to U.S. Census Bureau data adjusted to 2025 dollars.

Today, those figures have climbed to $87,460 and $126,700, respectively.

That's a 41% increase in median household income, compared with a 67% increase in the average—evidence of how income growth has become more concentrated toward the upper end of the distribution.

And that's where Social Security runs into trouble.

The program collects payroll taxes on wages, but only up to an annual limit. In 2026, workers and employers each pay 6.2% on the first $184,500 of wages. So someone earning $2 million pays the same amount in Social Security payroll taxes as someone earning $184,500.

As more wage income accumulates above that ceiling, Social Security collects nothing from those additional earnings, even as they contribute to the growth of the economy.

But the problem extends beyond how wages are distributed.

Between 1970 and 2023, labor compensation's share of GDP fell from 65% to 57%, as a larger portion of national income flowed to business owners and investors through profits and investment returns.

Unlike wages, most of that income isn't subject to Social Security payroll taxes. So as economic growth generates more profits and investment returns, Social Security doesn't necessarily collect additional revenue.

And those earnings are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest Americans.

Taxpayers earning $1 million or more represented just 1% of filers in 2023 but received 48% of all investment income, according to AARP's analysis of Internal Revenue Service data.

AARP also points to the growth of businesses whose owners can receive some of their compensation as profits rather than salaries, further reducing the amount subject to payroll taxes.

Together, these changes have allowed the U.S. economy to generate substantially more income without a corresponding increase in the share subject to Social Security taxes. As a result, the program has captured a shrinking portion of the nation's economic growth, leaving less revenue available to pay future benefits.

Millions of older Americans are already struggling to afford their homes, leaving them particularly vulnerable to any potential reductions in benefits.

In 2023, more than 12.4 million households headed by adults 65 or older spent over 30% of their income on housing, according to Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies. More than half of those households—6.7 million—spent over 50% of their income on housing alone.

"Even without any insolvency-driven benefit cuts, millions of seniors already struggle to pay for food, basic healthcare, and even housing," Shannon Benton, executive director of The Senior Citizens League, said in a Nov. 10 statement.

And retirees could face those cuts sooner than the combined trust fund projection suggests.

The separate trust fund responsible for retirement and survivor benefits is projected to exhaust its reserves in 2032, two years before the hypothetical combined funds. Without congressional intervention, incoming revenue would cover only 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits.

Based on the average retired worker monthly benefit of $2,089 in September 2026, a 22% reduction would amount to roughly $460 a month.

Now, advocates warn that decisions over Social Security's financing can no longer be deferred.

"The incoming class of senators face an enormous responsibility," Benton said, noting that their six-year terms will run through January 2033—past the point when Social Security's retirement and survivors trust fund is projected to exhaust its reserves.

Richard W. Johnson, vice president of financial security at AARP’s Public Policy Institute and author of the analysis, argues that strengthening Social Security requires bringing its financing into line with the modern economy.

"Strengthening Social Security does not require re-creating the economy of 1983," he said. "It just means updating Social Security's financing to reflect how Americans receive income today."

And it was a popular idea on the 2026 midterm campaign trail, too.

In October, Sherrod Brown, who won Ohio's Senate race, called for higher earners to contribute more "by raising the tax cap so we can extend the life of the program."

Troy Jackson, Maine's senator-elect, went further, calling for eliminating the cap altogether.

"Making sure that wealthier people pay the same rate that working class people do would definitely strengthen the Social Security system overall," Jackson said in a September TV interview.

The idea has also drawn bipartisan interest, with Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) jointly proposing the elimination of the cap in June.

Based on Social Security actuaries' 2025 assumptions, eliminating the cap could close about 67% of the program's 75-year financing gap if higher contributions didn't generate additional future benefits—or roughly half if they did.

Other proposals would tax certain business and investment income that currently falls outside Social Security's revenue base.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5629. Spec Versus Built-to-Order: Builders Navigate a Changing Market

For builders, the push and pull between speculative homes and built-to-order (BTO) homes is a classic struggle, reflecting the desire to balance operational efficiency against market demand. A favorable mix directly dictates a company’s profit margins, inventory risk, and customer satisfaction.

Spec homes allow builders to more directly compete with resale inventory, offering faster move-ins that can capture demand from buyers looking to move quickly. In strong markets, heavier spec exposure can increase sales velocity. In slower markets, builders with large levels of spec inventory are exposed to carrying costs and pricing risk.

A built-to-order approach reduces that inventory risk and offers buyers greater personalization in their final purchase. Built-to-order homes typically carry higher sales prices and translate into healthier margins while requiring buyers to wait longer to move in.

While several companies are steadfast in their approaches, such as the 100% spec commitments of Meritage Homes and CBH Homes and the 70% BTO target set by KB Home, the spec-BTO balance often shifts over time.

In the immediate post-pandemic period, many builders leaned more heavily into spec production. Unprecedented levels of demand and rapidly rising home prices set a backdrop for many large builders to offer more spec and quick move-in (QMI) homes because homes were absorbed at record levels. Similarly, the standardized production and simplified SKU packages helped builders guard against pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and labor shortages.

When mortgage rates began to spike in late 2023, a go-to-market approach with spec production remained prevalent to help buyers with certainty of price and move-in timing. Public builders at the time noted buyers were less willing to commit many months ahead given rate uncertainty and favored move-in ready homes. Builders favoring a heavier spec production mix were able to lean into financing incentives in the form of price cuts and rate buydowns to capture demand as economic uncertainty began to mount.

At the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026, one of the more notable themes to emerge is a more concentrated shift toward a higher built-to-order mix. KB Home began sharing its goal of a 70% BTO mix in the second quarter of 2025, noting the approach is customer-centric and that a design-forward, personalized approach is a differentiator in a market where incentives were prevalent.

“Our buyers choose their lot, floor plan, and personalized finishes. The result is a home that has a real specific value to the people who will live in it,” president and CEO Rob McGibney said during an earnings call with investors. “Homes built to customer specifications do not require heavy incentives to sell.”

Similarly, in the past couple quarters PulteGroup has highlighted its efforts to skew production more toward BTO homes, targeting a 60-40 mix.

“Our decision to build more spec homes once supply chains collapsed and build cycles effectively doubled was the right one at the time, but we much prefer having a growing backlog of sold homes,” PulteGroup president CEO Ryan Marshall shared during a recent earnings call.

The shift is not just occurring among large public builders, with Texas-based Stylecraft Builders reporting a shift toward the BTO model. After carrying essentially no to-be-built volume as recently as 12 to 18 months ago, the company is targeting a goal of 20% to 25% of sales from BTO orders.

Spec-heavy, BTO-heavy, and hybrid operators are all succeeding in the current challenging market. Rather than converging toward a single model, many builders increasingly view spec and BTO homes as complementary tools that can be adjusted based on market conditions, buyer behavior, and community characteristics.

For many builders, spec homes and BTO homes are not an either-or strategy, and a flexible approach that puts buyers front of mind yields the most successful results.

“They serve different customer needs and we want to execute both approaches well,” David Weekley Homes chief operating officer Ladd Fargo tells BUILDER. “The approximate mix depends on the market, buyer behavior, product type, and price point.”

The by-market approach is one that resonates strongly with Trumark Homes. As a private builder that serves as the western hub for Daiwa House, Trumark Homes leans into the local expertise of its division operators to meet the market with the best approach across its operating platforms in California, Colorado, and Washington.

“We know that we have strong operators in all our markets, and we trust our division teams to understand their buyer profiles, have a pulse on the competition, and utilize the data and tools available to plan accordingly,” Trumark Homes chief operating officer Steve Kalmbach says. “We will continue to be nimble and make the best strategic decisions for each community along the way.”

Fred McConnell, vice president of brand and performance marketing at Risewell Homes, tells BUILDER the company has become more intentional about creating built-to-order opportunities while maintaining a strong offering of quick move-in, spec homes. The mixed approach allows Risewell to be both consumer-led and market-responsive while aligning the company’s core brand platform, Built Well to Live Well.

“Our goal is to maintain the flexibility to respond to both the consumer and the dynamics of each individual market and community,” McConnell says.

Huntsville, Alabama-based Davidson Homes has seen a shift toward more BTO homes, but the company’s core strategy has not changed. CEO Brandon Jones says the company continues to meet buyers where they are, offering a solution for those who need to move in 45 days or those who want to choose every detail from homesite to interior finishes. He says the market has not picked a winner between spec or BTO and has instead rewarded builders who are disciplined about using both approaches.

“We start with the buyer, not the model. A lot of our industry has moved to one way of building,” Jones continues. “We’ve kept real personalization on the menu because buyers still want it, and we keep inventory on the ground because some buyers can’t wait. If we get the buyer right, the mix takes care of itself.”

CBH Homes has been a 100% spec builder since 2019, placing high value on the efficiencies gained in the building process and the simplification it provides to the buyer experience. The efficiencies gained early, from purchasing to scheduling trade partners, provide consistency and synergy that allows real value to be passed on to the buyers.

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable,” CBH Homes president and owner Corey Barton explains. “Our buyers can walk through a home, see the finishes, know the price, and know when they can move in. There are fewer unknowns.”

In the current market, where some builders are shifting approaches back toward a heavier BTO mix, Barton says CBH Homes still sees value in its 100% spec approach.

“When rates move or the right opportunity presents itself, our buyers don’t have to wait months for their home to be built,” Barton says. “On top of that, we know if a buyer has the option, they will want to make changes. Not allowing change orders allows us to keep costs down and construction efficiency high. Our goal isn’t to give the buyer a thousand decisions to make. It’s to do the work up front and create a beautiful, professionally designed home they can walk into and say, ‘This is it.’”

“Being a spec builder allows us to do what we do best: Build amazing homes quickly, efficiently, and at a price that keeps homeownership attainable.”

Meritage Homes made a similar transition to an all-spec approach in 2016, focusing on the entry-level segment and leaning into competition with resale inventory. The builder’s shorter cycle times allow it to start homes later while also maintaining its 60-day closing guarantee. CEO Phillippe Lord says that its trade relationships and limited SKU counts set it apart from other builders and provide greater certainty to its vendor partners. While the builder has been market responsive and has increased its portfolio of move-up product given market conditions, Meritage Homes remains committed to its 100% spec approach.

Houston-based David Weekley Homes has leaned more heavily into move-in-ready spec homes to respond to a buyer that is placing more value on speed and certainty. Fargo says the shift has been driven by changes in buyer preferences rather than operational considerations.

“In a more uncertain market, many buyers are less willing to commit far in advance. They want to know what they’re buying, what it will cost, and when they can move in,” Fargo explains. “With quick move-in homes, the goal is not simply to build more inventory. It’s to be thoughtful about which homes we start, where we build them, the price points we target, and when the homes will be available.”

Similarly, Kalmbach notes Trumark Homes is seeing more contingent buyers in the current market. For these buyers, knowing what homes are available within a given time frame can be an important factor when they are looking to move but still must sell their previous home. Spec homes represent a solution for this buyer.

For builders that have leaned more heavily into a BTO approach, most cite personalization, design, and customer centricity as core factors. By allowing buyers to choose lots, floor plans, and personalized finishes, says KB Home’s McGibney, the company is best able to serve its customers.

“Buyers are already invested in and feel a connection to the homes they created,” McGibney said. “This is in contrast to a speculative business model where incentives are used to create value. In that model, the builder increases the incentives to the point at which the buyers believe they have been adequately compensated for features and finishes they did not choose.”

Erlanger, Kentucky-based Fischer Homes has seen an increase in interest in BTO homes in 2026, with the builder noting many buyers are placing an emphasis on personalization. BTO homes utilize Fischer Homes’ Design Studio, giving buyers the opportunity to select finishes and details that bring a unique vision to life and allowing the builder to deliver a home that reflects the specific needs and preferences of a particular buyer.

“The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

Beyond design, KB Home’s McGibney said a BTO-forward approach provides visibility, predictability, and limits risk. When a buyer commits and the company locks in a price, the direct costs can be established before a shovel hits the ground and KB Home knows the margin it will achieve at delivery before a home is started.

“We view this as a fundamentally lower risk profile than a speculative model, where a builder starts a home with an assumption for the future sales price and then finds later, at the time of sale, that market conditions may require price reductions or heavy incentives,” McGibney said. “The visibility and predictability that BTO provides translates directly into more efficient operations and more dependable margins at delivery.”

PulteGroup’s shift toward increasing built-to-order homes reflects the preferences of move-up and active-adult buyers. The builder’s lower cycle time allows it to selectively use rate buydowns to facilitate BTO sales while still achieving higher margins than on spec sales.

“[Move-up and active-adult buyers] are individuals who expect choice, and our operating model allows them to choose their preferred lot and select the options and upgrades they desire,” Marshall said.

For luxury builder Toll Brothers, the company can provide a design-forward experience even to spec buyers given its timing and approach to sales. The builder is focused on selling specs as early as possible in the construction cycle to allow personalization through its design studios, providing an experience that is like the BTO experience in all but name.

Several builders say the spec-versus-BTO decision is often less about philosophy and more about the product being sold and the customer buying it.

Decisions are closely tied to what different buyer segments prioritize in the purchase process. For entry-level buyers, value is often concentrated in price, payment certainty, and speed, characteristics that favor a spec approach. Move-up buyers, by contrast, are often purchasing for the home itself and have greater flexibility to prioritize personalization and design choices over speed.

“A first-time buyer is usually solving for payment and timing. A move-up buyer is solving for the home itself,” Jones of Davidson Homes explains. “Spec answers the first. Built-to-order answers the second.”

Kalmbach of Trumark Homes adds that buyers who are seeking customization in the home buying process are more likely to have the resources and time to engage earlier in the purchasing process, beginning with lot selection and continuing through the full design process. Fargo of David Weekley Homes echoes this distinction: standardized, higher-density, and entry-level products generally lend themselves more naturally to move-in-ready construction while higher-priced, customizable homes are better positioned for BTO.

“In general, building from the ground up allows customers the opportunity to personalize their home and participate more fully in the home building process,” says Fargo. “The longer timeline also gives our team members more time to understand the customer, build a relationship with them, and help create a home that is right for them. That relationship and the experience we provide the home building process are things we value.”

Vincent Salandro is an editor for Builder. He earned a B.A. in journalism and a B.S. in economics from American University.

#5628. Meritage, PulteGroup Honor Veterans With Mortgage-Free Homes

Two national home builders are honoring military veterans and their families this fall with the gift of mortgage-free homeownership.

Meritage Homes, through its partnership with Operation Homefront, welcomed U.S. Navy veteran Maggie Coleman and her family to a new home in Gulfport, Mississippi, on Veterans Day. Meanwhile, PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes will present mortgage-free homes to U.S. Army veterans Carson Shaw and Ryan Heard and their families ahead of Thanksgiving.

The initiatives provide the families with greater housing stability while building on both companies’ long-standing efforts to support military families.

Meritage Homes and Operation Homefront presented Coleman and her two children with the keys to a new, mortgage-free home during a Veterans Day ceremony Nov. 11.

The approximately 2,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, three-bath home is located in Meritage’s Hidden Trails community in Gulfport, Mississippi. The donation marks the 23rd home Meritage has donated to a military family.

Coleman served 13 years in the Navy, including deployments to Italy and Kuwait. The home allows her family to put down permanent roots in her home state of Mississippi.

“I want to give my children everything I didn’t have,” Coleman said. “I want this home to be a place where my kids and I can share stories and make memories.”

“We’re proud to help welcome the Coleman family home to Gulfport,” Meritage Homes CEO Phillippe Lord said. “We recognize the service and sacrifices she and her family have made, and we’re honored to share in this special moment with them.”

The home was provided through Operation Homefront’s Permanent Homes for Veterans program, which works to help military families achieve long-term stability through mortgage-free housing and other support.

PulteGroup will continue the season of giving Nov. 18, when its Built to Honor program and Building Homes for Heroes present the keys to two mortgage-free homes at the builder’s Spencer Glen community in Riverview, Florida.

The homes will go to U.S. Army Sergeant Carson Shaw and his partner, Annalisa, and Purple Heart recipient U.S. Army Specialist Ryan Heard, his partner, Danielle, and their two children.

Shaw joined the Army in 2019 at age 18 and completed deployments to Iraq and Syria and to Africa. A line-of-duty motor vehicle accident in 2024 left him paralyzed from the waist down. He also lives with the effects of a traumatic brain injury and bilateral hearing loss.

Since his injury, Shaw has participated in six adaptive sports at the Warrior Games and plays wheelchair basketball with the Tampa Strong Dogs. His new accessible home will provide a stable foundation as he pursues a bachelor’s degree in finance and economics.

Heard enlisted in the Army in 2007 and completed two deployments to Iraq and one to Afghanistan. During his 2013 deployment to Afghanistan, an improvised explosive device detonated beneath Heard and three fellow soldiers. Despite sustaining a severe traumatic brain injury, Heard helped treat wounded soldiers and coordinate a medical evacuation before losing consciousness, according to the release.

Heard, who received a Purple Heart, also lives with PTSD, chronic migraines, hearing loss, and chronic pain. His new home will provide him and his family with a mortgage-free place to put down roots.

The two homes continue a significant milestone for PulteGroup’s Built to Honor program. Since its launch in 2013, PulteGroup has built and donated more than 100 mortgage-free homes valued at over $40 million to veterans and their families.

Building Homes for Heroes is also celebrating its 20th anniversary and expects to reach its milestone 500th home in December.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5627. Construction Site Next to Deadly Brooklyn Building Collapse Had History of Safety Issues

As authorities continue to search through the rubble of a deadly building collapse in Flatbush, Brooklyn, that killed eight, troubling details have emerged about safety concerns at a neighboring construction site.

On Wednesday afternoon, the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. collapsed, taking the shared wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave. with it, leaving the bedrooms and closets of residents in that building exposed.

The deadly tragedy occurred next to an active construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., where an existing structure had been demolished and excavation was underway to build a new residential building.

In a press conference at the scene of the tragedy, Mayor Zohran Mamdani vowed a full investigation into what preceded and caused the collapse, including whether the construction work underway at 2625 Bedford Ave. played any role.

"If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them accountable," the mayor said.

The construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. was purchased for $3.99 million by a pair of LLCs registered to Judith Swimer and Faigy Fischman in June 2024, just days after the duo purchased another property at 600 Utica Ave. in East Flatbush for $5 million, according to public records.

Public records show they initially planned to develop a three-story apartment building on the lot, but the project had been plagued with stops and starts over amendments to the building plan and safety concerns from city inspectors.

In March of this year, the Department of Buildings halted the demolition of a one-story building on the site after an inspector reported that demolition contractor N Tech Design of America had failed to take proper safety precautions, including installing netting and putting up sidewalk shields, records show.

A month later, inspectors returned to the site and found that the demolition had gone ahead anyway, in defiance of the stop-work order, according to city records. A $10,000 fine was issued.

In May, a city inspector issued additional citations and another stop-work order against the contractors for allegedly failing to ensure adequate protections of neighboring buildings and for deviating from approved construction plans. Within a week, the city lifted that stop-work order.

According to signs posted on the site, the construction and development management firm Promont is overseeing the project. Realtor.com has reached out to Promont for comment.

The alleged deviation from filed plans may have been related to a new permitting request submitted by Robert Fischman of WG Facility X LLC, amending the proposed project to a nine-story structure on the site with a ground-floor grocery store. That amended permit request has not yet been approved.

Fischman has a troubled history. In 1999, Fischman was charged in a real estate kickback scheme involving his company, M.S. Berkoff Co. Earlier this year, Berkoff Supply sent tenants of 1321 Flatbush Ave. a letter alerting them to the excavation work.

In March of this year, as a part of its survey of the property in advance of submitting the request for the revised nine-story build, Promont commissioned a pre-construction report from structural and geotechnical monitoring company Quiver Monitoring.

The report focused on the buildings surrounding 2625 Bedford Ave. and assessed the masonry on the north facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. as being in poor condition, "with a wide range of deficiencies noted" according to the report.

Jessie Kramer is a licensed professional engineer in Colorado. She has deep experience in forensic engineering, including uncovering the causes of building collapses.

Kramer tells Realtor.com® that an older brick building adjacent to an active excavation site immediately raises red flags.

“Tons of thoughts pop up when I see something like that,” she says. "My day-to-day is looking at collapsed buildings, looking at failed buildings, and saying, 'Why did this happen? How widespread is the damage?' And often, the answer involves multiple issues."

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani announced that the city would sweep 100 other properties associated with five entities tied to the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. The mayor and the city’s Department of Buildings commissioner declined to name those entities.

Isolag Realty Corp. purchased 1321 Flatbush Ave. in 2024, and Olufemi Falade signed the deed. The property consisted of four residential units and a ground-floor commercial space. A three-bedroom unit in the building rented for $3,550.

The 96-year-old building had 98 recorded violations dating to 1972, according to the city's Department of Housing, Preservation, and Development. Eleven of those violations were from this past year, including a violation for "unsafe electrical wiring" and a notice to "provide an adequate supply of water for the wet sprinkler and/or standpipe."

Falade has a tumultuous history of building ownership. In 2006, he spent 12 days in jail for failing to repair issues in numerous properties he owned. “In just 12 buildings he owns, there are more than 1,800 violations of the city’s housing and maintenance codes,” Housing Preservation and Development Commissioner Shaun Donovan told the New York Post at the time.

"I can't speak to what potential deficiencies might have been there before this happened," Kramer says. "But I can say on a building of this age, our modern codes differ a ton from what were the standards back then. So it's imperative to keep up with maintenance in these old buildings. And that's an active process. Owners have to be super on top of it.

“People obviously are wanting answers immediately, and that’s not going to happen,” Kramer adds. “This is going to be a yearslong investigation process to decide who’s at fault and what happened.”

Andrea Cavallier contributed to this report.

#5626. How Agents Can Chart a Course for No Buyer Remorse

The bidding war is over. Some of the decisions made are harder to undo. As an agent or broker, is it part of your professional obligation to discuss where the buyer might be in five years financially and family-wise? Probably, even if it might occasionally put them off a purchase.

A recent survey of 1,000 U.S. property owners found that 80% had at least one regret about their home, location or buying experience. Location bothered 45%, while 58% reported regrets about the home or homeownership itself.

For homeowners who bought during the pandemic frenzy, moving on can carry an added complication: the mortgage may be more attractive than the house.

A recent study in the Journal of Banking & Finance found that for every percentage-point increase between a homeowner’s fixed mortgage rate and current market rates, the probability of selling falls 18.1%. Researchers estimate mortgage lock-in was associated with 1.72 million fewer home sales between Q2 2022 and Q2 2024.

That pressure is particularly relevant now. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.28% in early October, its highest level in nearly three years.

For Nick Nastos, a real estate broker and founder of Chicago’s Property Shop, that creates an unusual form of buyer’s remorse.

“You can regret the house and still have a mortgage you’d hate to give up,” he says. “That’s what makes these decisions difficult. Someone may know the home no longer fits their life, but replacing a 3% mortgage with today’s rate can completely change the math.”

Nastos gives five reasons a pandemic purchase may feel different now.

Nastos says regret alone should not determine whether someone sells.

“Start with what you would change about the house, then price out what changing homes would actually cost,” he says. “Sometimes the answer is to move. Sometimes that low mortgage makes improving the home you already own the better option.”

Suzy Minken, a real estate advisor with Compass working out of Northern Virginia, said looking toward the future while purchasing a house today is key to avoiding buyer remorse.

“It’s not something that is talked about enough,” she says. “I’ve even had buyers speak to my architect (relationships are key) while touring the house to see if they could do an addition. The architect did a review of the property and said it could be done. The buyers submitted an offer (multiple bid situation) and bought the house. They proceeded with a two-story addition before they moved into the house.”

Minken stresses that there is a need to distinguish between buyer’s remorse and the frustration of having fewer options than originally anticipated.

“Consider the young family who purchased a starter home with the intention of moving to a larger home in five years,” she explains. “Perhaps they’ve welcomed another child and need an additional bedroom. But with higher home prices and mortgage rates, the move-up home they envisioned may no longer be financially practical.

“In many ways, today’s move-up buyer has become today’s renovation buyer. Rather than moving to a larger home, homeowners are looking for ways to make their existing homes accommodate their changing needs.”

But what happens when renovation isn’t an option either?

“When buyers fall in love with a home, I encourage them to think about whether it’s already ‘maxed out’ or has room to grow with their changing needs,” says Minken. “Is there room to expand? Could an unfinished basement become additional living space? Is there flexibility in the floor plan to accommodate a growing family?

“I also encourage buyers to look beyond the house itself. Why are the current owners selling? Did they outgrow the home after having another child? Is there something about the layout or the property that made adapting it difficult? These questions can reveal important clues about how a home might serve its next owners.”

Minken encourages buyers to think beyond what they need today and consider how their needs might change over time. That includes family circumstances, the need for additional space and even commuting considerations if their employer requires them to spend more time in the office.

“We can’t predict changes in interest rates, home prices or family circumstances,” she says. “But we can ask the right questions before they make one of the largest financial decisions of their lives. Sometimes the regret isn’t buying the wrong home. It’s discovering that the next step, whether moving to a bigger house or renovating, is no longer within reach.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5624. Housing Starts Pull Back, but Top Markets Hold Their Ground

Zonda’s third quarter 2026 data shows housing starts over the past four quarters declined 10% from the same period a year ago. More specifically, 22 of the top 25 housing production markets posted year-over-year declines, pointing to a broad-based slowdown. However, the national slowdown can translate into very different competitive conditions depending on geography.

Sarasota was the clear outlier, with starts rising 20% year over year to 9,691 during the four quarters through Q3 2026. Chicago also managed growth, increasing 1% year over year to 7,680 starts, while Boise was effectively flat at 7,303.

At the other end of the spectrum, Las Vegas and Provo posted the largest declines among the top 25 markets, with starts falling 22% year over year in each. Riverside/San Bernardino followed closely with a 21% decline. Washington, D.C., Nashville, Raleigh, and Jacksonville were also among the markets recording double-digit contractions.

Despite declining activity, Dallas and Houston continue to operate on a different scale from the rest of the country.

Dallas ranked first with 37,497 starts over the past four quarters, down 10% year over year. Houston followed with 34,996, down 8% year over year. The two metros operate in a league of their own, each producing more than twice as many starts as any individual market elsewhere in the top 25.

Phoenix and San Antonio were the only other markets to top 15,000 starts, at 16,770 and 15,531, respectively. The rankings also point to relative stability at the top. Every market in the top 10 retained its position from the previous quarter, even as housing production softened nationally.

For industry professionals planning for 2027, the numbers reinforce the importance of looking beyond national trends. The size and direction of the housing adjustment vary substantially by market. Production is still highly concentrated in the Sun Belt metros, but growth in markets like Sarasota and Chicago shows that opportunities remain even against a weaker national backdrop.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5622. Horizon3 launches Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab built on NodeZero attack data

Autonomous penetration testing company Horizon3 AI Inc. today launched its new Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab.

The lab will draw on data from NodeZero, Horizon3’s penetration testing service, which is used by more than 7,000 organizations including banks, federal agencies and hospitals.

Purdue University’s Z. Berkay Celik has been named the lab’s inaugural director. Celik is an associate professor of computer science at Purdue and co-director of the Purdue Security Laboratory. Much of his work deals with finding software vulnerabilities and building defenses for autonomous systems, and he has run joint projects with industry and government.

According to Horizon3, NodeZero tests now produce about 30 billion tokens of anonymized data a day. Gathered on customers’ live production networks, the data also shows how their defensive tools reacted to each NodeZero command.

Snehal Antani, Horizon3’s co-founder and chief executive and a former chief technology officer of Splunk Inc., said the company has “spent years collecting” the data. Putting it to use in research like this is the next step, he said.

The lab’s first projects include research on coordinated groups of AI agents used in attacks. Deception is another, building on a Horizon3 paper titled “Honeyquest for LLMs.” Also on the list, according to Horizon3, are “interruption and rollback mechanisms” for autonomous security agents.

Horizon3 published a paper on keeping such agents under control in May. Using Anthropic PBC’s Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Haiku 4.5 models, it tested a design that limited the AI to a fixed list of approved tools, and Horizon3 said the system never proposed an action outside that list across more than 420 deployments.

Trained separately for each customer, Horizon3’s cyber world models give its red and blue agents a shared memory, and the lab is expected to speed up their development. Horizon3’s Cyber Resilience Centers of Excellence, which focus on critical infrastructure, will also report to the lab.

Horizon3 said in October that it had passed $100 million in annual recurring revenue, with growth of 120% year over year. NodeZero has run more than 350,000 production-safe tests to date. Horizon3 said about 80% of its customers have moved from annual to monthly penetration testing.

Founded in 2019, Horizon3 raised $250 million in August at a valuation of more than $2 billion.

#5621. Former CFO Sues NAR for Withholding Retirement Payments

The National Association of Realtors® (NAR) may spend the holidays in court, as the association is being accused of failing to pay a former employee promised retirement based on the financial strain of previous legal issues.

John Pierpoint—NAR’s former and long-time chief financial officer, who was succeeded by Matthew Cendella in 2025—filed a lawsuit against NAR in the Circuit Court of Cook County in Chicago on Wednesday, Nov. 11. He claims that NAR has refused to pay him a retirement benefit that the association regularly provides to retiring senior executives.

According to a release from Pierpoint’s attorneys, NAR “improperly withheld one year of salary in retirement compensation despite having recorded the anticipated payment in its own financial records for more than a decade.”

The release also points out that NAR has maintained the executive retirement compensation practice for approximately two decades, and pays retiring senior executives a year’s worth of their base salary.

In 2024, Pierpoint received over $872,000 for his role as CFO, according to NAR’s 2024 990 form.

While the Burnett settlement burdened NAR with a $418 million payment, Pierpoint’s attorneys claim that retirement compensation is held in reserve, specifically set aside for those payments.

“Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” David Fish, an attorney representing Pierpoint, stated. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives. We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees.”

NAR had not yet commented on the lawsuit at press time.

This is a developing story. Stay tuned to RISMedia for updates.

#5620. Joanna Gaines Reveals How Her Approach to Holiday Decorating Has Evolved as She’s Gotten Older

Joanna Gaines keeps a beautifully decorated home year-round, so it’s no surprise that she pulls out all the stops for the holidays.

The “Fixer Upper” star recently shared her best holiday hosting tips as she prepares to celebrate the season with her family. She also noted the surprising way her approach has changed over time.

“The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” Gaines, 48, told USA Today. “I do think this is the one time of year where you can really go big if you want to—or keep things timeless and simple.”

While the Magnolia co-founder encouraged aspiring decorators to feel empowered to go big with their festive displays, she left room for those who prefer to take a more subdued route.

“There’s no right or wrong because the holidays really are so personal and sentimental,” she said. “It’s just a matter of what you love and how you want your home to feel for your family.”

Gaines also noted that she’s committed to upholding food traditions, using recipes she’s been working on since she and Chip Gaines wed in 2003.

“Food is really at the center of our holidays,” she said. “Thanksgiving especially is this day I feel like I can taste all year long because our family really does make the same dishes year after year.”

Gaines also detailed her approach to Christmas in the editor’s note she published in the Nov. 10 issue of Magnolia Journal.

“Every season holds a blend of the big and small, the milestones and the everyday, the photo-worth celebrations and the not-so-picture-perfect moments,” she wrote. “There’s something about the holidays that bridges the gap between these.”

She noted that as the years go by, she’s “come to realize” that the most important memories are the ones that might not be captured with a camera, and exist only in memory.

“Maybe there’s no physical evidence they happened at all, except for the fact that you were there—and you felt it,” Gaines continued. “It’s these softer moments that give us life and ground us in presence. The days that held no agenda, the mornings I took slow, the smiles you won’t see in my camera roll because I was simply bearing witness.”

Explaining that she’s choosing to prioritize holding space for both the major moments and the much more relatable ones, Gaines also reflected on being the “gatekeeper” of her family’s yearly traditions as she aims to “do the same things” they always have, “if not bigger and better” this year.

She wrote about the “dressing up” that is encouraged toward the end of the year and romanticized the “fresh delight” of decorating the home, hosting loved ones, and “trying to create standout experiences” that her “kids will remember and tell their kids about someday.”

The Gaineses certainly have their hands full with their five children: Drake, 21, Ella, 20, Duke, 18, Emmie, 16, and Crew, 8. But during a recent conversation on the “Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce” podcast, the proud mom revealed that they’d recently been discussing the idea of expanding the family once again.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

“He is telling everyone I’m pregnant. And just for the record, I’m not,” Gaines quipped, adding that her husband had even told their “grown kids” that she was expecting, and their eldest daughter said that she’s “not coming home” if the news is true.

The HGTV personality went on to encourage Kelce, a mom of four, to add another little one to her family.

“Five is a good number,” Gaines said, noting that she would “have more babies” if she “could.”

#5619. Qvyon launches with $8M to improve safety for physical AI deployments

Physical AI validation infrastructure and software development company Qvyon Technologies Inc. launched today with $8 million in total funding to help companies validate autonomous vehicles and robots before deployment.

MaC Venture Capital led the funding, with participation from BDC Capital, BKR Capital and Spotlight VP.

Physical AI is artificial intelligence that moves from digital brains to the real world, allowing smart machines to perceive, reason about and act within physical environments. This can include factory floors, retail shopping aisles, the kitchen or the roadway.

Before companies can deploy smart machines, such as robots or self-driving cars, into the real world, they must understand how these systems will operate under both normal and abnormal conditions. Reproducing strange, unlikely and dangerous conditions in the field is difficult and risky. For example, a car might suddenly pull in front of a truck during a rainstorm or a sensor array on a robot might become blocked or damaged while working on a production line.

To address these examples, Qvyon released Mimic Core, a platform that takes real-world sensor recordings into simulated environments to produce varied test scenarios, allowing developers and engineers to access data and test physical AI models and robotics setups in virtual environments without repeatedly collecting field data.

A single recording can allow an engineer to create many test variations to tease out where systems make mistakes. This allows development teams to catch problems before putting robots to work in the real world.

“We spent years building AI for vehicles and saw how hard it was to prove those systems were ready for the road,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Frantz Saintellemy. “Companies need to test what happens in their own vehicles and factories by using their own recordings.”

Qvyon’s system ingests camera, lidar and radar data. It uses this to reconstruct environments in 3D and time-sequence snapshots, capturing scenes and how they change over time. It uses this to generate challenging conditions to test AI models against the hardware they will drive in simulation. The platform produces traceable datasets and validation evidence that engineers can use to evaluate smart machines’ performance before deployment.

Mimic Core works alongside the same virtual testing tools that companies already use and helps them better understand the scenarios and conditions robots and smart machines will face.

The company offers the product as software-as-a-service and as a self-hosted solution for companies that want to keep everything in-house. Qvyon stressed that when using its cloud product, customer data is kept separate and is never used to train AI models for other customers.

Mimic Core is available today via Qvyon Cloud with a 14-day guided evaluation, or for companies to run on their own systems.

The company said the funding will support Mimic Core and its rollout through the United States, Europe and Japan. Qvyon is also developing Mimic Validation OS, planned for the first half of 2027, to help companies measure and document test results, and Mimic Learn, planned for late 2027, to help improve AI using information from machines already in operation.

#5618. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

#5617. DC Gym Shooter Kills His Building Manager After HOA Dispute Over Mold Issues

A Washington, DC, doctor who had been locked in a legal battle with his homeowners association over mold problems fatally shot the manager of his condominium during a shooting spree on Thursday, police said.

The fatal shooting incident was reported around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood in Northwest DC, about a mile from the White House, drawing dozens of heavily armed police officers to the area.

Matt Wade Lambert, 55, a physician living in a penthouse apartment at the Metropole Condos building on 15th Street Northwest, was identified by the authorities as the shooter who killed one and injured four others before taking his own life.

Lambert was suspected of going down to the luxury VIDA Fitness center housed inside the building, locating the building manager, identified las 46-year-old James Stuart, next to the treadmills and shooting him with a handgun from a point-blank range, DC Councilmember Brooke Pinto told reporters, according to WUSA9.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," gymgoer James Spellman told The Associated Press. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Dozens of people were in the middle of their morning workout in the gym at the time of the deadly attack, which triggered an evacuation and an order to shelter in place in the area.

While law enforcement officials have not revealed an official motive for the shooting, Pinto said that the building manager was "targeted" by the suspect.

During a press conference Thursday evening, Interim DC Police Chief Jeff Carroll said that Lambert then ran out of the gym, went up to his seventh-floor patio and opened fire from a rifle, striking two men and two women who were downstairs. Earlier reports said three of them were construction workers.

One of the victims was hospitalized in critical condition and three others sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Lambert eventually barricaded himself inside his condo at Metropole Circle and was on the phone with police negotiators when he ended his own life with a shotgun blast.

When officers breached the door, they found all three firearms used during the shootings, along with containers of flammable liquid.

DC Mayor Muriel Bowser described the incident as a "senseless act of gun violence."

Court records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that Lambert had been in a long-standing feud with his condo’s management and filed a lawsuit in March 2025. In it he claimed that he had not been able to live in his seventh-floor penthouse since Nov. 11, 2024, because of mold, moisture, foul odor, and related damage.

Lambert argued in the 12-page complaint that the problems in his unit were caused by repairs to the building’s facade that had been performed by a contractor, for which he paid over $15,000 as part of a special assessment.

According to the filing, Lambert had incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the HOA's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation."

A mediation in the case had been scheduled for March 2027.

Attorney Joel Braithewaite, who represented Lambert in the case, told NBC News that he spoke with him just yesterday or the day before and said that the 55-year-old was "in a good place" and about to start a new job on Monday.

#5614. Square takes Squaremates AI agent out of beta and opens up to sellers’ own AI software

Block Inc.-owned commerce platform Square today made its Squaremates artificial intelligence business agent generally available to sellers in the U.S., after the agent entered open beta in April under the name Managerbot.

For sellers who would rather stay in the AI software they already use, Square is also offering a new command-line tool and an updated Model Context Protocol server.

Running a business is “an endless string of judgment calls that are all on the owner,” said Willem Avé, global head of intelligence at Square. “We built Squaremates to help share that load,” he said.

Each seller’s agent now runs in its own secure workspace with access to cloud compute. Square said that gives it room for longer jobs. A seller could ask it to find customers who’ve lapsed over a given stretch of sales, for instance, and have it draft a discount to win them back.

A beta feature lets Squaremates build restocking orders directly on a supplier’s website, and the seller places them from there. Email access for its daily briefing is coming soon.

Fraser Thompson, who leads strategy and operations at Los Angeles-based Burgers Never Say Die LLC, put Squaremates to work on the restaurant’s house-made cheese sauce. “I dip my fries in it, I dunk my burger in it,” he said. “So I’m thinking, how are we not selling more of this stuff?”

Digging into attachment rates and customer segments showed that “our OGs, the regulars who’ve been with us since day one, love it.” The restaurant started promoting it on social media with what Thompson called “silly posts,” and he said that a few months later “we’d 12x’d our cheese sauce.”

“A lot of sellers already have an AI tool they like working in,” Avé said. The updated server, Square MCP, lets a third-party assistant answer questions about the business and make changes once the account is connected. Square CLI is aimed at sellers and developers who want to script or build on top of their accounts, and it gives their own tools and agents access to Square’s application programming interfaces.

Squaremates Apps are custom applications a seller writes with an AI coding tool and the CLI, which Square then hosts with a live connection to the seller’s business. Splitting cash tips by hours worked is one of the uses Square suggests.

Donnie McClanahan, who has four cafes around Knoxville, Tennessee, built a labor board app with the CLI and an AI coding agent. It pulls schedules and timecards from every location onto one screen. A lot of his mornings used to go to “playing catch-up just figuring out who’s where,” he said.

Sellers can try the tools at the Squaremates Tour, a run of in-person events Square kicked off recently. Apart from the features still in beta or coming soon, everything announced today is available to U.S. sellers at no additional cost. Squaremates itself is not yet available to sellers on Square’s Multi-Account Suite.

#5613. Inside Jensen Huang’s $53 Million Property Portfolio as the Nvidia CEO Resigns After Affair with Suspected Chinese Spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned after having extramarital affairs with a business executive—Alice Huang, who the U.S. government has determined to be working with Chinese intelligence—and a Nvidia employee.

Finance chief Colette Kress will work as the interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent replacement, Nvidia said Thursday.

External and internal candidates will be considered as the company searches for a Jensen's successor.

“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world," the statement read. "The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

The news follows a Nov. 8 statement from Huang, who admitted to the affairs.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang stated in a previous message to the company. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

While the board of Nvidia claimed it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” an external counsel will be selected to investigate

The revelation, first reported by the New York Times, is expected to have an economic impact not only on Nvidia—whose stock price has already taken a hit—but on the artificial intelligence industry as a whole, given the chipmaker’s influence.

The company was the first in the world to reach a valuation of $5 trillion after seeing unprecedented growth amid the artificial intelligence bom.

According to the New York Times, Nvidia is responsible for making "the most essential and expensive component in almost every A.I. scheme," a collection of hardware designed specifically to bolster artificial intelligence.

Its ascent to the pinnacle of tech success began as something of a slow burn in 1993, when Huang, 63, launched the company alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

At the time, Nvidia was viewed very much as a niche—and fledgling—tech startup. However, it has since grown into an industry giant, inking deals with all manner of brands and agencies, from the U.S. Department of Energy to Nokia, Samsung, and Sam Altman's company, OpenAI, the parent to ChatGPT.

Huang's own net worth has skyrocketed with that accelerated growth. He is currently one of the 10 richest men in the world with an estimated fortune of $174 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The number of men who can claim to top him in personal fortune can be counted on two hands—and include the likes of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Larry Ellison.

Like others in the exclusive "super billionaires" club—men and women with net worths exceeding $50 billion—Huang has invested his fortune across diverse ventures and companies, while managing to remain in this elite group.

However, he has also followed in the footsteps of his fellow tech titans by pouring a sizable chunk of his fortune into real estate—amassing an incredibly impressive portfolio of homes from Hawaii to California.

Huang, who was born in Taiwan in 1963, spent his early childhood in Thailand. He moved to the U.S. after his father visited America and vowed to bring his sons, he previously told CNBC.

Ahead of his move, his mom would teach him 10 words from the dictionary each day to help him learn English, despite not knowing the language herself.

At age 9, Huang and his brother headed to America to live with their relatives. His early life in the States was starkly different from the current lavish life he lives.

When he was a child, his aunt and uncle accidentally enrolled him in a Baptist boarding school in Kentucky, thinking it was a prestigious prep school.

While there, he became a target for bullies and teasing due to his long hair and accent.

As the future of Nvidia's stock remains unclear, Realtor.com® has lifted the lid on the tech tycoon's expansive property portfolio.

In 2017, the tech tycoon splashed over $38 million for a sprawling mansion in San Francisco's Gold Coast neighborhood.

Property records seen by Realtor.com reveal that the dwelling is tied to Riva LLC, which is managed by Michael A. Chojnacki, a tax lawyer who looks after the finances of Huang and his wife, Lori.

The luxe abode in the Pacific Heights neighborhood spans 11,400 square feet and boasts a curved roof, panoramic views of the Golden Gate Bridge, and many bedrooms and bathrooms.

The limestone mansion has a large terrace, a three-car garage, two wine rooms, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a theater, and a gym.

Developer Bill Campbell, of Marble Management, previously told the Wall Street Journal that construction on the dwelling took nearly four years.

Of course, Huang is also neighbors with Ellison and David Sachs.

Huang previously owned two starter homes in San Jose, CA. The first one, which measured 1,500 square feet and had three bedrooms, was sold for $185,000 in 1988—just five years before he founded Nvidia.

Elsewhere in California, the tech mogul owns a lavish dwelling in Los Altos, just 15 miles west of Nvidia's headquarters, which is in Santa Clara County.

He purchased the property in 2003 for $6.9 million. It measures over 7,000 square feet and has six bedrooms.

The elegant two-story estate features lush landscaping and a resort-style pool.

To top off his property portfolio, the businessman also snapped up a home on the south side of Maui in 2004.

The dwelling is situated in the Wailea Resort, which houses 14 other properties behind a gate and spans 10.5 acres on the ocean.

The home features seven bedrooms and was built in 2008. He paid $7.8 million for the abode.

The property spans 8,000 square feet and is surrounded by lush greenery.

In 2023, Maui experienced deadly wildfires, and the Huangs "donated significantly to local relief efforts,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.
