#5597. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns following affairs scandal

Nvidia Corp.’s board of directors today announced the resignation of Jensen Huang, now former chief executive and president of the artificial intelligence chipmaker, amid a scandal, naming Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO.

The news arrives following numerous industry reports that the board intended to replace Huang as CEO after revelations of a second extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia, coming mere days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

News initially broke over the weekend that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. and an alleged Chinese spy. The Information reported on Tuesday that Alice Huang facilitated $7.5 billion in chip sales to China. According to another report, Jensen Huang also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who serves as vice president of healthcare.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities concluded Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset. Upon revelations of the affair, the Associated Press reported that President Trump announced that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the allegations, while adding, “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Late Wednesday, the Nvidia board met to decide whether to oust Huang and discussed a potential replacement as CEO. Huang has no obvious single successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. Reportedly, the board sought counsel from an outside firm to find someone to fill the role.

With the announcement, Nvidia stock was falling more than 5% in trading today, backing off an even steeper loss at the opening. Yahoo Finance calculated that Nvidia has lost more than $600 billion in market value since the previous Thursday, likely with more shocks to come.

“Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Kress. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead.”

Kress has served as executive vice president and CFO since joining in September 2013. Her accolades include leading the company’s finance organization and working to build the company’s dominance in the AI chip industry. Before joining Nvidia, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco Systems Inc. and Microsoft Corp.

The CFO was intimately involved with Nvidia’s widespread financing of AI compute providers, in particular its backing of not only AI leaders OpenAI Group PBC and Anthropic PBC — the latter set to go public as early as next week — but also neoclouds such as CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV. Those financings have been criticized by some as “circular,” meaning Nvidia essentially invested in customers so they could use the money to buy more of its graphics processing units.

The potential successors to Huang, who had 30 direct reports, include no one obvious choice and a succession plan apparently was not in place. Candidates that some have speculated about include Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas, who worked at Nvidia years ago, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, and Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing and creator of its CUDA software considered the real moat for its business.

“The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang is about more than succession at the world’s most important AI chipmaker,” Forrester Vice President and Group Research Director Stephanie Balaouras told SiliconANGLE in an email. “Nvidia’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom. If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience. If its stock, financing relationships or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger.””

Balaouras added that “tech leaders shouldn’t overreact, but they should treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers and investment plans.”

Huang is best known for co-founding Nvidia in 1993 in a San Jose Denny’s and has served as its CEO since. His departure will likely send further ripples through the AI silicon and software industry. He has been deeply involved in Nvidia’s product strategy and built longstanding customer relationships, helming the company as it became the behemoth it is today.

Nvidia commands roughly 80% of the data-center AI chip market, although industry estimates vary by methodology. Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. puts its share of AI computing power shipped at 63% in the second quarter of 2026. Other market carve-outs include custom chips built by cloud companies within the broader supply, including Google LLC’s tensor processing units at 25%, Amazon Inc.’s custom silicon at 5% and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s AI hardware accelerators at 4%.

Nvidia is expected to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings on Nov. 17.

#5596. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5595. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5594. Khloé Kardashian Says Lamar Odom Is ‘Dead’ to Her After His Comments About Marrying for Family’s ‘Lifestyle’—Inside Their Former Marital Mansion

Khloé Kardashian is drawing a line through her relationship with her ex-husband, Lamar Odom.

On the Nov. 11 episode of “The Kardashians,” Kardashian got candid about what the former NBA star  said regarding their marriage in the Netflix documentary "Untold: The Death and Life of Lamar Odom."

“I did watch the Lamar documentary. I’m not too thrilled about it,” she said.

The mom of two, who was involved in the making of the documentary, previously expressed her “regret” in doing so on the April 15 episode of her podcast, “Khloé in Wonder Land.”

“I’m watching the documentary, and I’m like, 'Wait, I took time out of my life to sit here and do a favor for you,'” she continued on the family’s reality show. “I’m not being paid. I’m doing this ‘cause I’m trying to be nice.”

Kardashian found “many things” Odom said in the documentary to be “really distasteful.”

“You’re saying that you weren’t really in love with me, you married me just so you could be more popular in pop culture, all these things, which is so weird,” she explained. “Even if that is your truth, why don’t you say it without me being on the other side of these interviews? I just thought that was really, really lame.”

In the documentary, Odom said he found the Kardashian family’s “lifestyle” to be enticing. The couple married in 2009 just 30 days after meeting.

According to comments Odom’s friend Anthony “Pumpkin” Booker made in the documentary, on the day of the former couple’s wedding, the basketball player said he was “doing it to try to better his future” because the family had “mad connections.”

The Good American co-founder didn’t hold back when speaking about where she stands with Odom today.

“The bridge is burned, and there’s no more rope left to throw over. So he is dead to me,” she said. “This just solidifies what liars, con artists, cheats, thieves, trolls that men are. I just don’t want to be involved. Play with yourself, don’t play with me.”

Odom and Kardashian filed for divorce in 2013, citing “irreconcilable differences.” It was not finalized until 2016, as Odom had a near-fatal overdose in October 2015, prompting Kardashian to put the legal process on pause.

“He OD’d during the divorce, and I was his next of kin, even though it was still, the divorce was still—it was on the judge’s desk,” she said during a 2019 podcast appearance. “It was like, two years, or like a year or two of us trying to get the divorce going, and then this happened.”

She explained that the pause was “not for any romantic reasons.” It was so she could continue to “help take care of him and make sure that he would be OK again.”

After the split, it was reported that Kardashian kept the couple’s marital mansion, which was located in an upscale guard-gated community called Mulholland Estates in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Tarzana.

The former couple purchased the home for $3.95 million in December 2009, about two months after their wedding day.

The six-bedroom, 8.5-bathroom, Mediterranean mansion was heavily featured on both “Keeping Up With the Kardashians” and their spinoff, “Khloé and Lamar.”

All six of the en suite bathrooms were embellished with designer wallpaper, tumbled stone, mosaic accents, and custom closets. The primary suite also had a spalike bathroom and boasted expansive views of the city.

The 8,400-square-foot estate was equipped with all of the amenities you’d expect from a home of an NBA pro and a Kardashian: a home gym, a library, an office, and a theater room, among other luxuries.

Outside, a resort-like pool included stunning water features and was accompanied by fire pits and a spa.

The home was sold for $5.49 million in January 2014, with “The Big Bang Theory” star Kaley Cuoco snapping it up for nearly $1.5 million over the asking price.

Mulholland Estates wasn’t the only place Odom and Kardashian called home during their marriage. After Odom was traded to the Dallas Mavericks in 2012, they rented a posh condo at W Dallas Victory Hotel and Residences.

The $7,500-a-month dwelling had two bedrooms and two bathrooms and featured slate flooring, a wet bar, and bathrooms tiled with mother of pearl.

The building had amenities that included two fitness centers, a spa, an entertainment room, and a zero-edge infinity pool.

Following her separation from Odom, Kardashian purchased a $7.2 million Calabasas home in June 2014. The 9,214-square-foot estate was the former home of Justin Bieber.

Today, Kardashian lives in a stunning $17 million custom-built abode in Hidden Hills, CA, with the two children she shares with ex-boyfriend Tristan Thompson. The property is located right next door to her mother, Kris Jenner.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5593. Computer vision startup Tristar AI pulls in $12.4M to automate quality control for manufacturers

All too often, manufacturing defects seem to slip past human eyes, with the result that high-speed production lines turn into expensive scrapheaps. Computer vision startup Tristar AI Inc. has just raised $12.4 million in early-stage funding in order to try to put an end to these costly mistakes.

Today’s Series A round was led by Isogon Ventures and saw participation from Blackhorn Ventures, Ford Street Ventures, NextView Ventures, TenOneTen and Capgemini’s ISAI Cap Venture Fund.

Tristar AI is gearing up to transform quality assurance in manufacturing at a critical moment for the industry. Manufacturers have found themselves squeezed by a combination of rising raw material costs and growing labor shortages, and these problems have been made even more acute by the U.S. government’s insistence on bringing more manufacturing back home.

According to data from the Capgemini Research Institute, 48% of U.S. companies have invested in reshoring projects this year. But 83% say they’re worried about the lack of skilled industrial workers needed to fulfill those initiatives.

One of the major challenges for manufacturers is that they’re still encumbered by inefficient inspection protocols that rely on either manual checks, or in a best-case scenario, rigid, rule-based machine vision systems. Quality control is essential for any manufacturing operation, but the inefficiency of these protocols makes it a significant roadblock too.

It forces companies to take skilled workers off production lines and sometimes even bring their entire operations screeching to a halt. Yet there are many occasions where they still miss subtle flaws in their products, resulting in wasted materials, downtime, missed deadlines and sometimes even very expensive customer claims.

Founder and Chief Executive Salem Karani is all too familiar with the inefficiency of manual inspection. He told SiliconANGLE that while growing up, he would often accompany his father to his family’s plastic film manufacturing plant in Houston, turning up at all hours of the day and night in order to troubleshoot production issues that could spring up at any moment. Because the company’s margins were so tight, any period of extended downtime could threaten its profitability, so he would spend hours with his dad frantically troubleshooting line errors.

It was this experience that ultimately inspired Karani, who studied computer vision at Harvard and MIT, to develop an automated quality inspection system that can operate continuously without slowing down production. “The problem was never that people didn’t care about quality,” Karani said. “It’s that people catch problems after the fact, once they’ve already cost time, materials and customers. Tristar gives every production line a live record so teams can act when it matters most.”

Computer vision in manufacturing operations is not a new concept, but where Tristar differs is through its use of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models that can adapt to changing conditions, materials and defect types. The startup’s platform looks at machine telemetry, the quality of the products coming off the line and the activity of human operators, allowing it to uncover issues the moment they emerge and immediately understand where the problem is, and why it occurred.

Best of all, the system can integrate with factories’ existing systems, such as cameras, sensors, programmable logic controllers, enterprise resource planning systems and so on That enables them to get up and running without an expensive overhaul.

Isagon Ventures General Partner Paco Riberas said he’s backing Tristar because manufacturers are losing far too much money to avoidable defects. “In today’s industry, precision isn’t optional, and Tristar makes it possible,” he said. “Its AI vision catches defects in real time, directly on existing production lines. Salem and his team are building the quality standard for modern manufacturing.”

Tristar’s early traction has been encouraging. Its system already monitors more than 500 production lines across North America and Europe.

Customers include global packaging giants such as Amcor, DuPont and Klöckner Pentaplast, and also some of the biggest suppliers to automakers such as Toyota, Honda and Mercedes, Karani said. Those customers report defect detection accuracy rates of between 95% and 99%, and say the platform pays for itself in an average of just four months.

Karani said the goal now is to expand Tristar’s platform into new manufacturing sectors and enhance the capabilities of its computer vision AI to try and improve its accuracy even further. Ultimately, he sees the company as the operational system of record for factory floors, giving manufacturers more visibility into everything about their production operations, from the raw materials to the finished product.

“Physical AI will play a critical role in the future of manufacturing,” said Capgemini Ventures’ Matthieu Eyriès. “Tristar combines advanced AI capabilities with a strong understanding of industrial environments, addressing concrete manufacturing challenges with measurable impact.”

#5592. Realty Executives Associates Appoints New Executive Vice President of Agent Development

Realty Executives Associates (REA) has announced the appointment of J Lewis as executive vice president of Agent Development, a newly established leadership role focused on strengthening the success, productivity and long-term relationships of REA’s agents.

According to a release, prior to joining REA, Lewis served as CEO of Keller Williams for 13 years, bringing extensive experience in brokerage leadership, agent development and organizational growth.

In this new role, the company says Lewis will focus on helping existing agents increase productivity and profitability, strengthening agent relationships and retention and creating meaningful opportunities for professional development and business growth. He will work to provide agents with the resources, guidance and support they need to build sustainable businesses.

“One of the things I enjoy most is sitting down with an agent or a team, understanding what they’re trying to accomplish, and helping them figure out how to get there. That might mean looking at their production data, analyzing their financials, identifying opportunities they’re not seeing, or simply fine-tuning the way they run their business,” he says. “Every agent has different goals, and I enjoy helping them develop a plan to reach those goals and build a business that supports the life they want.”

“I’m incredibly excited to join the number one brokerage in East Tennessee,” Lewis added. “What really attracted me to REA is the opportunity to work with a company that understands the value of investing in its people. I’ve always enjoyed working alongside agents, understanding what they want to accomplish, and helping them find ways to get there. REA has created an environment where that kind of work is valued, and I’m excited to be part of it.”

“At REA, we believe our agents are our customers. Our responsibility is to create an environment where they can build successful, sustainable businesses and feel supported along the way. This position is an extension of that commitment,” said Justin Bailey, CEO and partner of Realty Executives Associates.

Bailey added: “Success isn’t simply measured by how many agents we have. It’s measured by the success of the agents who choose to call REA home. We want to be intentional about helping them become more productive, more profitable, and better positioned for the future. We have always believed that taking care of our people is what makes a great brokerage, and this is another way we are putting that belief into action.”

#5591. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5590. XRP Price Prediction: Brad Garlinghouse Faces $1.05 Test as Whales Buy $72M

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP whales accumulated $72 million over four days, but its price remains dangerously close to critical support. Meanwhile, spot XRP ETFs recorded $10.4 million in net outflows, their largest single-day withdrawal since March.

XRP is hovering around $1.05, a level that could determine its next major move. With selling pressure mounting, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse faces another test of confidence in the token.

Garlinghouse has spent years positioning Ripple as a major player in institutional payments. Its ambitions extend across cross-border transfers, financial infrastructure, and institutional adoption.

However, XRP holders still need those developments to translate into stronger token demand. Ripple’s business expansion and XRP’s market performance are two different things. That gap has widened as investors reconsider their exposure to established crypto. Institutional partnerships can strengthen Ripple’s business without automatically triggering additional XRP purchases.

The latest whale accumulation offers some encouragement. Large holders adding $72 million worth of XRP suggests certain investors see value near current levels. But ETF withdrawals tell a different story. The $10.4 million outflow shows institutional demand remains inconsistent, even as whales accumulate.

Bitcoin’s investment narrative is gradually expanding beyond digital gold. Developers are increasingly exploring ways to bring faster transactions, decentralized finance, and additional applications into its ecosystem.

That shift could create opportunities for infrastructure projects targeting Bitcoin’s limitations. Bitcoin Layer 2 networks aim to make the underlying ecosystem more useful without replacing Bitcoin itself.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project pursuing this direction. Its approach combines Bitcoin-focused infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine execution, targeting faster transactions and broader application development.

The project has raised $33.2 million at its current presale stage. Its current token price stands at a low $0.0136, with staking rewards reaching 35% APY. But its presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, putting a deadline on the current entry opportunity.

XRP represents an established payments-focused crypto, while Bitcoin Hyper targets an emerging infrastructure opportunity.

For investors seeking exposure to earlier-stage projects, the potential appeal lies in entering before an ecosystem reaches maturity. Established cryptocurrencies offer greater market recognition, but emerging infrastructure projects can attract attention through their expansion potential.

Bitcoin Hyper’s pitch centers on making Bitcoin more functional. That proposition could appeal to investors who believe Bitcoin’s next growth chapter will involve more than simply holding BTC.

The immediate XRP price outlook remains heavily dependent on the $1.05 support level. Losing this floor could expose XRP to another wave of selling. The next downside target sits around $0.99. A move below psychological support could further weaken confidence among short-term traders.

However, XRP’s Relative Strength Index has fallen to approximately 24. That places the indicator deep inside oversold territory, suggesting selling pressure has become unusually intense.

Oversold conditions can create opportunities for a relief rally, particularly when large holders continue accumulating. But buyers still need to demonstrate enough strength to reclaim lost resistance levels.

A recovery toward $1.30 would provide an initial bullish target. Stronger momentum could subsequently bring the $1.50 area back into focus.

For now, the XRP price faces two competing forces. Whale accumulation and oversold conditions offer reasons for optimism, while ETF outflows and fragile support keep downside risks alive. Defending $1.05 could give bulls another opportunity to rebuild momentum. Losing it would put $0.99 firmly on the radar.

#5589. With $23M in funding, Luminal is the latest startup to put Nvidia’s CUDA moat in its crosshairs

Luminal AI Inc. has outlined a plan to tear down Nvidia Corp.’s formidable software moat in the artificial intelligence chip industry after raising $23 million in early-stage funding.

Today’s Series A round was led by Standard Capital and saw participation from existing investors such as Y Combinator, SagaVC, Liquid 2 and Felicis, bringing Luminal’s total amount raised to date to more than $28 million. It comes about a year after the startup raised $5.3 million in seed funding.

Everybody knows about Nvidia these days. The chipmaker has ridden the generative AI wave to a staggering $5 trillion market valuation, surpassing rivals such as Apple Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. to become the most valuable publicly traded company in the world. But anyone who assumes that it’s solely Nvidia’s graphics processing units that set it apart would be mistaken, for the real reason for its dominance of the AI computing industry is not just silicon, but software.

For almost two decades, Nvidia’s proprietary Compute Unified Device Architecture or CUDA software framework has been the real differentiator, serving as a virtually impenetrable barrier that prevents rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Google LLC and Amazon Web Services Inc. from stripping away its market lead. Though those rivals have developed some very powerful GPUs and custom application-specific integrated circuits for running AI workloads at lower costs than Nvidia’s hardware, they haven’t been able to match the scale of Nvidia’s software ecosystem.

Virtually every major AI framework, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, has been built natively on Nvidia’s CUDA software, enabling developers to run their AI models on Nvidia’s GPUs without any modifications. But to run their models on alternative chips, developers need to rewrite much of the underlying code, which is challenging and time-consuming work. That’s why the vast majority of AI workloads still run on Nvidia’s chips.

Many developers don’t want to be paying the exorbitant fees needed to rent Nvidia’s GPUs or purchase them outright, but they also don’t want to spend months at a time fine-tuning their codebases to get their AI models to run optimally on alternative hardware, and it’s this challenge that Luminal intends to solve for them.

The startup’s solution is a two-pronged architecture platform that consists of its proprietary search compiler and a fully managed inference cloud that combine to eliminate the hassles of bringing AI workloads onto different chips.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Joe Fioti told SiliconANGLE that the compiler works by systematically exploring different ways of running neural networks on the target chip in order to come up with the most optimal path. It benchmarks each variation until it finds the best possible solution, and then it automatically generates the code developers need.

Once the code is ready, it caches the implementation so it can be reused across recurring inference workloads. In this way, it allows developers to run their AI applications across heterogeneous chip architectures with minimal fuss, Fioti said.

“We started out building in the open on GitHub as AI adoption took off, and quickly saw how much demand there was for a more efficient way to run AI models across different hardware,” Fioti said of the company’s origins.

Luminal’s compiler and inference cloud are designed primarily for running high-throughput, continuous-uptime AI applications that demand massively scalable inference. Think applications such as AI coding tools, automated image generation engines, AI video generators and real-time voice agents.

“The cost of running AI shouldn’t limit who gets to build it,” Fioti said. “We’re building the infrastructure to make high-performance inference more accessible, giving developers more choice beyond Nvidia’s ecosystem without forcing them to compromise on speed or cost.”

Luminal launched its compiler and public cloud-based inference infrastructure just four months ago and adoption is growing rapidly. It’s already processing more than 45 trillion tokens per month – a number that’s roughly equivalent to 10% of the total tokens consumed so far by Together AI Inc., an $8 billion-valued infrastructure unicorn that has been serving the market for more than four years already. The startup has established a strong partnership with AWS, and runs a significant amount of its workloads on that company’s Tranium processors.

Going forward, Luminal’s plans include expanding its engineering team, scaling its go-to-market operations and optimizing its compiler and inference infrastructure to support more chip hardware and AI models.

Standard Capital’s Dalton Caldwell said he’s betting on Luminal because AI inference is the fastest-growing market in the world. “We backed it because of its deep technical expertise and its demonstrated proof that it can squeeze fantastic performance out of heterogeneous hardware,” he said. “Luminal’s ability to get the most out of GPUs that have already been purchased … is incredibly high leverage.”

Though Luminal has had a promising start, it’s certainly not the only company trying to break Nvidia’s CUDA stranglehold on the AI industry. Both Google and AWS have their own things going on, notably launching alternative AI frameworks to PyTorch that make it easier for developers to create AI models and applications that can run on their native processors.

Luminal also faces competition from startups such as Spectral Compute Ltd., which offers a programming toolkit and compiler that enables CUDA-based code to run natively on any AI-accelerated chip. There are also open-source efforts such as the UXL Foundation’s OneAPI, which converts CUDA code into software that can easily run on any silicon.

#5587. Fed Governor Outlines Inflation Progress as ‘Disappointing,’ Sees Path to 2% Goal in the Next Year

Inflation seemed to be making good progress at the end of 2025 and start of 2026, with the Federal Reserve actually starting to cut interest rates. The start of the conflict in the Middle East in February, however, threw a wrench in that progress, as inflation turned course and began to elevate once again.

Now, after the Fed chose to raise rates at its September meeting, inflation has reached a “disappointing” state, as outlined by Federal Reserve Governor and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman.

In a speech to the Council on Foreign Relations focusing on the current economic outlook, Bowman said that the Fed’s “progress on lowering inflation has disappointed,” but bringing down inflation does remain a “priority” for the organization.

As inflation has elevated, housing has felt the strain. Mortgage rates have been on the rise, recently returning to the 7% range. Affordability has been constrained for buyers, not just due to rate, but also due to inflation affecting their purchasing power and ability to save up for down payments.

Bowman said she remains vigilant on “monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices” and their influence on risks to lowering inflation, and she continues to “focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.”

“While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated,” she continued. “It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions.”

Bowman said what is currently holding back progress on inflation is a “confluence of shocks,” stemming from Middle Eastern conflict, tariffs imposed from the Trump Administration and “AI-related price pressures.”

“It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations,” she said. “But today’s consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer.”

Bowman, appointed by President Donald Trump in his first term and elevated to vice chair in 2025, said the U.S.’s conflict in the Middle East continues to exert downward pressure on the economy, but pressure is also sourcing from the AI boom and “buildout,” as she characterized it.

As for how these two issues could affect inflation in the future, Bowman said that she can see “sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist.”

However, she also said she could “envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly,” in which case core PCE inflation (meaning price increases excluding volatile energy fluctuations) would return toward the Fed’s 2% target in a “timelier” fashion.

In terms of the Middle East, Bowman said that as the conflict persists, energy prices could remain elevated, keeping inflation on the rise “because of increased pass-through to consumer prices of higher production and transportation costs.” Additionally, if conflict were to escalate, she said it could have “more meaningful effects on real activity because of higher uncertainty and the larger impact of energy prices on lower- and middle-income consumers.”

On the potential of a “quick resolution” to the conflict, Bowman noted that it “may take some time for energy prices to normalize” even in the aftermath.

As for AI, Bowman said she “expect(s) the AI shock to play out over some time” as plans for new data centers continue to “surge.” However, she noted that as AI investment is “increasingly being financed with external funds,” there are other potential risks it presents to the economy.

One such risk is the potential of workers being displaced. Bowman said that even though any monetary policy can’t “address that transition directly,” it can still “support a dynamic labor market that facilitates the necessary retraining and mobility of workers across jobs.”

Another risk is the financing of AI, as Bowman said that “AI revenues have been rising quickly but are not yet sufficient to pay for the expense of maintaining existing and developing new AI models and data centers.” As such, she also noted that “AI-related debt has been rising rapidly, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit, and project finance, and is on track to exceed $800 billion this year.”

The rapid expansion of AI has also put some “upward pressure on a number of price categories,” as Bowman noted, specifically to the prices of memory chips, semiconductors, computers and more. However, she said that she expects “production capacity to catch up to demand gradually over time.”

Bowman did point out that the risks from AI “seem to be concentrated in only a few large firms that provide AI services.”

Overall, Bowman said that if “AI-related revenues fall short of sharply rising costs, especially as public sentiment and local opposition could lead to increased regulation and delays, we could see a sharp correction in equity prices for AI firms, higher financing costs, and reduced access to credit.”

“This shock would likely slow the AI buildout and soften both economic activity and inflation,” she concluded.

Bowman said that looking ahead, her expectation is that “policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence.” Such policies include “pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses.”

Bowman went on to say that she does expect the labor market, which has performed resiliently through most of 2026, to “remain stable.” She also expects for inflation to “slow” as “special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year.”

“Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices,” she continued.

Bowman said as these “shocks” to the economy and inflation fall back, her forecast is for “core PCE inflation to move closer to 2% next year.”

Right now, she said that the pressures persist, indicating that “there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5586. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5585. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5584. Vanta launches AI Governance, Risk Quantification and a Vanta Agent for entire jobs

Compliance automation company Vanta Inc. today launched AI Governance by Vanta, a product on its Agentic Trust Platform said to give security teams a single view of every artificial intelligence system in a company.

Also making their debut at VantaCon 2026 in San Francisco this week are Risk Quantification, Autonomous Vendor Assessments and a new version of the Vanta Agent that the company claims can take on entire jobs.

Vanta is pitching the new products at security teams that are under pressure to move faster on AI. According to job-title data compiled by Vanta, the number of AI security engineers and architects has tripled so far this year compared with all of 2025.

AI governance roles, which did not appear in the company’s figures before 2024, have grown tenfold in two years. A complete inventory of the AI tools in use is still out of reach for many security teams, Vanta said.

Chief Product Officer Jeremy Epling, who is due to demonstrate the products at a keynote later today, said security teams are usually being held accountable for AI with the same headcount they had before it arrived.

“Plenty of tools can list the AI running in your company,” Epling said. Vanta also checks whether that AI is doing what a customer approved, he added, with the Vanta Agent taking on the follow-up work once someone signs off.

Point products for AI security often detect threats without the business context to judge how much they matter, according to Vanta. The company claims to be the only vendor tying an AI agent’s live security telemetry directly to an organization’s compliance controls.

On the risk side, Vanta’s unified risk view, which draws on live signals from across a customer’s compliance program, now includes Autonomous Vendor Assessments. According to the company, Risk Quantification, also added to the view, is meant to show leaders the financial impact of their most critical risks.

Entire jobs can now be handed to the latest version of the Vanta Agent. Once it has learned how a customer runs its program, the agent is said to bring staff in when a decision calls for human judgment. Users can also reach it natively inside Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Slack.

Vanta also named Fredrick “Flee” Lee its new chief information security officer. Lee joins on Nov. 16 from Reddit Inc., where he led security before, during and after the company’s initial public offering. Gusto Inc., where he ran security before Reddit, was a Vanta customer at the time. At Vanta, he is expected to act as what the company calls “customer zero” in pushing the product road map.

The company has been valued at $4.15 billion since July 2025, when it raised $150 million in a Series D round led by Wellington Management Co. LLP.
