#5583. Historic New England City Reclaims Top Spot as America’s Hottest Market

A Connecticut metro known for its insurance headquarters and the Pratt & Whitney aerospace company has reclaimed its title as America's hottest housing market.

The Hartford, CT, metro area has shot back to the No. 1 spot in October for the first time since a summer run at the top from May through July 2026, according to the Realtor.com® October Hottest Markets report. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, claiming the crown eight times.

The Nutmeg State accounts for four of the top 20 markets, with Waterbury, New Haven, and Norwich joining Hartford with median list prices between $400,000 and $460,000, says the report.

The No. 1 market encompasses the cities of Hartford, West Hartford, and East Hartford, but also a large swath of quintessential historical towns that look like they stepped out of a Hallmark movie.

Those small towns—including Wethersfield, Windsor Locks, Avon, and Farmington—draw homebuyers with their small-town charm, stunning nature, and commutable locations.

They also offer relative affordability compared to the elite suburbs dotting the Long Island Sound, such as Greenwich, Westport, and Darien, which are closer to New York City.

But Hartford, the state's capital, is still close enough that it embraces some spillover from the more expensive areas. If residents need to commute to New York City only a couple of times a week, the approximately 2.5-hour drive or Amtrak ride may be worth it for the nature, safety, quiet, and relative affordability these small towns offer.

"Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country," says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

And home browsers are most definitely interested.

The Hartford metro had 4.1 times the viewers per property as the rest of the country, by far the highest. Median days on the market are a swift 37 (only one more than last year and a month faster than the national time) and the median list price is $440,000, the second-highest among the top 10, behind only Manchester-Nashua, NH, at $549,000.

Homes in the most wanted markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on the market of 37 days, more than three weeks faster.

The hottest markets for October 2026 are Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (4.1 times the national average); Kenosha, WI (2.8); Lancaster, PA (2.4); Rochester, NY (2.5); Manchester-Nashua, NH (2.8); Peoria, IL (2.4); Erie, PA (2.8); Rockford, IL (2.6); and Waterbury-Shelton, CT (2.8).

Incorporated in 1693, Glastonbury (named after the town in England) boasts the country's oldest continuously running ferry, to Rocky Hill across the Connecticut River. It also has the second-highest concentration of surviving pre-1800s Colonial homes, about 154.

An easy 15-minute commute to Hartford via Route 2, and abutting both West Hartford and East Hartford, Glastonbury has long been a home base for the higher-ups in both the nearby insurance industry and Pratt & Whitney ("Pratt rats," in local lingo).

The past few decades have seen major changes for the formerly rural town as sprawling, multimillion-dollar estates began flecking the hills that were only farmland and tobacco fields not long ago.

Glastonbury has managed to retain much of its historical and rural appeal even as the town gained both a Whole Foods and a Trader Joe's, and its median home price skyrocketed, currently standing at $530,300, a 6.2% increase over last year.

Wendy Anderson of William Pitt Sotheby's International Realty, who represents the town's most expensive listing, a $7.2 million French chateau-style estate in South Glastonbury, says the town continues to draw high earners not only from Hartford, but from New York City and New Haven as well.

"It's always been a strong market, a sought-after town," she tells Realtor.com. "It's an easy commute."

Beyond the commute, the town—which is fairly large for a "small town" at about 52 square miles, with three ZIP codes—seems to have it all.

Beyond its bustling commercial center—complete with shops, restaurants, coffee spots, and an urgent care clinic—the area still boasts working farms, orchards, two active wineries, a sandy-shored pond, and a riverfront park.

All public schools have a rating of 8 or higher out of 10 by Great Schools, drawing families.

The housing stock is diverse: In addition to the aforementioned Colonial homes, there are small ranches, grand estates, classic midcentury homes, newer townhomes, and upscale rentals. There are even senior and lower-income communities.

"A lot of towns in Hartford County have a lot of amenities and activities," says Anderson, who has lived in Glastonbury for 45 years. "And a great sense of community. There's town football, soccer, tennis. So many activities for children, and concerts. And it's easy to get to the shoreline, or to get to Boston or New York."

Anderson doesn't think the market will go up indefinitely.

"I think the market has peaked, the wave has crested," she says. "But the market is still holding strong."

Since listing the $7.2 million French chateau on nearly 2 acres in July, she has already shown the estate to a dozen potential buyers—and just closed on a $1.4 million home that was sold in less than a week.

Buyers, usually business owners, are lured to the town by its spectacular fall colors, its rolling hills and dense forests, its fruit orchards, its gourmet restaurants and cosy taverns—as well as its relative affordability.

Adds the agent: "I just saw a TikTok video that said, 'This town, Glastonbury—it's like Greenwich, but half the price!'"

West of the river, a mere 10 miles away from Glastonbury, is West Hartford. An undercurrent of rivalry has long existed between West Hartford and Glastonbury, with both attracting Hartford's top earners from the healthcare, insurance, and education industries.

Although less than half the size of Glastonbury, West Hartford offers many of the same charms with its mix of idyllic small-town life and modern convenience.

Both towns are considered very walkable compared to the average Connecticut suburb, have highly rated public school systems, and have beautifully maintained their share of pre-1800s historic homes.

West Hartford, however, tends to be more expensive at its high end, standing at a median of $712,000 for its 06107 ZIP code, a slight dip from last year.

Robert Levine of ERA Real Estate, who lives and sells in West Hartford and the surrounding areas, says the two upscale suburbs have a few key differences.

Glastonbury has larger plot sizes, with homes often sitting on an acre or more of land, and has room to grow. West Hartford, a more suburban enclave with no real room left to build, has a denser, more bustling center of town.

"We're a destination. People come from 15 miles away to have dinner in our center," Levine says.

As for the metro being the hottest one in the country, the agent says he isn't surprised—he still sees multiple offers on turnkey homes that check all the boxes: good location, backyard, basement, two-car garage, etc.

But he declares that the area is in a "transitional market," with some homes sitting for several months.

"Homeowners are scratching their heads, like, 'Wait, my home won't sell in a weekend?'" he says.

"We're transitioning to what I call an 'equilibrium' market," he adds. "It's not necessarily favorable to either buyers or sellers. It's all about the property."

As for why central Connecticut keeps luring buyers, the agent notes the scenery, the small-town vibes combined with modern ease, and the tight-knit communities.

Kiri Blakeley writes about trending news at Realtor.com. She has also worked at Forbes Magazine, Forbes.com, CafeMom, and DailyMail.com, covering everything from billionaires to celebrities to crime. Her work can be found in news outlets worldwide, including Yahoo, SF Gate, New York Post, Seattle-Post Intelligencer, Marie Claire, She Knows, Huffington Post, and New York Magazine. She has an M.A. in journalism from Columbia University. In her spare time, she writes psychological thrillers under a pen name. She lives in Brooklyn, and her cat foster Instagram account has over 4 million views.

#5582. Agile Robots raises $500M funding led by SoftBank at $8.5B valuation

German artificial intelligence robotics startup Agile Robots SE announced today that it has raised $500 million in new late-stage funding at an $8.5 billion valuation.

Japanese multinational investment holding company SoftBank led the Series F funding round. Other participants included AI chip leader Nvidia Corp., Japanese group Hitachi Ltd. and T Capital. The financing brings the total capital invested to $2 billion.

Founded in 2018 as a spinoff from the German Aerospace Center, Agile is one of Europe’s leaders in humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and dexterous robotic hands, along with the AI models needed to control them. The company combines robotic hardware with sensing, computer vision and AI software to automate physical work.

At the center of its hardware and software is force-sensitive manipulation. It allows robots to control how much force they use to handle delicate parts, perform precision assembly, and adapt to changing situations.

“Physical AI will fundamentally change how the world builds, moves and makes things,” said founder and Chief Executive Dr. Zhaopeng Chen. “Our vision is intelligent robots working alongside people in factories and warehouses everywhere, and Agile Robots is determined to lead that shift.”

Agile’s established flagship arm Diana 7 allows for precise manipulation and assembly; it includes torque sensors in all seven axes of movement that can detect and respond to the amount of force required to grab, lift and manipulate objects.

Agile One, the company’s humanoid robot, was publicly unveiled in November 2025 as an industrial-first platform. The launch extended the company’s approach into human-shaped platforms intended to carry out tasks across a production floor. It includes dexterous hands, advanced perception and human collaborative capabilities, allowing it to operate readily alongside personnel in manufacturing and logistics settings.

The company now offers an entire family of Agile One human-shaped robots, including the Agile One S, a compact humanoid reference platform built for research labs, universities, and developers. The company also offers Agile One SN, equipped with Dual Wuji five-finger hands and preconfigured for Nvidia Corp.’s Isaac GR00T AI models that act as robot “brains,” designed to let industry developers rapidly train, evaluate, deploy and test new robotic skills.

“We bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production, across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing,” added Chen.

The funding will support expansion into the United States, hiring more engineers and accelerating development of intelligent robotics applications. Additionally, the company said it intends to expand production, including in Germany, where it opened a facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, in early 2026 to meet rising demand. Agile said the site can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.

Agile has deployed around 20,000 industrial robotic solutions for customers across the automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. It boasts a growing portfolio of subsidiaries, including BÄR Automation, Franka Robotics, Idealworks and Krause Automation. Franka supplies manipulation technology, Idealworks develops mobile robots and coordination software, whereas BÄR and Krause build and integrate interaction capabilities.

In robotics, Agile faces stiff international competition from established automation suppliers such as Universal Robots A/S, ABB Ltd., FANUC Corp. and Yaskawa Electric Corp. Its Agile One humanoid faces rivals that include Figure AI Inc., Apptronik Inc. and Agility Robotics Inc.

#5581. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5580. Zillow Rental Market Report: Demand for Single-Family Rentals Surges

Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month.

“For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise.

Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.

In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down.

Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals.

Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%.

Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%).

For more information, visit www.zillow.com.

Paige graduated from Central Connecticut State University with a B.A. in Journalism and Public Relations.

#5579. A New Wave of Opportunity Zones Is Coming in 2027—and Home Values Are Already Surging in Key States

The United States has thousands of new Opportunity Zones, a designation that could bring rising values to many emerging housing markets.

The Treasury Department last week announced 6,576 new Opportunity Zones (OZ), which will maintain that status for the next decade. All 50 states and the District of Columbia have zones in the mix, and 2,594 of them are in rural areas. OZs benefit from enhanced economic incentives, and they're targeted at communities with the potential to grow.

“By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

This is the second round of OZs since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act established the program in 2017. The private sector has invested $110 billion in developing the first crop, Treasury said. The original OZs remain active through 2028, and the new ones begin in 2027. Some OZs were renewed.

States submitted nominations from about 25,300 census tracts eligible for the program, and leaders cheered their wins. There are about 25% fewer tracts than last time.

"Whether it's bringing new life to a downtown, creating great-paying jobs, or building housing for more families, these Opportunity Zones will help attract investments that can make a real difference in the lives of Ohioans," Gov. Mike DeWine said of Ohio's 260 new OZs.

“Virginia is ready to harness the potential of Opportunity Zones,” Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said of the state's 153 new OZs. “I worked closely with local leaders across Virginia to make sure we supported the priorities that mattered most to local communities."

Property data group ATTOM analyzed 3,805 OZ census tracts from the last tranche and found median single-family home and condo prices rose in 48.1% them. Compare that to home prices outside of OZs, which rose 51.6%.

Some OZs see their home values rise much more quickly. ATTOM found that about 9.4% of the OZ census tracts saw their highest median home value since the Great Recession in the third quarter of 2026. About 27.1% of them saw double-digit growth in home values year over year.

“Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80% of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so, home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.”

As far as states with a lot of OZ price growth, Maine came in first, with 64% of its OZs seeing median home prices rise. South Carolina (61.3%), Wisconsin (58.3%), Virginia (53%), and Oregon (52.3%) rounded out the top five.

ATTOM noted that many of the census tracts recorded a low number of sales, so the data can be volatile. Still, 79.5% of them had home prices below the national median. Outside of them, just 50.4% of tracts had prices below the national median.

Michael Tillman, CEO of OZ developer PTM Partners, tells Realtor.com® the program also gives developers time to experiment. His company builds workforce housing in Florida using cold-formed steel and vertical integration.

"These are not build-and-flip products; we want to be there as their family grows," Tillman said of the units. "That's stickier than high-end luxury. There's got to be more institutional capital with that long-term focus."

OZs tend to have higher poverty rates, lower median family income, and more housing cost burdens than a typical area. Some are in urban areas, and others are in rural ones.

Brookings Institute analyzed the OZ program and found half of the zones saw "accelerated growth." But it said the designation alone doesn't create success. Local market conditions and state and local regulations play a role. And, while they do often mean new investment, that can vary depending on the development already there.

"Investment alone is not synonymous with shared prosperity," Brookings said in the report. "In some places, OZ capital has expanded housing supply, supported business formation, created jobs, and leveraged underutilized community assets—while in others, it flowed toward projects with limited community benefits or into neighborhoods already on a growth path."

Brookings also noted the first round of OZs came when the country already saw increased building. What this means in the current, challenged market has yet to be seen. States should develop a strategy for how to develop each zone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5578. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5577. IBM Quantum and the race to make scientific advantage useful to industry

SPECIAL BREAKING ANALYSIS by Dave Vellante

QDC26 shows progress in the hardware, software and tooling around quantum computing as customers look for evidence of better outcomes.

IBM Corp.’s Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week marked a change in emphasis. IBM claims that researchers have demonstrated quantum advantage in 2026 by working with the classical computing community. Its public presentations showed progress in processors, error correction, scientific software and the integration of quantum with conventional computing.

The company’s quantum leader, Jay Gambetta (pictured), also set a new target. The next big milestone comes by demonstrating industry impact by 2028, conditional on collaboration across enterprise application researchers and the classical and quantum communities.

Our key takeaway is that IBM is assembling more of the full system required to turn a quantum experiment into useful scientific work. Hardware is important, but the real innovation will come from software. Importantly, the tools that help a scientist formulate a problem, run it across different computing resources, check the result and understand the economics are where much of the innovation is headed. These capabilities address several of the barriers customers described to us in our spring quantum tour of major scientific research labs; and the issues discussed with technologists on our Quantum 101 Series at theCUBE’s NYSE studio.

Despite the progress being made, the remaining gaps and challenges are many. Quantum science is advancing but impact on industries is still years away. Better software is the key to making dramatic improvements in quantum performance and a new service capability can attract researchers. But if a chemist needs to understand the deep nuances of quantum computing, it limits adoption. We believe the next phase of innovation will focus on abstracting quantum complexities and making measurable improvements in simplicity to drive further usage.

In this Special Breaking Analysis, we examine IBM’s public QDC proclamations through the prism of our spring interviews with six quantum and supercomputing experts. We add customer perspectives from our partner Qualitate, assess the implications of IBM’s foundry investments and consider what evidence would signal that progress is moving from scientific advantage to industry impact.

IBM’s progress comes into better focus when evaluating its milestones separately. IBM’s goal of demonstrating Quantum Advantage by 2026 is generally accepted as met, based on achieving particular computation superiority relative to today’s classical methods. But to truly show industry impact, IBM needs to show results make a difference to an organization. Milestones around fault-tolerant architectures will increasingly focus on the ability to sustain reliable computation in the face of errors. Progress in one category will definitely support another but it’s useful to look at milestones and proof points separately as shown below.

IBM deserves high marks for achieving that advantage but is subject to scrutiny. Gambetta’s keynote described classical researchers overtaking quantum results, claims being withdrawn as classical makes improvements, and subsequent quantum work moving the needle in favor of quantum again. This of course is how a competitive scientific ecosystem should operate. We’re eager to see the leapfrogging end and await a day where a quantum advantage becomes sustainable with clear evidence that classical computing has no chance of catching up for specified use cases.

Observers can rightly be concerned that incorrect inferences may be drawn from the term “advantage.” The phrase can sound like a statement of superiority. But if that advantage is not consistently held, then the broader industry might remain skeptical. The same applies to verifying that a customer outcome is attributable an underlying scientific model powered by quantum.

A public Allstate example is useful and illustrates the difference. IBM described underwriting-optimization results as comparable to classical optimization schemes. That can represent progress, but it does not show that quantum has delivered a superior underwriting outcome. Customers need to decide how much they are prepared to invest in learning before a measurable benefit appears. IBM, in our view, is working hard to simplify the heavy lift and broaden adoption.

The researchers we interviewed in spring 2026 for World Quantum Day were already thinking beyond the hardware. Their concerns included application selection, reliability, integration, software complexity and the ability to preserve optionality as hardware evolves. These were six independent editorial interviews conducted on theCUBE, made possible by Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., across five institutions, offering a view of the work required to make quantum useful. The discussions were hosted by this author and Paul Gillin, managing editor at SiliconANGLE.

The following table highlights the to priority stated by each researcher at the time and our take on how IBM has responded in the past 6-9 months.

IBM is directing effort toward problems that these practitioners identified months earlier. We believe that is a strong indicator of product relevance, an even more important than hardware milestones.

It also gives us a more reasonable test of true progress. A scientist must be able to attack a meaningful problem with less setup effort, run it more reliably and compare the result with a credible classical alternative. IBM’s public announcements show capabilities intended to support that progression and the gaps identified this spring by our researcher friends. Thus far, however, they don’t show how broadly researchers can complete their tasks without specialist assistance. IBM shared additional capabilities to a small group of industry analysts under NDA, which look encouraging.

Some of the most interesting material in Chicago concerned ordinary operational friction. In the public developer sessions, IBM described experiments interrupted by sleeping laptops, dead notebook sessions, running out of memory or tokens, and lost work in process. In quantum research, as with AI YOLO training runs, they add expense and blockers to work that already requires specialized expertise.

Managed workflows address this through simplification by moving execution into a hosted environment with conventional computing resources and tools to capture and save work in process. Researchers can associate quantum jobs with the workflow and monitor consumption across both quantum and classical support infrastructure. That creates a basis for repeating experiments and understanding where resources are consumed and how to optimize the complete process.

Take the chemistry approaches discussed at the event. Researchers can divide a larger molecular problem into smaller parts, use quantum or classical computing methods for appropriate parts and combine the results. At QDC26, IBM described improvements in classical algorithms that support the processing of quantum jobs. Classical solving steps can become a major bottlenecks and represent opportunities for optimization.

The relevant focus is increasingly the complete research workflow. Here we’re referring to the preparation, the quantum work, the classical processing and the validation. This expands the opportunity for IBM and its partners because more of the work can be supported through its software and services. It also shines a light on how the economic case needs to evolve, with a focus on the cost of an outcome.

Faster quantum hardware alone is not the answer. Conversely, better classical software can make quantum experiments much more productive. Both are developments that came into focus at QDC26. Customers need enough visibility to identify the bottlenecks and implement improvements.

IBM’s pronouncements about AI are expected to address barriers raised in our spring interviews – the complexity of translating domain knowledge into a working quantum experiment. IBM must provide skills that assist with choosing methods, workflows, applying classical algorithms and the like. And validating implementations before longer, more expensive runs take place. Our developer conversations at the event underscore demand for AI assistance with calls for simpler packaging and managed services.

We believe this marks is an important near-term relationship between AI and quantum. AI can help scientists use quantum computing more effectively before quantum delivers a broadly demonstrated improvement in AI itself. The immediate opportunity is to simplify – reducing the effort required to apply specialized software and infrastructure.

This requirement has implications for how scientific software is packaged. A library contains reusable code. Increasingly, skills will supply context and guidelines for selecting and applying that code. As skills improve, we expect more of the integration work to be assisted by software. The value of a mature library will still depend on its performance and suitability for the task at hand. The public QDC releases include libraries, mapping tools and AI skills together; they hint toward an evolution in how software will be used in the future.

Another gap is accountability. For example, what happens if a workflow executes but uses invalid scientific assumptions. An AI-generated configuration can appear valid while making a poor trade-off between accuracy and cost, for example. In our view, a useful abstraction must maintain the ability to understand those AI decisions and validate them in terms that a domain expert/scientist comprehends.

This is where customer evidence must become more specific in our view. For example, can a chemist repeat useful work without a vendor team guiding them every step? Can another scientist reproduce the result? Can the organization see what exactly changed between runs? We would place considerable weight on those conditions when judging whether easier programming translates into broader scientific adoption.

Chemistry and materials are fields that provide a strong connection between our spring interviews and the public QDC discussions. Johansson at CSC emphasized the challenge of modeling interacting electrons. Beck at Oak Ridge described materials and chemistry research with potential relevance to fusion and biology. IBM’s sessions discussed tools for decomposing problems and processing results across quantum and conventional systems working in tandem.

We view these fields as particularly credible places to look for early useful applications because the scientific problems involve quantum behavior. That is a reason to prioritize research that benefits from quantum. Problem scope, accuracy and economics (or feasibility) relative to conventional methods will determine the ultimate usefulness of quantum.

IBM’s performance progress is notable, but its points of comparison are instructive. Its headline 25-fold improvement in maximum circuit throughput compares Nighthawk r2 with Heron. Several application improvements also compare newer IBM quantum systems with earlier ones. Those figures demonstrate progress within IBM’s generations but a customer still needs a comparison with the best practical classical approach to the same problem.

The mot useful metric in our view is the cost and time required to obtain a validated outcome. The calculation should include all aspects of conventional preprocessing and post-processing, the quantum work done, job completion times and the intensity of the technical skills required perform and validate the result. Importantly, an important future measure is whether the process can be consistently repeated at scale.

Customers should absolutely invest before quantum consistently wins. The key is to identify those investments as a learning experience.

Post-quantum cryptography or PQC is a topic we unpacked at theCUBE’s Quantum Readiness Day this past September. Qualitate customer survey findings add another dimension to our PQC analysis. But don’t confuse PQC spend with quantum application adoption.

A query of Qualitate’s interview data on quantum adoption focuses heavily on PQC, a tactical topic that is top of mind for enterprises today. Organizations are spending to prepare existing information systems to resist future quantum-enabled attacks. The data include customers already taking action, as well as those evaluating.

“Now is the time we’re really starting to go all in on post quantum cryptography.”

The same participant, a technology lead at a professional services company, explains the rationale in terms of future loss avoidance:

“We anticipate that this will significantly save us on dealing with enormous crises in the future.”

Today’s enterprise focus as it relates to quantum is on modernizing cryptography. This is far ahead of investing to find useful applications for a quantum computer. Today’s practitioners are consumed with deploying and securing agents and making AI trustworthy. Quantum applications, other than PQC, are not top-of-mind for most enterprise customers. Security work to protect conventional systems is tactical and there’s little evidence of interest in running workloads on quantum hardware within organizations today.

NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024 and encourages organizations to begin transitioning. Its guidance also explains the risk that adversaries collect encrypted information today for possible decryption later. Unlike Y2K, which had a definitive date associated wth the risk, the timing of a capable quantum attack remains uncertain. As such, migration planning is sensible now, independent of IBM’s application and hardware milestones.

The following competitive signals are seen in the Qualitate data and are almost exclusively security-related:

The opportunity for specialists also remains open. One participant states:

“The field is still not crystallized. And probably we will not necessarily rely on the hyperscalers. Probably will rely on specialists.” – Global head of analytics, financial services and insurance, large U.S. corporation (Source: Qualitate)

Our take is that technical credibility and existing relationships, combined with the ability to affect a successful migration, may all influence these purchases. IBM has many assets, but customers are still evaluating alternatives. Success in quantum-safe security strengthens its commercial position without, by itself, resolving which quantum computing architecture or application platform will prevail when quantum goes mainstream.

Quantum computing also needs to progress from building exceptional devices to producing dependable systems repeatedly. The manufacturing announcements around IBM’s roadmap deserve scrutiny in that context.

In September, IBM acquired, Anderon, finalizing a $1 billion CHIPS award supported by an additional $1 billion IBM investment. IBM has reported it has an Albany, New York-based, 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry serving customers across the ecosystem, with initial wafers already running through the facility.

Our view is that the learning curve will be as important as any single milestone. More repeatable production can confer experience advantages to IBM (Wright’s Law), much in the same way Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has demonstrated its leadership in semiconductor manufacturing. Serving multiple customers could help support volume across shared infrastructure. Whether those benefits emerge depends on demand, process stability, yields and the ability to protect each customer’s intellectual property. In addition, IBM can learn from Intel’s missteps and its own foundry challenges.

The industry needs to watch for manufacturing progress alongside qubit performance. Capital investments are followed by innovation. IBM’s August acquisition of HRL Laboratories adds a related strategic chess move. The rationale explained by IBM is to acquire expertise in silicon-spin qubits, sensing, materials, cryogenics, controls, packaging and interconnects. IBM describes that expertise as complementary to its superconducting work and identifies opportunities to collaborate with Anderon.

We interpret the acquisition as a way for IBM to control its destiny in a return to its vertically integrated mainframe past. At the same time, it doesn’t have the volume economics to achieve its objectives purely as a captive/integrated systems player. So it must open up its manufacturing capability to other parties, including its competitors.

Taken together, the public announcements at QDC26 suggest a broader platform ambition. IBM is connecting access to quantum hardware and software with classical computing, application functions, development tools and the like. We believe this could increase its role in the customer’s research process and create more opportunities for ecosystem partners to package specialized capabilities.

The competitive advantage will come from making useful work easier to perform and repeat. A customer that can move from a scientific experiment to a reliable result at scale, with less effort, has a reason to stay with a vendor and invest more. That advantage still has to be earned through application quality, performance, service reliability and superior economics.

There is also a customer tradeoff – the classic lock-in risk. An integrated service can reduce operational complexity while increasing dependence on the provider’s tooling and ecosystem. Open-source tools help minimize the risk, but portability also depends on whether models, workflows, validation and operational models transfer to another platform. Our spring conversations with Kranzlmüller – and his emphasis on technological independence – along with Shehata’s interest in interoperable specifications – make that point clear.

We would not declare IBM as a decisive winner from this conference. But the company has presented an impressive combination of hardware, software and infrastructure progress. Customers will determine its value through repeated use and outcomes. Competing systems from specialists and hyperscalers – as well as progress from classical methods – will continue to shape the narrative.

If Jay Gambetta’s prediction holds true, the next two years will produce a more tangible conversation around industry impact. Look for significantly more quantum POCs, more named customers solving consequential problems and a measurable change in a scientific or business decision. We would also want enough evidence for an independent team to assess the contribution; and for the customer to explain the full cost of achieving an outcome.

For enterprise leaders, the sensible approach is to separate cryptographic readiness from quantum application programs tied to specific problems and economics.

IBM has made a stronger case that the surrounding machinery for useful quantum computing is coming together. The future test is whether customers can show what changed because of quantum. A demonstrably improved scientific result or an economically superior workflow would make the 2028 ambition impressive.

That is the evidence we will be watching.

#5575. Inside the $3.25 Million Pasadena Glass Pavilion That’s Still Studied in Architecture Classes Today

A three-bedroom midcentury modern home designed by Case Study architect Craig Ellwood has just come on the market in Pasadena, CA, for $3.25 million. It features a notable cantilevered glass pavilion.

Built in 1965, the Kubly House was originally constructed for less than $45,000. The 2,227-square-foot home has since been thoughtfully updated.

“What makes this house special is its architecture and design, and how true it has remained to the original,” says Chris Suarez, who is co-listing the property with Kimberly Benz of Suarez + Benz at Compass. “Nothing was significantly altered. Everything done was intended to restore the house to its original condition. The footprint, the floors, the glass—everything has remained true to the original design.”

Located in the Linda Vista neighborhood, the home has an iconic redwood, cantilevered glass pavilion that opens to a single-level floor plan. The private half-acre lot includes a pool and spa surrounded by lush landscaping with eucalyptus and oak trees.

With exposed post-and-beam construction, clean horizontal lines, and expansive walls of glass, the home was designed to give the illusion of floating above its natural surroundings. The deck was recently restored using specially milled wood.

“It was sourced from northern Washington and brought down here,” Suarez notes. “Everything was done painstakingly to avoid altering the house’s integrity, architecture, and design. That being said, significant work has been done, including updates to the roof, infrastructure, air conditioning, and electrical systems. All the major systems have been updated, but you wouldn’t necessarily know it because the work was done so carefully.”

Originally commissioned by ArtCenter College of Design alumni and educators Don and Sally Kubly, the home represents their understanding of design and the culture of the college community. It is still studied in classes there.

“Don was ArtCenter’s first president in Pasadena,” Suarez explains. “There’s also a connection through Craig Ellwood, who designed ArtCenter’s main campus building. The main campus is an incredible steel-and-glass building designed by Ellwood. Don played a significant role in moving the school from Los Angeles to Pasadena, where he served as president for many years. He’s very well known within that community, and this house is significant to the college’s history and culture.”

Based on available architectural records, the Kubly House is said to be Ellwood’s only documented residential project in Pasadena.

After remaining in the Kubly family for nearly six decades, the home changed hands for $3.6 million in 2022. Since then, the sellers have undertaken a preservation-minded restoration with Carl Bronson of Bronstruction, updating major systems to contemporary standards.

“A house that helped usher in much midcentury modernism was the Glass House, designed by Philip Johnson around 1948 or 1949,” Benz notes. “That design was definitely something Ellwood loved. You can clearly see that house’s influence here, which is important because it reveals some of the influences behind Ellwood’s work.”

Benz adds that the home’s design was also influenced by Ellwood’s peers, including midcentury designer George Nelson.

“A furniture plan developed for the house clearly referenced Mies van der Rohe and George Nelson, both important figures in midcentury modern design,” she says. “Even the deck and the steps leading to the house resemble a George Nelson bench. There’s actually a bench built into the concrete wall near the pool that resembles a George Nelson design. I don’t know whether Nelson designed or made it, but the influence is certainly there.”

The house is special because many of the original details have remained intact, she adds.

“You can see the influence of the people Ellwood admired throughout the house,” Benz says. “That significance is what makes this house important when you look at the midcentury modernist movement. All these examples are visible in the house and remain there.”

Some of the built-in furniture has a distinctive style, too.

“There’s a stunning floating credenza that looks like a George Nelson piece,” she notes. “We think it might be one of his designs. It’s in the living room. There’s also a built-in console that might be a George Nelson design as well. So, some of the furniture is actually built into the architecture.”

While some pieces are originals and others are reproductions, Benz says, “the most important thing was following the original plan. The history of this house is everything.”

When staging the home, she says they were “fortunate to discover an original interior design study among the blueprints, plans, and documents that came with the house. We were able to look at that study, and it became a guide and a road map for staging the property. Sourcing the furniture was a challenge because we had to find the specific pieces.”

The city of Pasadena has also identified the property as eligible for individual listing on the National Register of Historic Places.

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. #5574. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5573. BREAKING: Compass Sues 15 MLSs in 8 States Over Marketing Restrictions

As the next heated step in its nationwide battle against MLS incumbents, Compass filed more than a dozen federal antitrust lawsuits against 15 MLSs today, carrying out a promised threat to take a bitter, long-running dispute over restrictions on off-MLS marketing to the courtroom.

According to a release, Compass is accusing the MLSs in question of “fining and punishing agents who publicly market homes as their clients have lawfully instructed.” It also notes that said fines can reach up to $15,000.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson stated. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

One of the initial complaints obtained by RISMedia targets Hive MLS in North Carolina. The 45-page lawsuit alleges two violations of federal antitrust laws, accusing the MLS of conspiracy and an illegal group boycott.

“Homeowners should be free to choose how to sell their own homes without having a competition-killing real estate industry organization tell them how to do it,” the complaint begins.

The lawsuits are against six MLSs based in California:

And six MLSs are spread throughout the country:

Several of the MLSs targeted—including Hive MLS, ARMLS, REcolorado, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS and bridgeMLS—already sued Compass, asking a judge to preemptively declare their rules do not violate antitrust laws. They have characterized their various policies, which restrict how members can market listing off-MLS, as pro-competitive and pro-consumer, and claimed Compass is merely seeking to use its exclusive listings as a “competitive weapon.”

Compass, on the other hand, has repeatedly accused these MLSs of fighting purely to protect their own interests and claimed the MLS industry has long endured antitrust scrutiny from government regulators. It sent letters to many of these MLSs back in September, explicitly threatening to sue and force them to bear the legal costs if they continued enforcing the policies in question.

“It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” the Compass spokesperson said. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

Specifically, the lawsuit targeting Hive mentions restrictions on showings for “Coming Soon” properties and focuses on governance, describing the MLS as a “contract, combination, or conspiracy of competing agents and brokers.” It also points to Hive’s alleged licensing of data to third parties, something Compass has previously criticized.

“MLSs that are comprised of or governed by brokerages and agents with traditional business models have a strong financial incentive to impair the business models of innovators and mavericks who seek to offer marketing options to homeowners that eschew immediate and automatic sharing of their listings on the MLS regardless of the circumstances or preferences of the homeowner,” the lawsuit says.

Other lawsuits viewed by RISMedia, including complaints against San Diego MLS and REcolorado, appeared to be largely similar, though they incorporated at least some unique elements (for instance, the San Diego MLS suit quotes California law as imparting a fiduciary duty of “utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty” on agents, and notes that the Realtor® associations that previously owned REcolorado specifically cited worries about antitrust scrutiny when they sold the MLS to a private company back in 2024).

The lawsuits were filed right on the heels of Compass’ new Broker-to-Broker Cooperation Policy, which requires all Compass agents to cooperate with other brokers and agents unless otherwise instructed by the client in writing. Compass agents must also adhere to the policy when dealing with listings earmarked as Private Exclusives or Coming Soons.

Compass’ arguments against the 15 MLSs echo closely to the brokerage’s complaint in the ongoing lawsuit against the California Regional Multiple Listing Service (CRMLS), which it sued in mid-October.

Prior to Compass’ complaint, CRMLS took the initiative and sued the brokerage in early October. As outlined in its original complaint, CRMLS is asking a federal judge in New York to declare that the organization’s rules do not violate state and federal antitrust laws.

“The Cooperation Rules are straightforward: they require that when a broker publicly markets a property for sale—that property must also be submitted to the MLS for cooperation with other participating brokers,” CRMLS’ original complaint states. “What the rules do not permit is having it both ways—publicly marketing a property to attract buyers while simultaneously withholding that property from the MLS cooperative and the thousands of other brokers and their buyer clients.”

Compass, meanwhile, alleged that CRMLS’ rules were “illegal” and accused the organization of blocking the brokerage’s “better home marketing product to protect Compass’ competitors from having to compete,” in Compass’ original complaint against CRMLS.

“Instead of fixing its anticompetitive rules, CRMLS has escalated enforcement against Compass: by CRMLS’s own count, roughly a quarter of the CRMLS fines for public marketing in 2026 involve Compass listings,” Compass’ complaint continued.

Since then, several other MLSs have joined CRMLS in their lawsuit, or have filed their own against the mega-brokerage. OneKey MLS joined CRMLS in its legal battle late last month, while Texas-based Unlock MLS released its own letter alleging that Compass had mischaracterized its rules.

This is a developing story. Stay tuned to RISMedia for updates.

Jesse Williams contributed to this reporting.

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5572. Google retools Kubernetes for AI agents instead of building a new stack

Agentic workloads are pushing Kubernetes into territory its creators never planned for. Agents generate untrusted code on the fly, sit idle for long stretches and churn through pods at a pace that strains the orchestrator’s control plane.

Cloud providers are now rethinking how general-purpose a cluster should be. Google LLC’s answer is to stop treating every cluster as an infinitely flexible engine and tune each one into a runtime optimized for its workload, according to Jago Macleod (pictured, right), director of engineering for Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine at Google Cloud.

“There isn’t enough memory. There aren’t enough machines. So we have to get more efficient. And so one of the ways that we do that is to focus the Kubernetes cluster on the workload it’s running, and optimize it for that specific workload,” Macleod said.

Macleod and Jaana Dogan (pictured, left), principal engineer at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google is customizing Kubernetes for agentic workloads without fragmenting the open-source ecosystem. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes was built for microservices, then stretched to handle training jobs in which a single pod claims an entire node, Macleod explained. Agents are a different beast again, and some teams have resorted to building custom control planes just to cope.

“I think the agentic workloads are so different in the thrash and the churn that they represent is really not what we built Kubernetes for at all,” Macleod said. “And then agentic applications are almost the polar opposite, which is, you know, in the naive implementation, you just have as many pods as you can possibly fit, and so then the API machinery is running into limits.”

Platform teams have spent a decade making Kubernetes their compute fabric, and customers told Google they did not want agents to fragment it, Dogan explained. Google’s response is Agent Substrate, which runs AI agents in sandboxes directly on Kubernetes. The company donated the project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and recently released version 1.0. Because agents write their own code, that code is untrusted by default and needs sandboxing and network guardrails, according to Dogan. Customers also flagged a costly inefficiency.

“For example, our customers came to us, ‘Hey, majority of the time our agents are idle, but we have to allocate a sandbox all through the lifetime of a session,'” Dogan said. That means wasting a lot of CPU cycles, she explained.

Coding agents are also changing how engineers work, producing more prototypes and smaller, more focused teams, Dogan noted. As agentic workloads multiply, human judgment grows more valuable rather than less, according to Macleod.

“It’s not really, you know, fire off a prompt and forget it and walk away,” Macleod said. “It’s just a different level in the system where you’re applying your judgment and expertise. And that has never been more important.”

(* Disclosure: Google Cloud sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Neither Google Cloud nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)
