#5571. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5569. 4 insights from Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026: AI agents join the team as working colleagues

At Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026, AI agents moved out of single-player chat windows and into shared workspaces. There they work beside people as named, auditable members of the team. Block Inc. built these tools to run itself as an intelligence company, and it is now offering them to other businesses, building on Buzz, its open-source workspace for humans and AI agents. Block introduced Builderlab as a set of tools for teams and AI agents to work together.

The next phase will depend less on how capable a single agent becomes than on how well agents collaborate, share an organization’s context and stay inside firm security boundaries. Block plans to spread that model with open-source code, model-agnostic design and hosted infrastructure. The company is making that push while its core business delivers a third straight guidance raise.

“If you’re talking about making the whole organization more productive, you need to break down these distinctions between what the software does and what the people do,” said Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor of SiliconANGLE Media Inc.

Alison Kosik (left) and co-host Gillin spoke with industry experts during Block Builderlab Launch Event 2026 in San Francisco. The interviews covered Block’s open-source business model, agents with their own identities, the shift from prompting to overnight delegation and the security controls that let enterprises trust autonomous systems. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are four standout insights from the event:

Builderlab gives developers endlessly customizable agents on an open-source plug-in architecture, and the launch audience of application builders cheered the idea, according to Gillin. Agents in Buzz have names, avatars and personalities. That shifts the focus from switching among software-as-a-service applications to the work itself, and it could threaten SaaS companies. The revenue model follows the classic open-source pattern of giving the software away and charging for the convenience of a hosted cloud service, he explained. Block said little about commercialization or about Cash App, which brings in 60% of its revenue, according to Gillin.

Most AI tools are built for one person at a time, so each user becomes the bottleneck when results have to be shared with a team, noted Lucas Isaza, product lead of Buzz at Block. In Buzz, agents have their own identities, can be tagged like colleagues and leave an audit trail of every action. Plug-ins, added after the first version launched in July, let anyone reshape the interface. Nontechnical staff, such as account managers building personal dashboards, have been the heaviest users of the companion apps platform. Companies can self-host the open-source code, use a free tier or add funds for remote agents, models and extra storage, Isaza highlighted.

Builderlab sits as an interface layer above the models, so Buzz can use agents from any AI lab and switch to the newest frontier model as it arrives, emphasized Brad Axen, head of AI capabilities at Block. Remote agents run in central cloud environments that are easier to secure than laptops. People can hand them large assignments overnight and act as reviewers. Instead of soft guardrails, agents run on secure building blocks that never grant them permission for certain actions. Some teams have shipped software releases 50% to 75% faster. Axen expects agents to need much less human steering within the next year because they already sit inside the conversation.

Securing agents that act on their own does not mean starting over, because principles such as least privilege, isolated environments and egress controls still apply, shared James Nettesheim, chief information security officer and head of enterprise technology at Block. Builderlab gives every agent a full identity owned by a human, runs it in hardened cloud virtual machines and records its actions in a cryptographically signed ledger that cannot be altered. Block is also building information flow control, which tags data from sensitive sources so the security policy travels with that data and blocks leaks. AI already reviews Block’s code and sorts its security alerts. Nettesheim added that agents let defenders keep pace with attackers’ machine speed.

#5568. Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang's return after his resignation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

An internal post asking the board to weigh staff sentiment has drawn more than 1,600 comments, according to Wired

Nvidia $NVDA employees are urging the company's board to bring back Jensen Huang after his resignation as CEO, according to Wired, which reviewed internal correspondence at the chipmaker.

A longtime engineer submitted an internal suggestion-box post, before Huang resigned, asking the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to Wired. The post has since collected over 1,600 replies, and a number of them urge directors to figure out how to restore him to the role.

"If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," one anonymous commenter wrote, according to Wired. Another wrote: "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance."

One employee emailed the whole company to press for openness about why Huang departed, according to Wired. "I stand by Jensen," the staffer wrote, adding that supporting fairness need not require distancing oneself from a leader who has had such an impact on the workforce. Wired could not reach that employee, and the engineer who wrote the suggestion-box post declined to comment.

Within hours of the resignation, about two dozen employees voiced support for Huang on LinkedIn, according to Wired. Wired did not find any public messages from staffers at the chipmaker welcoming his departure.

An employee with roughly two years at Nvidia, who lacked permission to speak on the record, told Wired the wish to see Huang reinstated is widespread. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," the employee said, adding that the company will struggle in the absence of its founder and that directors need to reinstate him.

Many employees assumed the board would complete its investigation prior to any significant shake-up, according to Wired. The suggestion-box post asked that the board report what it uncovers to staff and officially request their opinions on Huang’s future as CEO. Huang exited right when the probe was getting under way, and staff are looking for the reasons.

Nvidia and board chair Harvey Jones had not responded to requests for comment from Wired.

Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspect is an agent of Beijing's spy agencies. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed Jones, a former Synopsys $SNPS CEO, as the board's first chair. The board is searching for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.

Huang, 63, admitted to infidelity in a note to employees on Nov. 8, the day the board opened an independent investigation.

#5567. Paris Signal Week looks to bridge crypto and institutional finance

Paris Blockchain Week is now Signal Week, a reflection of cryptocurrency’s global expansion.

The newly rebranded event is joining forces with RAISE Summit, the annual AI and networking conference, and Machina Summit, Europe’s leading physical AI event. Event organizers expect approximately 2,500 attendees, highlighting the growing profile of blockchain technology.

“The industry has changed a lot,” said Michael Amar (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week. “We really want to be the place where we bridge traditional finance and digital assets. It’s where the market is finally, and we are embracing it completely. We have the desire to go abroad to launch other conferences. So it made sense that … we join everything under the same roof, but different flows, different marketing and different ticketing.”

Amar and Charlie Meraud (pictured), chairman of RAISE Summit and co-founder of Signal Week, spoke with theCUBE host Gemma Allen, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed what to expect at the 2027 event and the evolution of cryptocurrency. (* Disclosure below.)

Signal Week is designed to cover the intersection between institutional finance and digital assets. Since its founding, the crypto market has grown to $40 billion in tokenized real-world assets, or RWA, according to Meraud. The week will also encompass the CXO Summit, a private gathering of C-suite executives.

“The CXO Summit is organizing a roundtable under Chatham House rules with these … crypto-native players discussing all sophisticated topics around what they are building and how they can partner all year long,” he said. “This is the kind of activation that makes people book a flight, buy a ticket and come to Signal Week. The industry needed a room for these players to connect and start actually doing business.”

Both founders see facilitating conversations between crypto leaders and traditional finance executives as one of the primary goals of the conference. The chief executive officers of Kaiko, Morpho and Fireblocks, all leading digital asset companies, are expected to attend. European Union regulators will also be present, Amar and Meraud emphasize, which will be critical for understanding the future of AI-powered finance.

“We’re creating those moments where people can get the most out of the conference,” Amar said. “If you talk about the C-suite, people coming from traditional finance and meeting the makers of the crypto industry, we’re creating the space where they will have talks in a very small room where actually we go very much into the details of the use cases of the implementation of a digital asset solution for a bank, for example.”

Another key topic at Signal Week and RAISE Summit will be custody, the safekeeping of private keys that allow a person to prove they control an address and the cryptocurrency it holds. Security has long been a divisive issue for cryptocurrency, spurring a variety of solutions.

“When we started … self-custody was one of the promised digital assets,” Meraud said. “A lot of players have been offering different ways of custodying digital assets. And having the most sophisticated solution coming to Signal Week, explaining all the new features, they’ve been building over the years is one of the reasons financial institutions are willing to connect and network with our audience.”

#5566. Nvidia heads for a sixth straight weekly loss as its market value sinks by about $1.6 trillion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday after reports of two affairs, and Nvidia stock fell 4.3% that day

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia $NVDA CEO on Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs, and the chipmaker's stock is on track for a sixth straight weekly loss.

Nvidia stock dropped 4.3% during Thursday’s session, leaving it down 11% across the week. The stock is down 29% across those six weeks, which erased roughly $1.6 trillion in market value and pushed Nvidia beneath Apple $AAPL. It is the stock’s longest weekly losing streak since 2012, according to CNBC.

The selling picked up in recent days, according to CNBC. Huang sent employees a letter on Sunday apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife," according to CNBC. The second affair, with an employee, was reported on Wednesday, and the board met late that night.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board looks for a permanent successor. Nvidia is due to post fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Huang, 63, stepped down as CEO and from the board, Nvidia said in a statement. Harvey C. Jones, who previously led Synopsys $SNPS, becomes the company's first board chair and will direct the search, which will consider candidates from inside and outside Nvidia, the company said. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993.

The affair Huang disclosed on Sunday was with a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence officials suspect the woman is an agent of Beijing's spy agencies.

Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation on Sunday. The board said nothing it has seen suggests Nvidia's trade secrets or U.S. national security were put at risk. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the allegation unsubstantiated.

Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

#5564. Did Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Just Expose Real Bitcoin Bottom in January 2027?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin’s cycle bottom is likely already in or very close, as a Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Bitcoin bottom prediction highlights a final low expected in the $60,000–$68,000 zone by late December 2026 or early January 2027 at the latest. As of November 11, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $73,700–$73,900, roughly 41% below its October 2025 all-time high around $126,000.

The market has been grinding lower after a failed recovery attempt into the low $80,000s, with recent sessions testing the psychologically important $73,000 level. While the short-term trend remains soft, longer-term structure and historical cycle patterns suggest the deepest part of the correction is largely complete.

Bitcoin is consolidating in a tight range after a multi-week decline. Immediate support sits at the $73,000 round number, which coincides with recent daily lows, the approximate 200-day moving average, and prior structural levels from earlier in the year.

A daily close below $73,000 would open the door to the next support cluster near $71,500 (prior swing area) and then the 50-day moving average zone around $68,500. Deeper support resides in the $62,000–$65,000 region, with the July 2026 low near $57,700–$58,000 acting as the major cycle floor.

On the upside, resistance is layered at $75,000, followed by the more significant $80,000 area. Momentum indicators such as the RSI have cooled into neutral-to-oversold territory on daily timeframes, leaving room for either a relief bounce or one final liquidity sweep lower before a more durable base forms.

Volume has been elevated on down days, consistent with distribution by short-term holders, but longer-term holder metrics and the 200-week moving average (historically a strong demand zone) continue to provide a structural floor.

Bitcoin | Net shorts just hit an ATH.The last 4 times we saw these levels, they marked a major bottom. pic.twitter.com/n9DkeYEYqy

My base-case view is that the primary cycle low was printed in July 2026 near $58,000. That level marked a roughly 54% drawdown from the prior peak, shallower than the 70–80%+ declines of previous bear markets, reflecting Bitcoin’s growing institutional base and ETF demand.

The current pullback into the low $70,000s looks more like a higher-low retest or secondary correction within a broader bottoming process rather than the start of a new leg down. If $73,000 fails, a final flush into the $62,000–$68,000 zone remains the most probable destination.

This area aligns with Fibonacci retracements of the 2025–2026 rally, prior demand zones, and the upper end of the July low region. I expect any such move to occur relatively quickly, within the next four to eight weeks, driven by residual profit-taking, macro uncertainty, or year-end positioning.

By late December 2026 or the first half of January 2027 at the latest, this process should be complete. A sustained defense of the $68,000–$70,000 area (or a higher low above $70,000) would strongly support the thesis that the bottom is in.

Conversely, a decisive break below the July low near $58,000 would invalidate the constructive view and open a path toward $50,000–$55,000, though that outcome currently carries lower probability given the maturity of the correction and the strength of long-term holder support.

In short, Bitcoin appears to be in the late stages of its post-2025 correction. The most likely final low sits in the $60,000–$68,000 range, timed for the remainder of Q4 2026 into very early 2027. Once that floor is confirmed with a higher low and a reclaim of $80,000, the stage would be set for a more meaningful recovery phase.

#5562. Kubernetes gets a second act as AI agents turn one prompt into thousands of inference calls

The rise of agentic AI systems is giving Kubernetes, long valued for its reliability and predictability, an unexpected second act.

As AI spending shifts from training models toward serving them and running agents, the open-source community is developing tools to handle the growing volume of inference requests. The orchestration platform was built from the start for dynamic, distributed workloads, which gave fast-growing AI companies a reliable foundation, according to Jonathan Bryce (pictured), executive director of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

“The AI boom has sparked a massive investment and a huge build-out of infrastructure overall,” Bryce said. “Having Kubernetes built from the beginning to handle really dynamic distributed workloads as those companies were growing like crazy — they had a really reliable, solid foundation to build on at the same time.”

Bryce spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how CNCF projects can meet rising inference demand, make better use of data center hardware and secure AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

New models grab headlines with benchmark scores in math and software engineering. But a model has no value until it can be served at high performance, and early chatbots made that look simple because each message triggered a single inference call, Bryce explained. Agents can make repeated inference calls to complete a single task, a shift the CNCF has put on the KubeCon agenda with its new AI inference and agentic track.

“We’re using coding agents to say, ‘Build me a system that does this,’ and it’ll spawn 10 sub-agents,” Bryce said. “Each of those are doing thousands of inference calls over the course of hours and just churning away.”

As inference demand fuels a data center construction boom and raises local concerns about resource use, the llm-d inference engine and Agent Substrate, which offers compact hosting for long-running agents, aim to get more performance out of existing hardware, Bryce said. Security and control pose another challenge because agents can make different choices when given the same task. OpenShell, a security project now under the CNCF’s neutral governance following Nvidia Corp.’s contribution, drew more than 300 contributing companies within months, a milestone which might once have taken two years to reach, he added.

“What I am constantly thinking about is, ‘How do we lower friction to collaboration?'” Bryce said. “How do we enable people to be able to move at the pace that the world and the industry is moving at, and how do we, while doing that, continue to drive that into collaboration around open solutions that can become those base and infrastructure components that we can all build on?”

#5560. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5559. SpaceX is launching Starship in its first attempt to catch both rocket stages today

Free daily briefing on global business news.

SpaceX said success would mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system, with the ship catch set for about 22 hours after liftoff

SpaceX plans to launch Starship Flight 15 from Starbase in Texas on Friday in its first attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage with its launch tower.

The company said the 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. ET. SpaceX has said the schedule is dynamic and could change, and a live webcast is planned to start about 30 minutes before liftoff.

If both catches succeed, it would be the first time an entire orbital launch system has been brought back intact, SpaceX said. Reusing both stages would allow the company to load fresh propellant and send those same vehicles back up, according to Bloomberg.

SpaceX set out a catch timeline for the flight. The booster catch is scheduled about 6 minutes and 35 seconds after liftoff. The ship is slated to circle the planet about 14 times at a height near 275 kilometers (171 miles) before its catch, which is scheduled about 22 hours and 32 minutes after liftoff.

This will be the first return and catch attempt for a Super Heavy V3 booster. Three V1 boosters were caught on earlier flights, and two of them flew again. SpaceX has not attempted a ship catch, which is harder than a booster catch because the ship flies a longer route at greater altitude and velocity.

The ship's return to the launch site depends on the flight control team confirming that the systems needed for reentry maneuvers, the landing burn and the tower approach are healthy. The flight profile lets SpaceX cut the flight short and bring the ship down in a splashdown if an engine problem or another issue arises, according to Gizmodo.

Starship will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Each adds 1 terabit per second of capacity to the constellation, and the satellites should begin serving customers a few weeks after launch at the earliest. Three of them carry cameras that will scan the ship’s heatshield and send imagery to operators.

Flight 14, on Sept. 28, was the first to send the ship to orbit, where it released 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The booster made a soft splashdown in the Gulf of America on that flight instead of returning to the tower, as SpaceX tested changes to improve engine relight reliability.

CEO Elon Musk outlined the double-catch plan on SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call last month. "I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk said. SpaceX is aiming for Starship to reach full capability around the end of 2027.

#5558. Procon Brings Robotics Technology to Port Canaveral's Cruise Terminal 5 Expansion

Following a successful pilot, Procon and Teleworker AI are bringing robotic 360-degree capture to active construction monitoring at Cruise Terminal 5

MCLEAN, Va., Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Procon Consulting, LLC (Procon), a construction management and technology consulting firm, has partnered with the Canaveral Port Authority to expand the use of robotic reality capture during construction at Cruise Terminal 5. The work is underway following a successful pilot that demonstrated how a four-legged robot could document changing site conditions through repeatable 360-degree capture walks.

The $78 million expansion and renovation will nearly double the terminal's size, from 90,000 to 170,000 square feet, to accommodate the world's largest cruise ships and enhance the passenger experience.

Using a robotic platform nicknamed "Sparky," Procon is providing Port Canaveral and its project teams with more frequent visual documentation of construction progress while reducing the time spent on routine site walks.

"Port Canaveral is making a major investment in its cruise facilities, and its project team needs a reliable view of progress as construction moves forward," said Jason Lopez, Senior Vice President of Procon. "Regular reality capture can help teams spot differences earlier, resolve questions faster and maintain better records. That value extends beyond construction: an accurate visual record of facility conditions can help facilities teams plan maintenance, troubleshoot issues and coordinate repairs more efficiently, helping minimize downtime, avoid unnecessary costs and keep operations running smoothly. That is the practical, long-term value we want to deliver through this work."

"Port Canaveral has always been a pioneer in utilizing data-driven tools to enhance our operations and provide a high-quality experience for our partners and guests," said Bill Crowe, Port Canaveral's Vice President of Engineering & Construction. "Working with Procon gives our team access to ongoing construction progress documentation throughout the course of Cruise Terminal 5 expansion and renovation, one of the most complex projects ever undertaken at the Port."

From a Successful Pilot to Active Deployment

The earlier pilot grew out of Procon's construction robotics research with Virginia Tech's Myers-Lawson School of Construction. The Multi-Agent Robotic System for Inspection On Site (MARIO) initiative explores how robots and remote monitoring can help project teams collect and use field information.

Procon is working with Teleworker AI, which developed components of the camera payload used for robotic reality capture. Teleworker's team also worked with Procon on assembly and setup, helping prepare the robot for deployment with limited hands-on intervention. The collaboration combines Teleworker's robotics expertise with Procon's understanding of construction workflows and the information Owners need.

"On a project like Cruise Terminal 5, a lot can change in a single day," said Stephen DeVito, CM-BIM, Director of Technology at Procon. "Daily capture gives the team a clearer record of what happened and when. That can help resolve questions about progress or site conditions before they turn into larger issues, while freeing staff to focus on work that needs their attention."

With Sparky conducting regular capture walks, Port Canaveral can compare site conditions over time, monitor progress between in-person visits and identify issues while they are easier to address. The resulting record can also help verify completed work and provide documentation if questions arise about schedule, change orders or construction claims.

The project is testing these benefits under real operating conditions. Procon is evaluating capture frequency, reliability and usefulness to the project team. The findings will help inform future uses of robotics on complex capital projects.

Procon's robotics work will be featured during Port Canaveral's 2026 State of the Port presentation on Thursday, November 19.  Sparky will take center stage ahead of the introduction of Port Canaveral CEO Capt. John Murray.

Procon Consulting, LLC is a construction management and technology consulting firm helping Owners plan, deliver and manage complex facilities and infrastructure. Through integrated capabilities in Construction & Program Management, Technology Solutions, Engineering & Technical Services, Risk Management & Claims Control, Project Controls and Facility Management, Procon provides the expertise, insight and tools needed to deliver better project and facility outcomes. Learn more at www.procon.com.

Led by the elected five-member Canaveral Port Authority Board of Commissioners and CEO Capt. John W. Murray, Port Canaveral is Florida's Premier Seaport with diverse business operations that include cruise, cargo, recreation and real estate, while serving as a supporting partner for commercial fishing and aerospace enterprises. Port Canaveral hosts more than 9 million cruise passenger movements and handles nearly 6 million tons of cargo annually, including bulk, break-bulk, project, heavy lift and containerized. The Port continues to build upon its leadership position as a gateway for global commerce through innovative initiatives like the Port Canaveral Advantage, a five-year, more than $1 billion capital investment program committed to improvements for all facets of its operations. For more information, visit www.PortCanaveral.com.

#5557. TikTok owner ByteDance is planning a buyback of up to $6 billion at about $400 billion

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The TikTok owner is proposing to extend by four years its deadline to go public or let outside investors sell back their stakes

ByteDance, the owner of TikTok, intends to repurchase as much as $6 billion in its own shares from investors, valuing the company at roughly $400 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The offer, outlined in a letter to investors, sets a price of $241.35 a share and implies a valuation 20% higher than the one used in a comparable program 12 months earlier, according to Bloomberg.

In the same letter, ByteDance proposed moving back, by four years, the cutoff by which it must list its shares or offer outside shareholders an option to sell their full stakes back to it, according to Bloomberg. The new deadline would be Dec. 11, 2030.

A ByteDance spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment on the proposals, according to Bloomberg.

The letter also lays out a plan to grant staff in ByteDance's artificial intelligence division 300 million stock units whose worth is tied to the performance of its AI business, according to Bloomberg. The company is stepping up incentives as it competes to hire and keep AI specialists, and it already gives those staff preferential equity terms unlike those offered to other employees.

Beijing-based ByteDance rose to the top of the startup rankings by value after algorithmic recommendations took hold through TikTok and its Chinese counterpart Douyin, according to Bloomberg. The company fell behind rivals when chatbots took off, but it has gained ground in AI after senior leaders called on employees in 2024 to step up their push. Its Doubao chatbot is China's most popular, and it runs a video-generation service called Seedance.

Co-founder Zhang Yiming has rallied the AI team behind a target of competing with the top U.S. labs within three years, according to Bloomberg. ByteDance is also preparing to roll out a personal AI assistant.

It remains uncertain at what point ByteDance, or any segment of its operations, might go public, according to Bloomberg. Certain current investors have priced the company at over $400 billion, and a number of secondary deals have pushed its implied value close to $500 billion.

#5556. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5555. Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong earnings results

Shares of artificial intelligence cloud operator Nebius Holdings NV dropped 17% today after it posted third-quarter financial results.

The company’s adjusted profit and revenue topped expectations. The selloff may have been sparked by its full-year forecast, which fell short of the consensus estimate. It’s also possible the sudden departure of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed. Nvidia is an investor in Nebius and many other AI and cloud companies.

Another possible factor: Nebius increased its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion. According to CNBC, that’s $4.15 billion higher than what Wall Street had expected. The company’s plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year surpassed the consensus estimate by an even wider margin.

The surging expenses may be related to its shift away from colocation facilities. Today, about 90% of the company’s infrastructure is located in rented data centers. In contrast, the next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity that it plans to bring online will be mostly powered by internally operated data centers.

“Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term,” said founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh. “We will continue to invest across the business – in our capacity and infrastructure buildout, in our platform and products, and in the team that takes this to market.”

Nebius swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year ago to a $90.9 million adjusted profit. The latter figure breaks down to adjusted earnings of 31 cents per share. The company’s profitability surprised analysts, who expected a loss of 69 cents per share.

Revenue growth was another bright spot. Sales jumped 517% year-over-year, to $980.8 million, which put the company well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus estimate.

One of Nebius’ main growth drivers is its Token Factory service for running open-source AI models. Developers use it to host both post-training and inference workloads. Nebius says that the offering, which launched a year ago, is nearing a “multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate” after logging a 17-fold quarter-over-increase in contract value.

Nebius’ largest customers played a particularly important role in its strong quarterly performance. The company signed $12 billion worth of contracts in the three months ended Sept. 30. The haul included multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and other major tech firms.

The company uses customers’ contract prepayments to finance its data center projects. The company says that the value of the prepayments it received in the third quarter exceeded its capital expenditures. However, the ratio of prepayments to capital expenditures is expected to decline as Nebius ramps up its data center spending. That detail may be yet another factor in today’s stock selloff.

Nebius expects its full-year revenue to be “at the low end” of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range. Analysts expected $3.37 billion. For 2027, Nebius is forecasting $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue.

#5554. Microsoft 365 outage stretches into a second day with Outlook and Teams disrupted

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Microsoft is working to restore service as the outage disrupts government offices, traders and businesses in more than 70 countries

Microsoft $MSFT said users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services, as problems with Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI tool dragged on for a second straight day Friday, according to Bloomberg.

Microsoft said administrators may be unable to reach the admin center for service health information, so it posted details on its public status page. The page lists both Microsoft 365 for business and enterprise customers and Microsoft consumer products as experiencing service degradation.

The problems began Thursday afternoon, according to Bloomberg. Microsoft has posted updates almost every hour as it tries to shift users onto servers that are still functioning. "A core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss," the company said, according to Bloomberg. Microsoft said it has found nothing to suggest the disruption was malicious.

In a Friday status update, Microsoft said service was beginning to recover in Asia and that its next priority was bringing the same improvement to other regions, according to Bloomberg. Few earlier disruptions at Microsoft have stretched beyond a few hours.

Microsoft stock slid roughly 2.1% before the market opened on Friday.

Users spread across over 70 countries said they had trouble using Microsoft products, according to Bloomberg. Security software, services for sharing files and tools used by administrators also suffered interruptions.

The number of people affected is unknown, according to The Associated Press, which put the ceiling at 430 million, the number of people Microsoft says use Microsoft 365 apps.

Richemont and Workhorse Group postponed earnings releases this week because of the outage, according to Bloomberg. Richemont has filed its report.

The U.K.’s National Health Service pushed back certain procedures because the outage hampered its communications, according to Bloomberg. Several police forces in the U.K. said they were unable to accept online reports of crimes, according to Bloomberg, which cited The Guardian.

Japan’s Finance Ministry said no incoming email reached it through much of the day, according to Bloomberg. Government ministries there put up printed announcements to let reporters know the day’s schedules. Euronext cautioned that it could not be reached by email.

At the Reserve Bank of Australia, Outlook was unavailable across departments, though essential functions continued as usual, according to Bloomberg. New Zealand immigration officials halted work on every visa application.

#5553. In HelloNation, Insurance Expert Ben Parsons Breaks Down What Affects Auto Insurance Costs

FORT COLLINS, Colo., Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Why do auto insurance costs vary so much for drivers in Fort Collins, and what can be done to manage them effectively?

A HelloNation article featuring Insurance Agent Ben Parsons of Fort Collins, CO, provides a clear explanation of what affects insurance premiums and how drivers can find the right balance between cost and coverage.

The article begins by pointing out that while it may be tempting to choose the cheapest auto insurance policy available, that choice can come with financial risks. Inadequate coverage options could leave drivers exposed in the event of an accident. By understanding how premiums are calculated and which factors are within your control, Fort Collins residents can make smarter decisions about vehicle protection.

Driving history is one of the most important influences on insurance costs. The article notes that drivers with clean records are more likely to receive safe-driver discounts, which reduce insurance premiums. On the other hand, past accidents or violations tend to raise rates. In Fort Collins, maintaining a solid driving history can have long-term benefits, both in cost savings and in showing insurers that you're a lower-risk customer.

Vehicle choice also matters. The article explains that newer or high-value cars typically require both comprehensive and collision coverage to protect them, which increases insurance premiums. However, selecting a vehicle with strong safety features and a lower risk of theft can help offset some of those costs. Fort Collins drivers are encouraged to consider both safety and reliability when choosing a car to keep insurance costs in check.

Coverage options play a major role in shaping auto insurance expenses. Colorado law requires liability coverage, but minimum limits may not offer enough financial protection. The article advises drivers to review their liability coverage carefully and consider adding comprehensive and collision coverage, especially if they want broader vehicle protection. These choices affect not only monthly premiums but also how well you're covered in case of damage, theft, or natural events.

Deductibles are another key factor. The article suggests that selecting a higher deductible can lower monthly insurance premiums, though it also means paying more out of pocket when filing a claim. Conversely, a lower deductible increases monthly costs but reduces financial stress after an accident. Finding the right balance based on your budget and comfort level is an essential part of managing insurance costs.

The article also explains that where you live in Fort Collins can influence your rates. Areas with higher traffic, more frequent accidents, or greater risks of theft may lead to higher premiums. Seasonal risks like snow and ice are also considered in rate calculations. Understanding how your local environment impacts insurance helps in choosing appropriate coverage levels.

Discounts can make a meaningful difference. The article highlights safe-driver discounts, as well as savings for bundling policies, taking defensive driving courses, or maintaining low mileage. Student and loyalty discounts may also apply. Exploring all available discounts helps Fort Collins drivers maximize savings without reducing the protection they need.

Comparing quotes is strongly encouraged. Since rates, coverage options, and available discounts can vary between providers, shopping around ensures that you find the right match for your needs. The article also points out the value of working with a knowledgeable agent who can help clarify policy details and spot opportunities to save.

Finally, the article stresses the importance of reviewing your policy regularly. Life events like adding a teen driver, moving, or purchasing a new car can impact premiums and coverage needs. Keeping your auto insurance policy up to date ensures continued protection and helps avoid surprise costs down the road.

Understanding Auto Insurance Costs features insights from Ben Parsons, Insurance Expert of Fort Collins, CO, in HelloNation.
