#5534. UWM rolls out 40 bps year-end pricing bonus, expands Bilt partnership

United Wholesale Mortgage introduced “40 to the Finish,” a year-end pricing incentive that adds 40 basis points to all products for loans with 700+ FICO scores when brokers use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools through Dec. 31. At the same time, UWM expanded its partnership with Bilt to integrate Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing platform.   AI Summary

United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) this week announced the launch of a year-end pricing incentive for broker loans and an expansion of its partnership with Bilt.

Effective immediately through Dec. 31, brokers who use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools will receive 40 basis points on all agency and nonagency products when the borrower has a credit score of at least 700, UWM said.

The incentive is intended to give brokers more pricing flexibility in the final weeks of 2026 while encouraging use of the lender’s underwriting and closing technology. Year-end pricing specials are common in the wholesale channel as lenders seek to pull volume into the current year, clean up pipelines and help partners hit production goals.

UWM – which was more aggressive on pricing in the past but is seeking to deleverage its balance sheet amid a deal with Oaktree Capital Management and the Ishbia family – saw its gain-on-sale margins decline to 124 basis points in the third quarter, down from 133 basis points in the second quarter.

UWM chairman, CEO and president Mat Ishbia told analysts he expects margins to be steady, adding that “people don’t use UWM because we’re the lowest rates” and arguing that competitors offering lower rates are not good partners.

Separately, UWM said it’s expanding its partnership with Bilt, a neighborhood commerce and rewards platform, to bring Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing ecosystem.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is designed to help businesses reach customers and build loyalty through neighborhood-level experiences. Through UWM, it links mortgage servicing with homeownership tasks and local commerce, while keeping independent brokers visible to borrowers after closing.

“The broker who helps you buy your home should be your first call when you’re ready to take the next step, whether that’s refinancing, accessing equity or buying again,” Ishbia said in a statement. “With Bilt Neighborhood OS, we’re making the servicing experience more valuable to homeowners and creating more reasons for them to stay connected to their broker between those major decisions.”

UWM already services hundreds of thousands of loans through Bilt, giving these homeowners a single place to manage their mortgage and access rewards. With Neighborhood OS added, UWM said the experience will extend into more day-to-day homeownership activities, from finding a local contractor to exploring neighborhood offers, or reconnecting with a broker about a home equity or refinance opportunity.

Bilt said it has delivered more than $1 billion in value to its 8 million members, who redeem rewards toward travel, housing payments, student loans, dining and other categories. The company also says it powers one in four U.S. rental homes, primarily through the Bilt Alliance of large owners and operators.

#5533. Iraq's oil output climbed to its highest level in seven years, the IEA said

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Gulf crude exports reached 18.4 million barrels a day in October, still 26% below pre-war levels, the IEA said

Iraq pumped 4.6 million barrels of crude a day in October, an increase of 540,000 barrels a day from the previous month, the International Energy Agency said in its monthly oil market report on Friday.

That was the highest level since September 2019, according to Bloomberg.

Iraq's output ran 170,000 barrels a day above its implied target of 4.43 million, the IEA said. The agency put the country's sustainable capacity at 4.87 million barrels a day.

Gulf producers excluding Oman exported 18.4 million barrels a day in October, which is 26% below pre-war levels, the IEA said. Those exports rose by 950,000 barrels a day from the prior month, according to Bloomberg. Producers in the region are sending some cargoes on low-profile tanker runs across the Strait of Hormuz and are shipping other crude by alternative export routes that never touch the strait.

Global oil supply rose by 2.3 million barrels a day to 105.4 million in October, the IEA said. That followed a 3 million barrel-a-day increase in September. The agency said the gains came from high Gulf exports despite continuing attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers.

Saudi Arabia produced 9.99 million barrels a day in October, up from 8.93 million in September, the IEA said. Kuwait produced 2.03 million barrels a day, up from 1.58 million.

The IEA's estimates differ from figures that Gulf producers submitted to OPEC. Iraq told OPEC it produced 4.888 million barrels a day in October, above the IEA's 4.6 million. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 10.563 million barrels a day, compared with the IEA's 9.99 million.

The recovery in Gulf output follows disruption from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which began in late February.

#5532. Lanvin Group Receives Continued Listing Standard Notice from NYSE

SHANGHAI, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Lanvin Group Holdings Limited (NYSE: LANV) ("Lanvin Group" or the "Company"), a global luxury fashion group, today announced that it received a notice from the New York Stock Exchange (the "NYSE") on November 10, 2026 that the Company is not in compliance with the NYSE's continued listing standard requiring a minimum average closing price of US$1.00 per share for its ordinary shares over a consecutive 30 trading-day period.

The Company has notified the NYSE within ten business days of receipt of the notice of its intent to cure the deficiency. Pursuant to the NYSE's rules, the Company has a six-month period following receipt of the deficiency letter to regain compliance with the minimum share price requirement.

The Company intends to consider available alternatives, including but not limited to a reverse stock split that is subject to shareholder approval, if necessary to cure the stock price non-compliance.  The Company can regain compliance at any time during the six-month cure period if, on the last trading day of any calendar month during the cure period, the Ordinary Shares have a closing price of at least US$1.00 per share and an average closing price of at least US$1.00 per share over the 30 trading-day period ending on the last trading day of that month.

The NYSE notice has no immediate effect on the continued listing of Lanvin Group's ordinary shares on the NYSE and is not anticipated to impact the Company's ongoing business operations. The Company's ordinary shares will continue to be listed and trade on the NYSE under the symbol "LANV" during this period, subject to the Company's compliance with the NYSE's other continued listing requirements.

Lanvin Group is a leading global luxury fashion group headquartered in Shanghai, China, and Milan, Italy, managing iconic brands worldwide including Lanvin, Wolford, Sergio Rossi and St. John Knits. Leveraging its unique strategic alliances with industry-leading partners in the luxury fashion sector and its access to the fastest-growing luxury fashion markets, Lanvin Group strives to expand the global footprint of its portfolio brands and achieve sustainable growth through strategic investment and extensive operational know-how. Lanvin Group's ordinary shares are listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol "LANV".  For more information about Lanvin Group, please visit www.lanvin-group.com, and to view Lanvin Group's investor presentation, please visit https://ir.lanvin-group.com.

Multichannel lender Newrez partnered with financial technology firm Upgrade to offer unsecured personal loans to eligible mortgage servicing customers, giving homeowners another option to access cash without tapping home equity or refinancing.

The loans, originated and serviced by Upgrade and issued by its partner Cross River Bank, do not change the existing Newrez mortgage. Newrez funded $12.9 billion in mortgages in the third quarter and reached $878.9 billion in unpaid principal balance across its mortgage servicing rights (MSR) portfolio at the end of September.

#5530. Canada is threatening to sue Stellantis over Brampton plant sale

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Stellantis has 30 days to address a notice of default tied to a federal funding agreement

Canada warned it may take Stellantis $STLA to court over the automaker's plan to sell its shuttered factory in Brampton, Ontario, giving it 30 days to resolve Ottawa's objections. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told a Toronto news conference on Thursday that Ottawa had formally notified Stellantis it is in default.

"We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them," Joly told reporters, according to CNBC.

Joly said Stellantis broke the contractual promises it made to Ottawa and to Brampton's workforce when it revealed it had struck a deal to sell the facility to Roshel, which makes armored vehicles. She said the company is "on the hook" for several hundred million dollars.

Stellantis, the parent of Jeep, Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, announced on Monday a deal to sell the plant to Roshel, though it did not disclose the price. The company said it recognizes what it owes the facility's employees and is ready to negotiate a settlement for union-represented workers in talks with Unifor, Canada's largest private sector union.

Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said on Thursday that the automaker will give back C$24 million in subsidies it received from Ottawa, according to CNBC. That figure falls short of what the government estimates Stellantis owes.

"We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," Longley said, according to CNBC.

A Stellantis spokesperson was not available for comment on Friday morning, according to CNBC.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the situation at the plant “unacceptable” and a “betrayal” of its workers, according to CNBC.

Stellantis had dropped its plan to build the Jeep Compass at Brampton, moving future output to an Illinois factory as U.S. auto tariffs and other pressures in the market weighed on the company, according to CNBC. The U.S. and Canada are in a trade dispute, and President Donald Trump has urged carmakers to shift their vehicle manufacturing to the United States.

#5528. CNCF data shows cloud native is the on-ramp to AI, and maintainers are paying the price

The global population of cloud-native developers has topped 21 million, but the headcount tells only part of the story. Artificial intelligence is changing what those developers build and how open-source projects absorb their work.

Fresh research is putting numbers on that shift. The latest State of Cloud Native Development report from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData Ltd. counts more than 21 million practitioners, or 41% of developers worldwide. Yet that figure likely misses many people who rely on cloud-native infrastructure without knowing it, according to Bob Killen (pictured, right), director of technical program management at CNCF.

“The big thing is it actually might be undercounting a significant amount of them,” Killen said. “Because there’s a very large amount of people that are essentially consuming cloud-native applications without even realizing it.”

Killen and Liam Bollmann-Dodd (left), principal market research consultant at SlashData, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the latest State of Cloud Native Development findings, AI adoption, the strain on open-source maintainers and the shift toward cost discipline. (* Disclosure below.)

The report’s most striking finding concerns AI. About 75% of cloud-native developers use AI in some form, compared with only about 55% of other developers, Bollmann-Dodd noted. The gap mirrors a broader trend of agentic AI pushing Kubernetes into a second act.

“It’s a massive difference,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “So somehow being cloud native enables you and your organization and your personal stack to do AI in all its forms.”

The same AI wave is straining the people who keep the ecosystem running. Sustainability dominated the Maintainer Summit ahead of KubeCon, as maintainers face a flood of pull requests frequently generated by agents, Killen explained.

“How do we as maintainers keep up with the flooding of PRs and issues and things like that?” Killen said. “Especially when many of them are frankly just slop. And the real frustrating part is they’ll be just good enough.”

Cost discipline is the next shift. Just as financial operations practices followed rising cloud bills, cloud-native developers will soon manage model and token spending closely, according to Bollmann-Dodd.

“I think token maxing is dead and it’s going to stay dead forever,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “And I think it’s going to become much more focused on how you spend your money and how you spend your tokens.”

#5527. Reverse mortgage executives read the tea leaves to decipher the industry’s next chapter

At NRMLA Annual, executives said reverse mortgage growth hinges on distribution through forward lenders and better LO education, supported by new prospecting and qualification tools. They also pointed to rising proprietary loan share and a 2027 pivot as traditional purchase and refi volumes remain pressured.  AI Summary

At this week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio, executives offered their thoughts on the evolving product landscape and efforts to expand the sales force while cautioning that hurdles around consumer misperceptions remain.

In a panel discussion held Tuesday and moderated by former NRMLA board member and current Texas Mortgage Bankers Association CEO Scott Norman, executives covered a wide range of topics including proprietary reverse mortgages, distribution efforts with traditional forward lenders and the potential for a broad marketing push to consumers.

“I think one of the things that’s held us back is our lack of distribution,” said Jim Cory, managing director of Guild Mortgage‘s reverse division. “It’s such a sea change in our business to suddenly have to go from this beloved group that we have here and begin adding to it. And literally thousands of loan originators now have access to this product.”

At a time when federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) have dropped to their lowest levels in about 10 years, private-label loans have stepped up to fill the void. Data compiled by New View Advisors showed that proprietary products accounted for 60% of all reverse mortgage volume in September 2026 — a share that is expected to continue growing.

Melissa Macerato, the newly appointed president and chief commercial officer at Longbridge Financial, said that these products have changed business for the better and that the industry would “be in a very different place” without them. Longbridge has been among the lenders to introduce private-label solutions in recent years through its Platinum suite and HELOC for Seniors.

Macerato said she expects to see more hybrid reverse mortgage products developed soon, with a focus on giving borrowers higher proceeds alongside mandatory but flexible payments.

“In order to get that broader distribution, in order to have more exposure for our products, we’re going to have to start speaking the language and developing products that more mainstream mortgage entities and loan officers really understand,” she said.

Jonathan Scarpati, chief production officer at Finance of America, told NRMLA attendees that the products “from 10 years ago are not reverse mortgages that everyone is selling today.” His company has also been at the forefront of product innovation with its HomeSafe suite — including a second-lien option that allows borrowers to tap into their home equity without touching their low-rate first mortgage.

But Scarpati believes that new products are meant to “cast a wider net” rather than replace the traditional HECM that’s been the industry’s cornerstone since the program was authorized in 1987. Mike Kent, senior vice president of corporate development and industry relations at Onity Mortgage, agreed.

“The reason we have proprietary products is that [the HECM] set the baseline, it set the standards, it ushered in the appropriate regulation and safeguards for the product, and it kind of cleared the way for us to begin to innovate,” Kent said.

Scarpati also pushed back against the notion that more competition in reverse mortgages is a bad thing.

“I think 2027 is a very pivotal moment for the industry in general,” he said. “I think as the products continue to evolve, some of them are looking closer to the forward industry. … The closer we have our products look to what the forward industry is used to, the more growth and the more adoption we’re going to get.”

Cory said that lack of distribution has been a longstanding obstacle for the industry. But many of the large independent mortgage banks (IMBs) — including Guild, Rate, Fairway Home Mortgage and CrossCountry Mortgage — now have a visible presence in the space. According to Cory, the six largest IMBs have about 17,000 originators today, and business would expand significantly if this group alone put more resources into reverse.

Jesse Allen, president of the 55+ lending division at Rate, said that while the largest IMBs have reverse mortgage options to offer borrowers, the ongoing hurdle is to get more engagement from loan officers. That work falls to reverse specialists, who must do a better job of sharing their knowledge and building relationships.

“If you want other people to trust you, you have to really know your craft,” Allen said. “Language matters. And so, as a reverse industry, I would encourage all of you to think about the language you use when you walk in with a traditional mortgage loan officer and a real estate agent. Use language that feels familiar to them and that will start to build trust.”

Some companies are introducing technology solutions to engage LOs who are unfamiliar with reverse products.

Earlier this month, Nationwide Equities Corp. launched ReverseReach, a tool to help uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in existing customer databases and referral networks. And in July, Reverse Market Insight expanded its loan qualification tool to include Smartfi Home Loans‘ proprietary products, part of Smartfi’s push to get more traditional LOs involved.

Scarpati said many lenders are looking for new opportunities as traditional purchase and refinance is expected to decline in 2027. Home equity lending, including reverse mortgages, presents a massive opportunity as U.S. homeowners hold roughly $35 trillion in equity, including $15 trillion among those 62 and older.

Lenders that don’t diversify beyond traditional products may find tough sledding if liquidity issues and consolidation continue over the next 12 to 18 months, he added.

“Originators are starving to find new opportunities to continue to succeed in mortgages in general. I think it just makes so much sense for a forward originator to start looking back at their client base,” Scarpati said. “We just have to continue to double down on education and technology to sort of help bridge that gap and make it easier for them to originate our loans.”

Audience member Melinda Hipp, a San Antonio-based Certified Reverse Mortgage Professional at Reverse Mortgage Authority, relayed some relevant information to the panelists on stage.

She said she recently recorded seven hours of conversations at two senior expos near San Antonio. People who passed by her booth frequently said they have no need for a reverse mortgage because their home is paid off, or that they “would never do that.” These comments feed into the laundry list of misunderstandings about the products.

While reverse mortgages often serve needs-based clients who want to access their home equity for repairs, healthcare expenses and other costs of living, their use cases also involve affluent clients who want better retirement tax strategies and cash-flow solutions.

The industry also continues to push for greater awareness of reverse for purchase transactions, which give seniors with large amounts of home equity a path to buy their next home without the burden of a monthly payment.

Hipp also suggested that the industry might look to do a broader advertising push, a reference to past efforts through celebrity spokespeople like Tom Selleck, Robert Wagner and others.

Allen offered his thoughts, saying that “marketing and messaging” is one of the industry’s “three big rocks” alongside product development and distribution. He said that any efforts through digital media or social media need to be different than what was done 10 years ago, since the addressable market has changed significantly.

“What’s the saying? ‘Many hands make light work.’ Well, many hands and it still won’t be light work,” Allen remarked. “We have to really figure out how to speak in a different way to the marketplace. … I think it has to be at an enterprise or an institutional level.”

If Dogecoin breaks through and holds above the resistance cluster of $0.075 to $0.080, it could pave the way toward the $0.12 to $0.15 range and, in a fully risk-on environment, possibly toward previous cycle highs.

Momentum indicators remain neutral to oversold on intermediate timeframes, suggesting significant potential for a sharp price increase once buying pressure returns.

In a true market frenzy driven by cultural narratives and structural mining support, measured moves and Fibonacci extensions from the multi-year base could project price levels well beyond previous peaks.

Combining the upcoming Litecoin halving dynamics, the early utility push from Dogecoin Labs and DogeOS, and Dogecoin’s unique cultural appeal creates favorable conditions for a potential extreme upside scenario, provided the right catalyst emerges and the broader crypto market supports it.

Dogecoin is now available on IOS for crypto payments.Massive move. pic.twitter.com/OBGux9JwY4

Away from the Claude AI Fable Doge price prediction, the Scrypt ecosystem’s mining economics reveal an underappreciated catalyst. Litecoin’s next halving is anticipated around late July 2027, reducing its block subsidy from 6.25 LTC to 3.125 LTC.

In contrast, Dogecoin maintains a fixed reward of 10,000 DOGE per block with no halving. As both networks share hashrate through merged mining, miners currently earn about 80-85% of their combined revenue from DOGE.

After the Litecoin halving, this percentage is expected to rise, making Dogecoin the primary economic incentive for miners using the Scrypt algorithm and strengthening network security.

The Dogecoin ecosystem also continues to evolve. In October 2026, the Dogecoin Foundation launched Dogecoin Labs, integrating the MyDoge wallet, the EVM-compatible DogeOS, and the Such App payments tool under one entity.

The DogeOS public testnet is live, enabling the development of DeFi, gaming, and consumer applications that utilize DOGE. These initiatives represent a significant effort to convert Dogecoin’s brand recognition into tangible utility.

Any traction in real payments or on-chain activity with DogeOS could bolster the perception of DOGE evolving beyond a mere meme.

Claude Fable Doge price prediction calls for Dogecoin to reach somewhere between $1.80 and $3.50, with a stretch case testing levels above $5.00 in the most euphoric version of this narrative, by January 1, 2027.

This remains a probability-weighted bullish outlook, not a certainty. Macro conditions, liquidity, and risk appetite will ultimately determine Dogecoin’s path.

#5525. Applied Materials posted record revenue, up 53%, topping expectations on AI chip demand

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The chip equipment maker expects fiscal first-quarter revenue of $11.1 billion, plus or minus $500 million

Applied Materials $AMAT reported record fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $10.41 billion on Thursday, up 53% from a year earlier, as demand for semiconductors tied to artificial intelligence grew, the company said.

Net income was $2.72 billion, or $3.40 a share, up 43% from a year earlier. Non-GAAP earnings per share reached a record $4.16, up 92%.

Analysts had forecast adjusted earnings of $4.06 a share and revenue of $10.30 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Semiconductor Systems revenue rose to $7.996 billion from $4.879 billion a year earlier. Foundry and logic made up 58% of the segment's revenue, DRAM 33% and flash memory 9%. Applied Global Services revenue was $1.896 billion, compared with $1.506 billion.

GAAP gross margin was 50.4% and non-GAAP gross margin was 50.6%, up 240 and 250 basis points from a year earlier, respectively.

"AI continues to fuel strong incremental demand for semiconductors," President and CEO Gary Dickerson said in a statement. He said Applied expects its Semiconductor Systems business to expand by more than 40% in calendar 2026, a period the company defines as running from the second quarter of fiscal 2026 through the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

For the fiscal year ended Oct. 25, revenue was a record $34.45 billion, up 21%. Non-GAAP earnings per share were a record $12.89, up 37%.

Cash from operations was a record $3.30 billion in the quarter. Applied returned $2.42 billion to shareholders, including $2.00 billion in share repurchases and $421 million in dividends. Chief Financial Officer Brice Hill said the buyback was the largest quarterly repurchase in more than eight years.

Applied expects first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $11.1 billion, plus or minus $500 million, and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share of $4.35, plus or minus 20 cents, the company said. Analysts had forecast $10.85 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $4.24 a share, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Applied scheduled an earnings call for 4:30 p.m. ET on Thursday.

#5524. Why QXO sees homebuilders as its mainstay of future growth

QXO wants to become a broader supplier to production and custom homebuilders, using cross-selling across building materials and installation. The company cited improved pricing, daily sales growth, and plans for procurement consolidation, private label expansion, and AI-enabled systems.  AI Summary

QXO, which aims to have $50 billion in annual revenue within the next several years, is counting on homebuilders as a launchpad for growth.

Chairman and CEO Brad Jacobs said Monday on a conference call that the company wants to supply builders with far more than lumber and trusses. QXO, which reports full Q3 2026 earnings after the market closes Thursday, has overhauled sales incentives, technology and pricing to become a primary supplier to production and custom builders.

The push follows its acquisitions of TopBuild and Kodiak Building Partners this year and Beacon Roofing Supply in 2025. Collectively, these acquisitions gave QXO exposure to a wide range of building products, including residential and commercial insulation, roofing materials, waterproofing, lumber and building materials, siding and exteriors, drywall and interior finishes, installation services, and tools and equipment such as fasteners, compressors and safety gear.

That broader footprint comes as the company’s core business is showing momentum. With $4.9 billion in combined revenue last quarter, the firm is well on its way to achieving Jacobs’ lofty annual revenue goal.

QXO, which generates roughly 50% of its revenue from residential construction, reported preliminary Q3 2026 results earlier this week showing organic revenue per day improved for the second consecutive quarter. Companywide pricing rose 2.2% year over year, with nine of 11 business areas posting positive pricing, and daily sales were up 5.4% year over year by the end of October.

Roofing and Waterproofing, QXO’s longest-held business after its April 2025 acquisition of Beacon Roofing Supply, grew daily sales 9.1%. Jacobs credited better on-time deliveries, invoice accuracy and inventory management for Beacon’s performance. Insulation was another strong performer, largely because of data center demand.

Beyond those gains, Jacobs said during the conference call that homebuilders represent a big growth opportunity. He outlined how QXO plans to capture more of their business, along with several ways QXO plans to grow in 2027.

During the call, Jacobs made it clear that QXO plans to cross-sell more to homebuilders, an important and growing customer segment.

“Our strong relationships with production homebuilders are typically rooted in our truss and wall panel capabilities, as well as insulation, where we solve some of their greatest needs. At the same time, it creates an opportunity for us to expand share of wallet by becoming their primary supplier for a wider range of building materials, with the added value of scale to support their growth,” Jacobs explained.

The company’s $17 billion acquisition of TopBuild, announced earlier this year, gave QXO an installation business with a presence at roughly 22,000 job sites every day. QXO, with an established distribution business, plans to leverage TopBuild’s installation services to supply more building materials, coordinate additional trades and manage more work and installations on individual job sites.

QXO’s $2.25 billion acquisition of Kodiak Building Partners, announced in February, additionally gave the firm exposure to building materials like lumber, engineered wood, doors, windows, trusses and gypsum products. These materials are essential to the company’s plans to sell more to Kodiak’s many existing homebuilder customers.

To incentivize cross-selling, Jacobs explained that QXO is changing its sales compensation structure to reward employees for selling customers a broader range of products across its businesses. Salespeople will have a financial incentive to introduce existing customers to other parts of QXO’s portfolio, including building materials and installation services.

“Homebuilders are a big opportunity,” Jacobs said. “One of the main reasons we bought Kodiak is that they brought phenomenal relationships with the big production homebuilders and the custom builders. And they were mainly selling them lumber or trusses or engineered products. So, we’re building on those great relationships, and we’re going to sell them much more. We’ve already started talking to many of these customers about this. There’s a lot of appetite for this.”

Cross-selling to homebuilders comprises just one focus area among QXO’s growth plans. Jacobs named five other areas where the company expects to improve margins and market share, including stronger supplier relationships, additional acquisitions, pricing improvements, smarter use of private-label products and technological improvements.

As QXO continues to integrate and improve its Beacon, Kodiak and TopBuild acquisitions, the combined company intends to leverage its larger scale in negotiations with suppliers.

The business has about $12 billion in combined spending, including about $11 billion in direct spending on products and materials. About $7.6 billion of that spending is with suppliers that serve at least two of QXO’s legacy businesses, including about $5 billion to suppliers serving all three.

QXO plans to consolidate its supplier base to capture that overlap, which could allow the company to push for better pricing and rebates and standardize purchasing agreements across the businesses.

“We want deep relationships with a smaller number of strategic supplier partners,” Jacobs said. “We want to be important partners with them and preferably their most important partner. And there’s quite a lot of overlap among the key suppliers across the three acquisitions we’ve recently done.”

If QXO strengthens its supplier relationships, its homebuilder clients could see better product availability and service, making the company a more appealing primary supplier for builders, particularly as it expands its offerings through additional acquisitions.

Jacobs sees additional acquisitions as a key way to expand its product portfolio, customer base and geographic reach. Following its blockbuster acquisition of TopBuild, QXO is now eyeing smaller, highly accretive acquisitions, but Jacobs did not identify specific acquisition targets or product categories.

Any future acquisitions could add complementary building-material categories, installation capabilities or regional relationships, all of which could support QXO’s push to become a primary homebuilding supplier and deepen QXO’s reach with builders.

QXO’s leadership changes also signal that it continues to eye acquisitions. On Thursday, the company named Dev Ahuja its next CFO, effective in January, succeeding Ihsan Essaid, who will become Vice Chairman. Essaid brings M&A experience from Novelis, where he helped complete and integrate the $2.8 billion Aleris acquisition.

During the call, Jacobs described pricing as one of QXO’s largest company-specific levers for expanding profitability. The company is moving to data-driven pricing based on demand, elasticity, inventory, fulfillment and customer profitability. Better service and availability, he said, can give QXO room to charge more, but the goal is value-based pricing, not blanket price increases.

“I’m not just talking about raising prices; it’s optimizing prices. I think we’re on a good trajectory to getting price where it needs to be, and I think we have an excellent pricing team,” Jacobs explained.

For homebuilders, a broader product and services offering could make QXO a more valuable supplier. However, the company also signaled that it is eyeing strategic price increases, and its expanding offerings, market share and value could give it the leverage to do just that.

QXO launched its private-label brand TRI-BUILT in 2024 and is now actively trying to grow the brand’s sales. Because it’s an original brand, it has stronger gross profit margins – about 2,000 basis points higher – than comparable branded products.

TRI-BUILT accounted for a record 10.6% of Roofing and Waterproofing sales in the third quarter, all from Beacon. QXO wants to expand the brand into more product categories and grow sales to more than $2 billion over the next three years, while also extending private-label offerings across Kodiak and TopBuild.

To support the push, QXO is redesigning sales incentives to encourage employees to sell more private-label products, and the company’s new compensation structure will also reward salespeople for selling private-label products.

QXO is integrating its acquired businesses into a connected technology platform that includes a new ERP, point-of-sale system, warehouse management system and AI-enabled CRM. The systems are meant to make it easier for customers to check inventory, receive quotes, place orders and track deliveries.

“When this is fully rolled out, our employees will be able to get their work done in one connected, AI-enabled environment. They’ll spend less time entering the same information into different systems or tracking down information that will be readily available. The new ecosystem will give our people more capacity to serve customers and run the business,” Jacobs explained.

The public can get a fuller look at whether these strategies are already translating into results when QXO reports full third-quarter earnings after the market closes Thursday.

#5522. AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment

LangChain Inc., a startup with a set of popular open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG fund led the round. It was joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. LangChain is now worth $3 billion.

San Francisco-based LangChain is best known for the eponymous open-source framework it released in 2022. The software reduces the amount of work involved in building AI agents. LangChain makes it relatively simple to connect an AI agent to a large language model, integrate it with tools and add a system prompt. The framework also enables developers to customize details such as the format of prompt responses.

LangChain’s second open-source tool, LangGraph, is designed for situations where a task is too complicated to be automated by a single agent. LangGraph can link together multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single automation workflow. It can also add in other elements such as a mechanism that requires humans to approve sensitive actions.

The third component of LangChain’s open-source portfolio is Deep Agents. It extends LangChain and  LangGraph with features that make it easier for agents to perform complex work. There’s a virtual file system in which agents can keep data, a work planning tool and a subagent generation feature.

LangChain generates revenue with a suite of paid products called LangSmith. Developers can use it to not only build agents but also to maintain them once they’re in production.

An AI agent usually goes through multiple iterations before it’s released to users. LangSmith enables software teams to save those iterations in a centralized repository. If an update introduces a bug into an agent’s code base, developers can use LangSmith to quickly restore an earlier, bug-free version. Furthermore, they can compare the output quality of different agent versions to identify the one that should be deployed to production.

LangSmith also includes a set of observability features. It generates traces, logs that describe every single step of the workflow through an agent processed a prompt. LangSmith analyzes those traces to find technical issues. From there, it prioritizes them based on their severity and generates code fixes.

After its previous funding round last year, LangChain disclosed that its open-source tools were being downloaded about 90 million times per month. Its LangSmith suite, in turn, is used by Autodesk Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and a long list of other tech firms.

LangChain reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. The company will hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers.

#5521. Builders are looking for a bottom. 2027 plans can’t wait that long

Builders are balancing incentives, margins, and cash recovery as resale inventory rises and rental options improve. Key signals include a 5.5% drop in existing-home sales, 5.1 months of supply, and widespread builder discounting.  AI Summary

We’re at that agonizing moment in a housing market downturn when finding “the bottom” becomes the first next thing to hope for.

The trouble is, market bottoms tend to reveal themselves only in the 20/20 clarity of hindsight, not in any set of measures we can confidently decipher in the present.

For America’s homebuilders, residential developers and investors, this creates an uncomfortable predicament. They’re not just competing with the clock. They’re competing with other parts of the residential continuum –rentals and resales – that are also competing with the clock. They must make decisions that will determine their performance in 2027 before they know whether the worst is behind them.

Decisions, for instance, like how much to build, where to commit capital, what prices will move homes, and what sales pace will sustain profitability.

The evidence accumulating as 2026 nears year-end offers little or no assurance that the housing market has found solid footing. Weakening household demand, rising competition in the resale market, increasingly attractive rental alternatives, and persistent uncertainty about employment, incomes, and home values are making it harder to balance pricing and sales pace sustainably.

The question for builders is not whether they can predict the precise moment the market turns. It is whether they can adapt their businesses to current conditions, preserve financial and operating flexibility to withstand further weakness, and position themselves to benefit when household demand eventually stabilizes.

The latest evidence points to a market that is still losing momentum

Thursday’s report from the National Association of Realtors offered another indication of the challenges facing the housing market. Existing-home sales fell 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, down 8.8% from a year earlier and the weakest reading since August 2010.

The number of existing homes for sale increased to 1.59 million, up 4.6% from October 2025. At the current sales pace, that represented 5.1 months of supply, compared with 4.4 months a year earlier and the highest level since November 2015.

The national median existing-home price, meanwhile, rose just 0.4% from a year earlier to $416,700. That combination of declining transactions, rising months’ supply and relatively stable reported prices illustrates a housing market in which buyers and sellers have yet to agree on home values under prevailing financing and economic conditions.

Telling data points came through in this analysis, breaking out trends that speak to a softening market:

The numbers reveal a critical point of distinction. A rising months’ supply does not necessarily mean homeowners are flooding the market with listings. It can result from sales falling faster than inventory is being absorbed. Both dynamics are relevant to builders, whose homes compete with an increasing selection of existing properties for buyers.

The latest data offer little encouragement to builders expecting a quick rebound in household demand. The National Association of Home Builders reported that September new-home sales fell to a 676,000-unit annual pace, 5.3% below the year-earlier level, while the supply of new homes for sale remained elevated at 8.4 months.

The October NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index fell to 29, its lowest level since June 2012. Forty-three percent of builders reported cutting prices, while 65% continued to offer sales incentives.

Those findings point to a persistent problem for homebuilding companies: Builders continue to make meaningful concessions to stimulate sales, but households’ response remains insufficient to establish confidence in a sustained recovery.

Mortgage rates remain an important constraint, but the industry’s demand problem is increasingly difficult to explain through financing costs alone.

Cotality Chief Economist Dr. Selma Hepp points to the cumulative financial pressures facing prospective buyers. Elevated mortgage payments, tariff-related construction costs, insurance premiums, property taxes, utilities, and everyday household expenses are affecting households’ ability and willingness to take on the obligations of ownership.

“For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market,” Hepp says.

Her observation highlights a sharp difference between qualifying for a mortgage and deciding that buying a home makes financial sense.

A household may technically qualify for a mortgage yet still find that the monthly payment, down payment, and ongoing ownership costs leave too little room for savings, unexpected expenses, or other financial commitments. For households concerned about job security or declining home values, waiting may seem increasingly prudent.

The broader economy complicates that calculation. Higher-income households with substantial savings, accumulated home equity, or financial assets may be able to absorb elevated housing costs, whereas entry-level and middle-income households have far less flexibility.

That unevenness helps explain why a national decline in mortgage rates might boost sales only modestly. Some prospective buyers need lower monthly payments. Others need greater confidence that their incomes will remain secure, that their other living expenses will stabilize, and that the home they purchase will retain its value. These concerns are not necessarily resolved by a builder’s offer of a temporary mortgage-rate buydown.

The Federal Reserve’s latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey underscores the demand problem. Banks reported weaker demand across all residential mortgage categories in the third quarter, even as lending standards remained largely unchanged for most mortgage products. Banks also reported weaker demand and tighter lending standards for construction and land development loans.

The implications extend beyond individual homebuyers. When expected sales absorption weakens, the financial justification for developing additional lots, opening communities, and committing construction capital becomes more difficult.

One of the most important changes in homebuilding’s competitive environment has been the reversal of several conditions that supported new-home demand during the pandemic and its aftermath.

During that period, builders benefited from an unusually tight existing-home market. Homeowners who had secured historically low mortgage rates had little incentive to sell, limiting resale inventory and directing prospective buyers toward new construction.

At the same time, elevated rents in many markets made homeownership relatively more attractive. Builders with available lots, construction capacity, and mortgage financing relationships were positioned to capture buyers with fewer alternatives.

The appeal of renting is not limited to households that cannot afford to buy. For some households, renting lets them keep their savings, preserve geographic flexibility, and avoid the risk of buying a home before local prices have stabilized.

Existing homes are also becoming more formidable competitors. In markets where resale listings have increased and homes are taking longer to sell, prospective buyers can compare new construction with a wider selection of existing properties. Sellers who need to relocate, settle estates, or complete other transactions may be increasingly willing to negotiate.

Builders therefore face a three-way competitive challenge that was less pronounced during the pandemic-era housing boom. They must compete against other builders, existing-home sellers and rental operators, each offering a different mix of price, location, amenities, monthly cost and financial commitment.

This competition is especially intense in markets where builders have substantial inventories of completed homes and developed lots. A resale seller may have the financial flexibility to postpone a transaction, whereas a builder must continue to carry land, construction, financing and overhead costs until inventory converts to cash.

This pressure can prompt builders to adjust their effective prices sooner than many existing-home sellers. Yet lower new-home prices can also influence resale sellers’ expectations, triggering another round of competitive adjustments. The process may continue for some time before either market reaches a sustainable balance.

For builders, the most immediate challenge is determining how much pricing flexibility is needed to maintain sales velocity without sacrificing the profitability required to sustain their businesses. Reducing prices and offering incentives may increase orders, but those measures can also erode gross margins and reduce returns on capital already committed to land and construction. Maintaining prices may protect reported margins on individual transactions, but it can leave completed homes on the market longer, increase carrying costs, and delay the recovery of invested capital.

Neither approach necessarily produces a better outcome without understanding the relationships among sales pace, effective pricing, inventory costs and cash generation.

The problem becomes more difficult when household demand continues to weaken. Pricing decisions that seem sufficient to generate sales in one month may need to be reconsidered the next as competing builders adjust incentives, resale sellers lower expectations, or rental operators offer more attractive terms.

The industry’s challenge is therefore to find a lower price at which buyers will purchase homes and to determine whether homes can be produced, marketed, and sold at that price while still generating acceptable returns. Not one or the other, both. That distinction directly impacts 2027 budgets.

A community that achieves an acceptable gross margin with three sales per month may generate inadequate returns if absorption drops to one or two sales. Conversely, a lower-margin community that turns inventory quickly and requires less capital may outperform one with stronger nominal margins but slower cash recovery.

These tradeoffs will vary by market, product type, land basis, construction costs, and financing structure. A single national assumption about mortgage rates or home-price appreciation cannot resolve them.

The industry’s search for a bottom should not become a reason to postpone decisions about how businesses will operate if demand remains weak. Instead, the uncertainty should drive builders to test their 2027 plans against a broader range of outcomes, including scenarios in which conditions deteriorate further before improving.

The first priority is a more precise understanding of household purchasing power and competing housing alternatives in each community’s trade area.

Builders need to know not only which prospective customers qualify to purchase, but also what they are willing to pay when comparing a new home with available resales and rental properties. That analysis should include the full monthly cost of ownership, the incentives required to attract buyers, and the potential impact of additional competing supply.

The second priority is reassessing land commitments, community-opening schedules, and construction starts.

Projects approved under stronger demand assumptions may no longer meet their original return requirements. Builders should evaluate whether development schedules can be phased, whether lot deliveries can be adjusted, and whether to defer capital commitments until sales absorption justifies additional investment.

The third priority is to maintain the financial and operational flexibility to respond when conditions change.

That means closely monitoring completed-home inventory, construction cycle times, cancellation rates, financing costs, and cash recovery. It also means identifying opportunities to reduce product and construction costs rather than relying indefinitely on incentives to bridge the gap between household purchasing power and home prices.

These are practical operational decisions, not substitutes for a stronger housing market. They can, however, determine how much financial strain a builder faces while waiting for demand to stabilize. They may also determine which companies are positioned to invest as better opportunities emerge.

Hepp identifies the upcoming spring selling season as an important test of whether housing activity can begin to recover.

“Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner,” she says.

Homebuilders cannot control when household demand stabilizes. They can control how quickly they recognize market changes, how effectively they adjust their cost structures and capital commitments, and how well they prepare their businesses for conditions that may remain difficult longer than expected.

The bottom will become clear in hindsight. The work of getting through it – and of emerging stronger – waits for no one.

#5520. A Democratic senator wants Congress to assess if Nvidia is 'too big to fail'

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Sen. Jack Reed wants analysis of how a possible Nvidia failure would hit U.S. banks and credit markets after CEO Jensen Huang resigned

Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, is asking Congress to examine whether Nvidia $NVDA counts as “too big to fail” and what a collapse at the chipmaker could mean for U.S. banks and credit markets, according to Reuters.

Reed said on Thursday that Nvidia “has backstopped the AI ecosystem through complex financing transactions.” He called for more disclosure about those deals.

"We need full transparency into these deals, an assessment of whether the company is 'too big to fail,' and an analysis of how these events may affect the U.S. banking system and credit markets," Reed said.

"Millions of Americans also have economic exposure to Nvidia through their retirement accounts and pension funds," Reed said.

AI-linked stocks traded lower around the world on Thursday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company.

Huang resigned as CEO and as a board member on Thursday, the company said in a statement. Nvidia stock was down about 10% after the opening bell, and it had fallen by more than a fifth over the past month.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor. Harvey C. Jones, a former Synopsys $SNPS leader, becomes Nvidia's first board chair and will direct the search, which will consider internal and external candidates, the company said.

Huang's departure followed reports of two extramarital affairs. He admitted to infidelity in a note to employees on Sunday.

Nvidia’s revenue for fiscal 2026 reached $215.9 billion, up 702% from $26.9 billion in fiscal 2022. The company is set to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

#5519. Leading AI Models Still Missing Critical Details When Giving Financial Advice, New Research Finds

New benchmarks from Vals AI and NextLadder Ventures, advised by the Financial Health Network, tested 28 AI models across 256 simulated financial counseling scenarios involving eviction, medical debt and other challenges facing low-income families.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, Vals AI and NextLadder Ventures released a new benchmark analysis examining general-purpose AI models' performance in providing financial advice in high-stakes scenarios often faced by low-income Americans, compared against best practices identified by financial counseling experts. The evaluation tested 28 models across 256 simulated financial counseling scenarios developed with practicing financial counselors.

The benchmarks are part of a broader effort spearheaded by NextLadder Ventures to accelerate the development of AI tools tailored to the unique needs and challenges facing low-income Americans navigating fork-in-the-road moments with disproportionate impact on their economic mobility.

"Every day, millions of Americans are struggling to make ends meet on tight budgets without much guidance or support," said Ryan Rippel, CEO of NextLadder Ventures. "Effective financial guidance that helps families make sense of their unique circumstances with reliable, tailored recommendations can make a world of difference. But too little of that guidance is available to low-income families, and the counselors who do work with these families are wildly over-stretched. AI-powered financial health tools have monumental potential to make a real dollars-in-pockets difference for low-income families, but far too many gaps remain in the general-purpose models that most people turn to today. We should not accept that the true measure of success for leading AI models means shattering the frontiers of mathematics, but not whether they can do the kitchen table math that faces tens of millions of families. It's our hope that these benchmarks will provide unbiased and actionable insights on how to make these tools better equipped to help low-income Americans move up the economic ladder."

"I'm optimistic that AI can make useful financial guidance available to more people," said Rayan Krishnan, Vals AI's cofounder and CEO. "Our evaluation shows there is still work to do. Models sometimes gave advice without understanding someone's circumstances, missed important deadlines or failed to connect them with available help. Independent evaluation makes those gaps visible and gives developers a way to measure whether their systems are becoming more reliable."

Vals AI worked with practicing financial counselors to develop 256 test scenarios drawn from the questions people bring to financial counselors. Twenty-eight AI models were tested in the role of financial counselor between September 14 and October 12, 2026. A second AI played the client and disclosed key facts, including income, debts, deadlines, family size, only when the counselor asked about them. Each of the 7,167 completed conversations (one per model per scenario) was scored against a checklist developed by financial counseling practitioners. An AI model did the grading; on practitioner-graded checklist items, it agreed 85% of the time.

The benchmark tested models from 11 developers: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Terra; Google's Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite; Meta's Muse Spark 1.2, Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Spark 1.3 Max, Wonder and Wonder Full; Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1; xAI's Grok 4.7; DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash; Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 Max; Moonshot AI's Kimi K3; Zhipu AI's GLM 5.3; Xiaomi's MiMo V2.6 Pro; and MiniMax's MiniMax-M3. Each model was tested directly at its standard settings, outside the consumer apps that run on it. The results measure model performance in simulated conversations, rather than the complete experience offered by consumer apps.

#5518. Exclusive: ARA forms AI Task Force to back licensee-in-the-loop laws

The American Real Estate Association launched an AI Task Force, chaired by Dmitriy Kruglyak, to advocate licensee-in-the-loop rules. The group plans white papers and state-by-state outreach to require licensed supervision of AI actions in real estate transactions.  AI Summary

The American Real Estate Association (ARA) has launched an AI Task Force focused on advocating for and advancing “Licensee-in-the-Loop” legislation in all 50 states.

Jason Haber, a co-founder of ARA along with The Agency’s Mauricio Umansky, said the legislative effort was inspired by a contributor article published on HousingWire by Dmitriy Kruglyak, a self-described software engineer turned real estate broker. In the piece, Kruglyak argues that the growing use of agentic AI in real estate could put consumers at risk by allowing unlicensed automated systems to perform tasks traditionally handled by licensed agents, including negotiating contracts and guiding transactions.

“I think this could be the defining issue for our industry in 2027,” Haber told HousingWire. “I read Dmitry’s oped and I was glued. I immediately understood the implications of what he was writing about. It struck me as a gigantic red flag in our industry and no one was talking about it.”

Haber said Kruglyak is now chairing ARA’s AI Task Force, which will be meeting for the first time in the coming weeks. The group will work on white papers focused on the issue, along with AI policy analysis and advocacy, with “licensee-in-the-loop” being the first issue the group will focus on.

“AI has no fiduciary, it holds no license, it has no errors and omission insurance and when something goes wrong, there is no real estate board to file an ethics complaint with,” Haber said. “So what happens is you have a consumer that has no idea how the AI model has been trained. For example, maybe it has been trained to benefit the seller and not the buyer so it convinces a buyer to make a higher offer.”

However, if a real estate licensee is involved, the whole situation changes, Haber said. ARA views “licensee-in-the-loop legislation as a guarantee that anyone who buys, sells or rents a home has a licensed, accountable real estate professional standing behind the transaction.

“We’re saying, if you have an act performed by an automated system on behalf of the consumer for a real estate transaction, it has to be supervised by a responsible licensee that’s identifiable to the consumer with a name and license. And, before any offer goes in or counter offers are transmitted, it’s really reviewed by someone who holds a license and that the autonomous system is backed by the licensees fiduciary responsibilities to a client,” Haber said.

He said ARA views this as the responsible way to embrace AI technology, as it enables consumers to hold someone accountable if something goes wrong in their transaction. Although the share of consumers buying or selling their home solely with the help of an AI model or an AI real estate agent product is still the minority, Haber said he believes the industry will see more of these AI real estate agent platforms popping up in the next year, which is why he feels it is important for ARA to get ahead of the issue.

“We are looking to future proof for the consumer in the industry,” he said. “We see this coming and we want to have regulatory and statutory framework in place so that we don’t have to react after the consumer has been harmed. So, we think by moving now we are in a better position.”

Haber also noted that these efforts take time, especially because there are no federal real estate licensing laws. Due to this, Haber said ARA is going state-by-state talking to legislators regarding this issue in hopes that they will be willing to introduce this legislation in their state.

“We are tapping our state association chairs and working with our federal lobbyist to connect us with elected officials around the country,” Haber said. “It is going to take some time and just getting one bill through one state is Herculean enough, but now we are trying to take this already very challenging thing and do it 50 times.”

While Haber acknowledges that this will be a tall order, he believes it is a great opportunity for ARA to show what it is doing to help agents and American consumers at a national level.

“I think it is going to be interesting to see how it plays out, it is a long process, but we think we will have legislation introduced as early as the end of the year or early January in some states,” Haber said.

#5517. Microsoft stock slips as global outage knocks out Outlook, Teams, and Copilot

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Microsoft said it has no indication the outage stems from malicious activity as it works to repair affected infrastructure

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Microsoft $MSFT stock slid 2% before the open on Friday while the company raced to bring services back online following a global disruption of Outlook, Teams and Copilot.

Microsoft's service health page said users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services. The page listed service degradation for Microsoft 365 business and enterprise products and for consumer products. Microsoft posted the information there because administrators may be unable to reach the admin center for service health details.

The stock is heading toward its weakest closing level since Nov. 2 and its poorest weekly showing since the week that ended July 24, according to MarketWatch.

Microsoft reported in a Friday update that the disruption touches many Microsoft 365 products tied to Exchange Online and email, according to The Associated Press. Users reported that Outlook, Teams and Copilot were down, the AP said.

Microsoft said it has no indication that malicious activity caused the outage and is using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure,” according to the AP. The company said in an earlier post that the adjustments it rolled out to boost serviceability were “not taking as expected,” the AP said. A more recent Friday update said, “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.”

Roughly 130,000 users reported problems accessing Outlook on Thursday, according to the AP, citing the outage tracker Downdetector. New reports have dwindled since that high point. Microsoft says its Microsoft 365 apps have a user base exceeding 430 million.

Workhorse Group pushed back its quarterly earnings call as a result of the outage, according to the AP. Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government emails were down. The Philippines' Supreme Court said the outage affected some operations, including email responses. Japan's government said the outage affected its IT infrastructure and that it secured alternative tools such as telephones.

IndiGo said the outage disrupted its email support services but not flight operations. Air India said its flights were unaffected and that it temporarily rerouted email services. OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, according to the AP.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke of Australia said Microsoft had likened the outage to the 2024 CrowdStrike $CRWD incident. "They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack," Burke told reporters in Sydney, according to the AP. He said Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar to an update that "has gone awry."

The decline follows a rally in which Microsoft stock climbed as high as $551.13 in mid-October, approaching its first record since October 2025. The stock was up about 14% for 2026 at that point.

#5516. Surging AI chip revenue and Microsoft deal boost Cerebras Systems stock by 17%

Artificial intelligence chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc. delivered third-quarter revenue that comfortably beat expectations in its latest financial report today while announcing a new deal with Microsoft Corp., sending its stock up almost 18% in late trading.

The company reported a loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of 67 cents per share, trailing Wall Street’s guidance of a 14-cent-per-share loss, though because of some accounting idiosyncrasies, its numbers are not directly comparable with that guidance. Meanwhile, core adjusted revenue for the period came to $230.9 million, up 70% from a year earlier and surpassing the Street’s target of $214.7 million.

The adjustments in Cerebras’ revenue are the result of some of the quirks in its accounting procedures. The company includes some pass-through revenue that’s subtracted from the total, and it also issues warrants to its major customers, which are then amortized as noncash reductions in revenue based on standard accounting rules, and so these are left out of the adjusted number.

Despite these complexities, investors were clearly impressed with the company’s growth over the quarter, and perhaps even more so by its progress toward profitability. Though Cerebras has not been able to show a profit yet, its adjusted operating margin of -14% was still significantly better than its earlier guidance of -24% from three months earlier.

Chief Executive Andrew Feldman (pictured) told analysts on a conference call that the company has an advantage over its competitors, which are struggling to keep up with customer demand and dealing with growing order backlogs. “I think there is opportunity created, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us,” he said, referring to Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units.

Cerebras does have a significant backlog for both hardware and cloud services itself, and that number rose from $25 billion in August to $26 billion at the end of the quarter. However, a significant portion of that backlog is related to the deal it struck with OpenAI Group PBC, Feldman said. This implies that other customers don’t have to wait so long for their orders to be processed.

Meanwhile, the chipmaker continues to expand its customer base. After recently signing deals with Amazon Web Services Inc. and Oracle Corp., the company today announced a new customer in Microsoft Corp., although it didn’t provide many particulars about that agreement. The small increase in its backlog doesn’t do much to settle concerns that all of those deals are on the small side, however.

“We believe revenue begins to show up in quarter one of fiscal 2027,” Feldman said after explaining that the agreement with Microsoft was signed and sealed a month earlier.

Feldman also explained that the company is now evaluating its financing options to find ways to meet customer demand and make inroads into its order backlog. It’s not clear what that financing will look like, as capital has become much harder to secure in recent months amid growing nervousness about the insane amounts of cash being spent on AI infrastructure buildouts.

Cerebras may perhaps be able to benefit from the uncertainty at its biggest rival Nvidia, which still dominates the AI chip industry, accounting for over 90% of all chip sales, according to some analysts.

Nvidia is in turmoil following the shocking resignation of its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s believed that Huang was likely forced to hand in his resignation after being outed for having an affair with an executive of a Singapore-based data center infrastructure firm, who is believed to have been acting as a spy for Chinese intelligence and a conduit for illegal shipments of GPUs into that country. Huang also had a second affair with one of Nvidia’s executives, according to reports that emerged yesterday, and reportedly a third one too.

It may take a while for Cerebras and other chipmakers to take advantage of the disruption to Nvidia, which is seeking to maintain stability through the appointment of longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO, but in the short term its prospects still look good. The company said it anticipates a core gross margin of 47% to 49% in the fourth quarter, with revenue rising to between $310 million and $330 million. Wall Street analysts are looking for a core gross margin of just 42.1% on sales of $271 million.

Moreover, Feldman told analysts on the call that the company believes its revenue will triple by the end of fiscal 2027. If that holds true, it would mean full-year revenue of around $2.85 billion, slightly below Wall Street’s long-term forecast of $2.92 billion in fiscal 2027.

NOIDA, India and SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest), the Agentic AI Quality Engineering platform, today released the State of AI in Quality Engineering 2026 report. It finds that 81% of software teams have merged AI-generated code or tests they did not fully understand, and 44% report more escaped defects or production incidents as AI-written code has grown. AI now writes much of the code and many of the tests, yet most teams still verify that work with a person after the fact, or with another AI model.

97% of teams surveyed now use AI in testing or plan to. For most of them, the open question is how AI-generated code and tests get verified before they ship.

Key findings from the State of AI in Quality Engineering 2026 report:

"Software teams now rely on AI to write their code, generate their tests, and increasingly determine whether both are ready to ship. Verification, however, has not kept pace with that shift. We believe any output AI produces should be validated by a system independent of the model that produced it, before it merges and every time it changes. The teams in our survey that already follow this discipline see fewer defects reach production, and we expect it to become the standard for engineering organizations shipping with AI", said Asad Khan, Co-founder and CEO of TestMu AI

#5514. California cities get firm notice: follow new housing laws, or else

California housing fights are increasingly happening before a vote, with nonprofits sending letters that cite HAA, density bonus law, and CEQA reforms. The goal is to warn officials and create a record that can be used if a city rejects or reduces a project.  AI Summary

A 135-townhome project cleared the Rancho Cucamonga Planning Commission on Tuesday on the planning department’s recommendation.

That is the outcome state reforms are meant to produce: more housing, including affordable units. Warmington Residential Homes’ project includes seven for very-low-income households. Still, the meeting showed how these disputes now run. Before a decision, a pro-housing nonprofit reminds the city to follow the law, creating a record it can cite if officials ignore the warning.

In Rancho Cucamonga, the California Housing Defense Fund sent a three-page letter citing the Housing Accountability Act, the state Density Bonus Law and last year’s California Environmental Quality Act reform. Rejecting the project or cutting its size, it warned, would require written findings of a specific health or safety hazard.

The Rancho Cucamonga letter was one of at least five CalHDF sent that day, along with letters to Santa Clarita, Whittier, Escondido and Twentynine Palms. Four concerned projects of 17 to 146 units. One addressed an ADU ordinance.

Those letters are a fraction of the total. James Lloyd, the organization’s director of planning and investigations, told HousingWire the number reaches about 100 a year.

They serve as a first step toward making sure cities implement state housing reforms properly, according to the organization.

Broadly, the letters pair legal warnings with a pitch to local officials: new housing helps a city’s finances and existing residents while meeting the state’s need for more homes.

“While no one project will solve the statewide housing crisis, the proposed development is a step in the right direction,” the organization writes.

Lawmakers have spent years trying to speed housing construction to improve affordability. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 130 to reform CEQA and SB 131 in 2025, exempting qualifying infill housing from environmental review and narrowing review for projects that nearly qualify. Legislators also tightened the Housing Accountability Act, which limits when cities can deny or shrink projects that meet zoning.

Neighbor suits have not disappeared. They have shifted to different arguments. Attorneys at the legal publisher CEB expect litigation to focus on whether a project qualifies for a CEQA exemption at all, rather than on the adequacy of an environmental report.

Builders and advocates pose a growing risk for cities that resist state law. Cities frequently lose when they test the rules in court, and the losses can be costly. Under Senate Bill 1037, penalties can reach $50,000 per unit for willful Housing Accountability Act violations.

La Cañada Flintridge refused to process a builder’s remedy project. A judge ruled against the city in March 2024, and the city dropped its appeal a year later rather than post a $14 million bond. It paid CalHDF $1,262,500 in fees and costs last year.

A small project in Pacifica shows the stakes. Neighbors sued over an eight-townhome project, arguing it needed a full environmental impact report instead of the lighter review the city used.

A trial court sided with them, rescinded the approvals and awarded nearly $1.3 million in attorney’s fees. In December 2025, an appeals court vacated the fee award, saying the judge had wrongly discounted the project’s housing value. It sent the question back to the trial court.

But when it came to a recommendation, staff tracked the laws CalHDF cited. They wrote in their staff report that the project qualified for waivers under the state density bonus law, which limits when a city can deny them. Staff also noted the project was exempt from environmental review under CEQA guidelines.

#5513. Texas's incoming attorney general vows to scrutinize a SpaceX-Tesla merger

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nathan Johnson, who takes office in January, said he has no qualms about examining Elon Musk's ties to the state

Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson vowed to scrutinize any merger between Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla $TSLA, the state's two highest-valued companies, he told Bloomberg on Thursday.

"Any merger of companies of that consequence warrants tremendous scrutiny," Johnson said, according to Bloomberg. He would not get into details about a possible SpaceX-Tesla combination.

SpaceX and Tesla are progressing in merger negotiations and could announce a deal as soon as December, with an announcement in early 2027 also under discussion, according to Bloomberg. The deal would be the biggest ever, and the combined company would span carmaking, battery storage for energy, and rocket and satellite businesses. SpaceX is valued at over $1.9 trillion, and Tesla's valuation is roughly $1.5 trillion. SpaceX and Tesla had not responded to requests for comment from Bloomberg.

Johnson said Musk has benefited from his ties to the Republican Party. "I think he's received a great deal of deference due to his alignment with the Republican Party and the tons of money he spent for the Republican Party," Johnson said, according to Bloomberg. "I have no qualms about examining his relationships to the state."

"I don't want anybody to have such control of the public sector that they can bend public power to their private gain," Johnson said of Musk. "I think his empire is at great risk of crossing that line."

Johnson said neither he nor his transition team has contacted Musk. "If Elon wants to talk, we can talk," he said.

Johnson, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa and Sen.-elect James Talarico have pledged to rein in Musk’s influence, according to Bloomberg. Democrats, who will control Congress starting in January, have promised to investigate Musk’s dealings in both business and politics.

Johnson will take office in January. He has promised to focus on the "nuts and bolts" of the office, including consumer protection and antitrust litigation, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla and SpaceX stock extended a selloff last week after Democrats won majorities in both houses of Congress and key offices in Texas. Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott $ABT in the governor's race. Musk's election spending totaled at least $474 million, including $224 million in Texas, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Abbott lost.
