#5488. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5487. Baldwin Group CEO: The biggest AI disruption in insurance is the advisor

Artificial intelligence is going to disrupt insurance brokerage. There is not much question about that. The question that matters is what gets disrupted, and how differently firms are preparing for it.

Most firms are approaching AI the way they approached every prior wave of technology: take the work as it exists and do it faster. But AI is dramatically changing the economics of gathering information, comparing coverage and facilitating transactions. A firm whose value lives in those activities is competing in a race to the bottom.

A firm built on specialized expertise, deep client relationships and experiential human judgment can change the paradigm, turning risk into opportunity for clients. Firms that make that leap go from being a vendor of downside protection to a business partner that helps a client achieve the fullness of their ambition. Their value becomes constrained only by what their clients can achieve.

Showing up that way requires the fortitude to completely rebuild how the work gets done. At Baldwin, alongside our partners at Dell Family Office and Sequence Holdings, we have launched into that journey. We call it Refounding.

Consider a middle-market renewal: gather exposure data, prepare the submission, market it, compare quotes, build the proposal, and present. Weeks of cycle time, most of it waiting on the next hand-off. Apply AI to each step and you compress each one a little. Redesign the work around what AI does well and you compress the entire cycle, and you hand the recovered time back to the client advisor for the only parts a client will pay a premium for: understanding the business, anticipating what could go wrong and structuring solutions that unlock potential.

That is the work underway through Catalyst, our firm-wide transformation program. Over 17 weeks, we completed more than 47,000 AI-assisted tasks at quality rates above 98 percent while standardizing 27 processes in our Client Experience teams. Those numbers matter only for what they free up: capacity redeployed into advisory work, not simply banked as cost savings.

Three things happen when you make that shift. Cycle times compress meaningfully. Throughput rises because the same team carries more complexity. And complex knowledge work gets sharper. In one early claims-review application, AI identified coverage gaps in minutes that led to $71,000 in additional claim payment for a client. A professional still had to evaluate what the technology surfaced and decide what to do. That is the model: technology ingests and processes; the human provides the judgment; and experienced professionals remain accountable for every decision that carries real financial consequences for a client.

AI drives the marginal cost of information toward zero, and when information is free, the premium shifts to what you do with it. Clients will have more data than ever. What they will not have is someone who has seen 200 versions of their problem, who knows which carrier will actually show up when a claim is contested, and who will tell them the uncomfortable truth about a coverage gap before the loss rather than after. That is judgment, earned through experience. The relationship that lets a client hear that perspective and act on it with conviction is earned the same way.

It is also why insurance advice has to move earlier in the conversation. Too often, insurance enters the discussion after the consequential decisions about risk have been made. With AI compressing the mechanics, the best advisors will move upstream into the room where those decisions happen, helping clients understand how risk affects their investments, their capital and their growth. That is where the advisor’s value was always supposed to live. The transactional work got in the way.

For generations, early-career insurance professionals built judgment by doing the foundational work: reviewing policies, preparing submissions and sitting beside experienced colleagues. That apprenticeship was never efficient, but it worked. AI will eliminate the tasks it is built on. Remove those tasks and do nothing else, and we will produce a generation of advisors who can operate the tools but cannot challenge them. Judgment comes from working through hard situations, seeing the consequences of decisions and learning from people who have been there before. We have to redesign the apprenticeship for a world where the old on-ramp no longer exists.

At Baldwin, we are transforming how we work, and early-career colleagues are among the first to benefit. They now encounter real client challenges sooner than the traditional path allowed. We have begun retooling our internal university, The Azimuth Institute, using AI as a training environment where a new advisor can pressure-test a coverage program, or ask why a senior colleague structured a placement a certain way, and get a substantive answer in seconds. Because AI absorbs time-consuming tasks, these colleagues are now beginning to learn higher-level insurance concepts earlier and spend more time on client relationships and complex coverage questions. We are also committed to more structured mentorship, not less, because experienced advisors are best placed to teach how to rigorously interrogate what the technology produces. And we are rethinking performance: when a day’s work takes an hour, the question is no longer how fast a task was completed, but how well the day was spent on problem-solving and critical thinking for client solutions.

Five years from now, the role of the insurance advisor will look substantially different, and I expect the advisors who meet that moment to be more valuable than any generation before them, because what they bring is the one thing the technology cannot: experience, judgment and a relationship the client trusts.

The firms that win will not be the ones that focus on AI purely to drive efficiencies. They will be the ones that changed the work, then built the people who could do the new work well. That is the work in front of us, and we intend to get it done.

#5486. DeepX plans to spend more than $100 million on a Samsung-made AI chip for robots

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The South Korean startup sent final DX-M2 designs to Samsung's foundry and expects first silicon by March 2027

DeepX, a South Korean startup, intends to commit upward of $100 million to a next-generation AI chip that will be fabricated on Samsung Electronics’ 2-nanometer process, according to Bloomberg.

DeepX has completed work on the chip, called the DX-M2, and handed the finished blueprints to Samsung's contract-manufacturing arm so that production can begin, according to Bloomberg. The company anticipates getting its first working chips by March 2027, followed by testing by customers and large-scale production in 2028.

The estimated cost of more than $100 million covers performance verification and production engineering expenses, according to Bloomberg.

DeepX is aiming the DX-M2 at three markets: robotics, factory and other industrial machinery, and PCs with built-in AI capabilities, according to Bloomberg. The chip is designed to handle generative-AI workloads while drawing only about 5 watts.

The project signals DeepX's wager that AI models are better run on the devices themselves than on servers in far-off data centers, according to Bloomberg. That approach can cut power consumption, expense and latency by avoiding round trips of data to the cloud.

DeepX's semiconductors are aimed at AI tasks and uses beyond the data center, a type of facility that is drawing growing pushback over how much electricity and water it uses, according to Bloomberg.

#5485. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

#5484. Detroit’s innovation lesson: what kids hear about careers vs. what they actually do

Anika Goss is president and CEO of Detroit Future City.

Angelique Power is president and CEO of The Skillman Foundation. Their organizations co-produced Career-Connected Learning: Investing in Detroit’s Future Talent (May 2026), the report cited in this piece; Skillman funded the research.

Some of America’s most influential leaders will soon gather in Detroit for the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum to discuss innovation, the pace of change and what it takes to compete. In classrooms across the same city, the workers their companies will need a decade from now are hearing about careers they may never get to try.

When Detroit Future City and The Skillman Foundation surveyed 83 young Detroiters in 2025 about career exposure, 78 percent said they had heard from a guest speaker or professional mentor. Fewer than half had done an internship or paid work experience. Just 35 percent had received hands-on training.

Detroit’s teenagers are not short on talk about work. They are short on chances to do it.

Jordan, a composite of students in our focus groups, shows what that costs. At 14, she loved sketching buildings, rooms and imagined cities. But no one suggested her interests might point toward a career in architecture or design. She discovered architecture years later, by accident, and realized there were pathways she could have explored in middle school.

Her story is common. A student who loved performing did not learn about physical therapy until nearly graduating. A true crime enthusiast had no idea criminology was a career. Students in skilled trades programs wished they had discovered those opportunities earlier.

Some youth are best suited for college, while others may pursue careers directly after high school. Both need opportunities to explore options and find a path forward.

Across the country, employers report trouble finding the right skills and experience. In a 2025 U.S. Chamber of Commerce survey, just 38 percent of hiring managers said finding candidates with the right skills was easy; 37 percent said the same about experience. The report, produced with the College Board, also found that 84 percent believe most high school graduates are not workforce-ready.

That points to a blind spot. Workforce programs focus on the late stages: choosing a major, enrolling in training, applying for a job. By then, young people like Jordan have already formed assumptions about which careers exist and where they belong.

Our May 2026 report, which Skillman funded, started with young people themselves: surveys and focus groups with nearly 200 Detroit youth, along with conversations with educators, employers and community leaders.

What we heard was consistent: Young people want earlier career exposure, mentors to explain different pathways and opportunities to connect school with the world beyond it. They are not asking adults to decide their futures. They want the possibilities to be more visible and accessible.

That is not just a Detroit challenge. According to NAF’s 2025–2026 Student Survey, 47 percent of students who did not participate in work-based learning cited a lack of awareness of available opportunities. Meanwhile, 79 percent of students who participated said those experiences helped them identify and develop skills for their future careers.

Exposure alone is not enough. In Detroit, talk is plentiful and practice is scarce.

Businesses can build on Career and Technical Education programs by offering workplace exposure, mentors, internships, apprenticeships and other forms of work-based learning. These experiences help students test their interests, build skills and understand career requirements.

Apprenticeships show the payoff. According to the U.S. Department of Labor, more than 800,000 people participate in apprenticeship programs annually nationwide. And the department’s April 2026 ApprenticeshipUSA fact sheet reports that 93 percent of apprentices who complete their programs retain employment, demonstrating the value of connecting education with hands-on experience and career opportunities.

Business cannot do this alone; educators, workforce organizations, higher education, philanthropy and community partners all have roles. The goal is to help young people see their options, not steer them toward one path.

Detroit Public Schools Community District’s High School Redesign strengthens connections between education, career exploration and life after graduation. Beginning in the 2026–27 school year, it expands advising, academic supports and college- and career-connected experiences across neighborhood high schools.

Henry Ford Health’s RYSE MED program offers another example, providing hands-on opportunities to explore careers in medicine and health care. From 2022 to 2026, the program enrolled 120 high school students, including 45 who attended DPSCD schools.

If businesses want stronger pipelines tomorrow, they cannot wait until students graduate to begin building them. They need to become visible earlier, in classrooms, in after-school programs, in summer internships, in middle schools, through meaningful opportunities for young people to learn by doing.

Detroit’s executives will spend the Forum talking about innovation. The students in the city around them are already hearing plenty. What they need is the chance to try the work, and business can give it to them.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, the S&P 500, and the Nasdaq $NDAQ are all tracking toward their strongest weekly showings since the start of August, even after all three fell Thursday when Nvidia $NVDA founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.

The Nasdaq has gained 3.2% so far this week, with the S&P 500 on course to finish up 2.9%. The Dow is on track for a gain of nearly 2%. Heading into Friday's session, Dow futures were up 78 points, a 0.2% gain, while S&P 500 contracts were 0.2% higher and Nasdaq-100 contracts edged up 0.1%.

#5482. Google Cloud takes aim at the cost of keeping idle AI agents running on Kubernetes

Kubernetes has become the go-to platform for distributed training and inference, but what happens to the compute bill when it runs AI agents that spend most of their time waiting?

When an agent’s container or virtual machine stays provisioned, customers pay for the wait as well as the work. To help customers control those costs and make agent workloads more predictable, Google LLC has donated three projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, according to Allan Naim (pictured, left), director of product management, AI infrastructure, at Google Cloud. For Kubernetes itself, the new challenge is freeing up compute between bursts of activity while letting each agent pick up where it left off.

“Act 2 is a few years back; Kubernetes became the de facto for inference and training,” Naim said. “What’s really interesting right now is we’re embarking on this Act 3 … where the typical patterns are very, very different from how Kubernetes was designed.”

Naim and Gari Singh (right), product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google Cloud is using open-source tools to cut compute costs when AI agents sit idle. (* Disclosure below.)

Cost presents a serious problem in agentic workloads, with agents sitting idle 90% to 95% of the time waiting on models, test runs or human approvals, Naim explained. Google developed Agent Substrate, an open-source runtime that hosts AI agents in isolated environments on Kubernetes. When an agent is suspended, the runtime saves a snapshot of its memory and local files and frees up its compute for other agents. When work resumes, it restores the agent from that snapshot in an available sandbox.

“It helps from an economic standpoint,” Naim said. “We’ve seen 10x reduction in cost in terms of running Agent Substrate on Kubernetes versus running these agents directly on dedicated virtual machines and containers.”

Security is another concern. In response, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018, which sits on top of the host kernel to block or audit every system call an agent makes, according to Singh.

“Agents and agent harnesses are designed to solve a problem — and to try to solve a problem — until they can’t solve the problem,” Singh said. “They will find all kinds of clever workarounds. They know everything that’s around. You want to make sure that it didn’t go make some low-level change to [your] low-level security, didn’t make an outbound network call, didn’t try to open a file that it shouldn’t.”

Google is also working with Anyscale Inc. on KubeRay, which runs Anyscale’s Ray platform natively on Kubernetes so platform teams can offer distributed training and inference to many research groups, Singh noted. OpenRL brings that approach to reinforcement learning, which teaches post-trained models guardrails, Naim added.

“In the past, to do reinforcement learning, you needed to hire a dozen research scientists with PhDs,” Naim said. “Our goal was, ‘How can we bring reinforcement learning into the world of platform engineering so that you can run reinforcement learning on your Kubernetes environment and take advantage of it to actually do continuous improvement for your agentic workload?'”

#5481. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5480. This Ford sculptor has carved cars out of clay for 40 years. AI and VR just cut his work time in half

John “Rex” Allen is 68, wears cowboy boots, a black baseball cap, and he’s spent four decades building life-size cars out of clay. These days he builds inside a virtual-reality headset, too.

He does his work upstairs at Ford Motor Company’s gleaming new headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, where the bird sounds in the yard aren’t even real. Just over four miles away, the 109-year-old Rouge Plant looks much the way it did in the 1920s, except with 3D-printed parts patching the factory together and a “Green Roof” overhead that is one of the world’s largest.

The new Ford World HQ opened in November 2025 as a 21st-century expression of the Ford Rouge logic, according to Ford Land CEO Jim Dobleske. World HQ stacks modern teams vertically the way Henry Ford stacked steel and assembly at the Rouge. It used to take 30 minutes to move a car from one end of the old design center to the other; now it takes “just over three minutes.” The birdsong in the courtyard is piped in, predator calls included, to keep Michigan’s ever-present geese away from workers wolfing down their lunches. “Those are not real birds,” Dobleske said, “that’s all fake.”

Fortune visited Ford in 1947 to document the “rebirth” of the company, when founder Henry Ford died and his grandson, Henry Ford II, was leading the postwar modernization of the iconic American manufacturer. Nearly eight decades later, Detroit as a whole is 13 years on from its historic bankruptcy process, but General Motors was the only member of the “Big Three” auto firms to post a net profit in 2025.

All three OEMs, or original equipment manufacturers, announced major pullbacks in their electric-vehicle strategies in 2025 as the federal government scrapped subsidies, prompting Ford CEO Jim Farley to (accurately) predict that the EV market would be cut in half as a result. In December, Ford announced about $19.5 billion in charges and pivoted to another rebirth: a race against the calendar.

Upstairs at Ford World HQ, Allen is looking at his clay cars, his monitors, his plastic models and his virtual reality glasses.

The Ford modeling studio is massive, with ceilings 25 to 30 feet high and a wide-open, blank space that feels like an empty Hollywood studio, awaiting a Gilmore Girls set or a replica of the Titanic.

Allen, with his thin white mustache complementing his mane of white hair, is doing what he’s always done: building cars out of clay.

Like most Michiganders who still work in auto manufacturing, Allen has an unimpressed air about his remarkable, unusual career. Asked how he joined the ranks of elite auto sculptors, he explains that he felt forced into it by fear of automation. “I used to be a machinist, and then it started becoming robotic, so I got out of that business real quick.” He reasoned that he’d always been a “bit of an artist,” and in high school loved comic books and cars and ran a side hustle airbrushing the “Rat Fink” mascot and other Kustom Kulture motifs onto T-shirts for other kids. Sort of a Mickey Mouse by way of R. Crumb, Rat Fink was a neon-green rodent mascot that exemplified the proto-punk vibes of Southern California car culture of the 1960s, but Allen said his tastes also ran a bit less gonzo — he used to carve Disney characters out of wood and clay for extra credit in art class, along with watercolors and oil paintings for extra credit in art class. “I made good money in high school,” Allen shrugs. “I loved doing that stuff.”

He didn’t set out to become a clay-man, either. “Somebody told me they created cars out of clay,” he explains, “which I had no idea of, so he introduced me to a guy that owned a business. And I mean, I fell right into it.” Allen recalled that he “tried it once” and the results spoke for themselves. He was 26 and soon found himself working 100 hours a week, pulling down roughly $100,000 a year.

Allen wasn’t in-house at Ford, then. At that time, Detroit had a dense web of small model shops that handled overflow work for the Big 3 — Ford, General Motors and Chrysler (now Stellantis), along with their suppliers — and Allen worked at a half-dozen of them. Work was steady. “You could grab a job any day of the week in one of these places,” he said, recalling that he worked on the original concept for the Dodge Viper at a Chrysler satellite studio. He’s now been at Ford for 24 years.

So, why clay? Allen and his colleagues, Nick Navarro, Shawn Fairall and Michael Smith, explained that it’s been that way for nearly a century. “Having the physical property in front of you to have the conversation with multiple people has always been a key part of the process,” Fairall said. “There’s always kind of this general misconception that computers have taken over car design,” Fairall said. “Clay has never really gone away.”

Smith, who leads research and development for Ford’s design team, always describes it to interns the same way. “We don’t sell pretty pictures of cars,” he said. “We sell vehicles.” He said a director might look at the clay and say, “you need to pull this back three more inches.”

It used to take about two weeks for one modeler to sculpt one full-size model, Allen said, and every change meant more weeks of work to do by hand. About six years ago, that changed with virtual reality and 3D printing. Now Allen can knock out a design’s theme in five days.

Allen said he’s seen a lot of upgrades in 40-odd years. First came “sweeps,” templates that modelers could drag along a car’s side. “That was a wow factor there for a while,” Allen said. Then came machines that could map the body, cut pieces out of it, and eventually shape an entire side. Now the team can rough out a car in clay, scan it in about 20 minutes, put on a headset to refine the shape digitally, and have a mill carve out the new surface over a few shifts, then continue working the surface by hand for the finishing touches. They call it hybrid sculpting. “This one is leaps and bounds,” Allen said, “further than anything we’ve ever done.”

“Because of technology, we’ve reduced the people over the years, so there’s less and less of us,” Allen said, adding, “we still have the same amount of work.” He said he thought this “virtual reality way of working would help keep us employed, basically, and it seems like it has, because we’re able to flip more designs now because of it.”

Those saved weeks matter because of what Ford is trying to pull off.

So what is the shape of the new Ford being born? The answer is in four parts. Ford sold about 650,000 fewer vehicles in the U.S. than GM last year, yet brought in slightly more revenue: $187.3 billion to $185 billion. The difference is mainly Ford Pro, the commercial arm that sells trucks and vans to businesses and governments earned $6.8 billion before interest and taxes in 2025 at a 10.3% margin. That’s more than double the earnings of Ford Blue, the gas and hybrid business, which made $3 billion, while the EV unit called Model e, lost $4.8 billion.

Kumar Galhotra, Ford’s chief operating officer, explained to Fortune how Ford’s next plan for Model e started with a skunkworks operation in California. “We tore down multiple Chinese OEM vehicles,” he said. “It was clear that because of the labor advantage and certain subsidies and battery areas, that their batteries are cheaper than ours.” So the team stopped trying to win on battery cost and designed around a smaller battery instead, with cleverer aerodynamics, fewer frictional losses and more efficient motors. “In the end, we’re pretty much equal in total system cost,” he said of Ford’s projection against China’s BYD, calling it “first principles thinking.”

The first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal EV platform is the Fathom, a $28,350 midsize electric pickup due in 2027. Ford says it will be able to send more than 10 kilowatts into a house during a blackout without the expensive wall-mounted inverter the F-150 Lightning needed. Asked how Ford makes money on that, a spokesperson said: “We see it as a compelling reason to buy Fathom.”

The rebirth includes a brand new business, Ford Energy, built to get a return on the billions Ford has sunk into batteries. By around March of 2025, veteran executive Lisa Drake could see that her battery plants just “weren’t full,” but Ford had already licensed lithium-iron-phosphate cells from China’s CATL and was building batteries in Marshall, Michigan. The same chemistry turned out to be close to ideal for energy storage for utilities and power developers racing to meet demand from data centers and an aging grid. “We actually were very fortunate,” Drake told Fortune. “I had a license for the best tech on the planet and the right tech for storage.”

In December, the board gave her $2 billion to start Ford Energy and she is retooling a Kentucky plant that used to make F-150 Lightning batteries, reusing about 30% to 40% of the equipment, with production set to begin in late 2027. The target customers are utilities, renewable energy developers and even data centers and hyperscalers, which don’t buy batteries directly but need power.

It’s part of Ford’s giant race against the calendar — Galhotra said Ford will end up “refreshing about 80% of our North American portfolio” between 2027 and 2029. And that’s where Rex Allen comes in. Every week saved in the clay studio will get to that refresh quicker.

Allen isn’t the only unlikely face of innovation at Ford. Over the river in Dearborn, another wears a giant Luigi-shaped mustache. His name is Greg Foresi.

The Ford Rouge Plant shows its age in a good way — a living museum, the first fully integrated auto factory in the world, still turning out cars in minutes through a century-old assembly line. And walking around, like a friendly engineer beat cop, is Foresi, the 3D-printing guy.

Foresi, who wears the horn-rimmed glasses of a Buddy Holly or a young Elvis Costello, got his signature look when he shaved off his eight-inch beard to play Luigi to a friend’s Mario one Halloween. When “mustache guy” shows up, he takes random requests from nearly everyone on the factory floor. That’s because he manages the 3D-printing lab, where roughly a dozen machines whirr away, steadily adding to nearly 300 tools and components in Foresi’s database, including about 50 individual socket covers.

“I’m out on the floor all day talking to people, trialing tools, evaluating equipment,” said the 35-year-old Foresi. Sometimes he gets five requests in one day, and sometimes nothing for five days. Foresi and his team point me toward a factory-floor wheel that isn’t black like the other ones, but a bright royal blue. This is a specialized part that filled a gap in availability during a supply-chain disruption. When Foresi saw the shortage coming, he printed his own.

Foresi explained that they didn’t have time to test the part. The choice was either trying the blue wheel and potentially creating a line stoppage — or not trying and definitely creating a stoppage. Some versions of the wheel failed, but Foresi said iterative improvements were made. “We avoided the problem entirely,” he said. Galhotra explained that Ford makes a new F-150 every 54 seconds at the plant, making Foresi’s blue wheel a hugely important component, but also not inherently scalable.

“One of the most radical things about 3D printing is that it decentralizes your logistics,” Foresi said. Galhotra put the limits plainly, saying that right now it’s “good for patches here and there,” like when a part is back-ordered or only can be flown in from somewhere else. Foresi agrees: “It’s not remotely close to replacing our conventional supply chain,” he said, adding that he gets “crazy requests” he has to turn down constantly. Some people think 3D printing is a joke, and other people “think that you can just 3D-print anything.”

Foresi had his own doubts at first. After stints at a supplier and a Ford stamping plant in Kansas City, he landed at the Dearborn truck plant as the only mechanical engineer in the final assembly department — ”a pretty intense job,” he said. “I’ve seen everything in the plant break and fixed everything,” Foresi said, recalling a line of people always waiting outside his cubicle. So when his talent was recognized as a fit for 3D printing (his “boss’ boss asked,” he said), his first instinct, like Allen’s, was fear for his job. His first instinct was that the job wouldn’t last, that 3D printing would lose favor and he’d be moved to a new role.

“I was worried that it was just a fad with the company and that it would lose energy and I would get laid off or something,” Foresi said. “They were like, ‘Too bad, you’re doing it anyway.’” Foresi hastened to add that he never felt pushed into taking the job or truly feared that he would be laid off; but he did think he might get reassigned. “After two or three months it became clear both to management and myself that printing was becoming so useful that a full-time position was needed.”

Mike Aragon and Alicia Boler Davis are both newcomers to Ford’s C-suite. The two Amazon veterans said have grown close, Aragon said, as their teams depend on each other and they bond over similar big-tech career transitions. Aragon recalls showing up for a leadership meeting five minutes late and CEO Jim Farley turning to him and saying, “Hey Mike, I want you to take on this AI initiative.” Boler Davis, a Detroiter who spent nearly 25 years working at GM before seven years out of manufacturing, said her return was like “drinking out of a firehose” and that she’s still “relearning the language, learning the culture.”

Boler Davis described the services and efficiencies that come from her use of smart data connected to a nationwide fleet and said she’s working toward a Ford Pro that can predict when a car will need a repair, or provide AI-enhanced advice to customers. As president of Ford Integrated Services, Aragon leads the teams that develop and scale digital products. “This is another reinvention on top of the reinvention that we already had to do,” he told Fortune.

At the Ford Accelerate event in Detroit in late September, Farley described to Fortune during a media briefing how Ford Pro actually uses AI to help dealership technicians, citing the example of an engine removal from a Ford Super Duty truck. “It’s like a two-day job” to take apart a Super Duty, he said, and AI is invaluable in walking customers through the process. “We are using AI for them to say, ‘Okay, do this, do that,’” he said. “They’re good mechanics, they just don’t know. They’ve never done it before.”

Galhotra was more measured about how far Ford has to go. There’s the AI that software companies talk about, on the one hand, and then “AI that’s going to change factories of how we build physical things, and in that second category, I haven’t seen really good execution yet. And even ourselves, we’re at the beginning of that journey.”

Boler Davis said some of Ford Pro’s fleet customers have pushed back. “We have some customers that, you know, don’t want you monitoring the vehicle or connected or don’t want to use the AI,” she said. Stressing that the cost of downtime can be hundreds, even thousands of dollars per vehicle on a given day, she said Ford Pro wants to empower fleet managers to help unlock the potential for their business. The tool isn’t to “get rid of the fleet manager,” she said, but to “make their job easier.”

Part of Ford’s pull for Aragon is personal. He said he remembers being driven to school in his grandfather’s 1963 F-100 truck. “I just remember the smell, which is like the smell of the nylon, and the dust — and then the Camels [cigarettes].” He said he’s planning to rebuild a model from the early ‘70s, which he’s planning to drive to work every day.

He’s not the only one at Ford with a project in the garage. Fairall restores old Volkswagens — he’s finished an ‘84 Westfalia Bus and is working on a ‘65 Split Window Bus. Allen is building his own car on the side, and he’s 3D-printing its front end. Asked whose intellectual property that makes it, Allen immediately responds, “It’s my car. “

Allen once feared the future enough to steer his son away from clay, though. Years ago, he brought his son, Derek, into a satellite studio and paid Derek to work six hours a day for him. “He started heading down this path,” Allen said, “he was getting pretty good at it. But I wanted him to be much more than just a modeler because I was worried about where modeling was going.” He steered him into engineering instead. “I always thought virtual reality would be there, but not in my lifetime,” he said. “I didn’t think I’d be part of it exactly.”

Allen says he thought he was ready to retire eight years ago, but now he’s excited to train the next generation of modelers in both virtual reality and clay. “I’m very excited about this whole chapter in my life,” he said. “I hop out of bed in the morning so I can come to work.”

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5478. Costco is recalling Kirkland Signature whipped cream in 12 states over cleaning chemical

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Members reported a chemical smell and taste in one batch; no serious adverse effects requiring medical care have been reported

Alamance Foods is recalling a batch of Costco $COST's Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream sold in 12 states over possible contamination with trace amounts of a sanitizing agent, the company said in a Nov. 7 notice to Costco members.

Alamance Foods said it is recalling the product "out of an abundance of caution." Members have noticed an odd chemical odor and flavor, but the company said it has received no reports of serious health problems that needed a doctor's care.

The recall covers 15-ounce (425-gram) cans with Costco item No. 1777000 and item code AC50, in a case pack of 8CT/3PK. Affected cans are marked with an April 2, 2027, best-if-used-by date and a timestamp falling between 00:35 and 02:45.

Costco records show members, or their add-on members, bought the item between Oct. 11 and Oct. 31, the notice said. It was sold in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin.

Members who have the affected product should stop using it and bring it back to a nearby Costco warehouse to get all their money back, the company said. Alamance Foods asked members with questions or concerns to email [email protected].

The notice neither named the chemical nor described how it may have ended up in the whipped cream, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

The recall arrives as Thanksgiving approaches, a holiday when whipped cream is a common finishing touch for pumpkin pie, according to Fox Business.

#5477. Our bank accounts had exactly one signer. Then the Navy called

Keith Presley is the co-founder and CEO of GUDEA, a narrative intelligence company that identifies inauthentic activity and foreign influence campaigns as they move through online conversation. He continues to serve in the Navy Reserve.

In October, the company I co-founded pitched on the main stage as a top 20 finalist at TechCrunch Disrupt, drawn from thousands of applicants. I was not in the audience or in the wings, because four days earlier the Navy had sent me mobilization orders. While Matt Chase, our senior vice president of global sales, delivered the most important pitch in our company’s history, I was in Norfolk, Virginia preparing to deploy. The mobilization was eventually canceled before I deployed, but, by that time, Matt was already being mic’ed up to get onstage.

I have thought about that week every day since, and I have come to believe the orders were the most honest test a CEO can face: proof, on a date I did not choose, of whether I had built a durable company or a team that could not function without me. The startup world quietly treats reserve service as a liability, but my experience that week convinced me the industry has it backwards.

There’s not much I can say about the mobilization itself, so this is a story about what the orders demanded of the company rather than where they were sending me.

Orders arrive via phone call with a report date and no room to negotiate. Questions a leader would normally settle over several quarters had to be settled in days. Investor relationships I had managed personally moved to Jonathan Sperber, my cofounder and our chief strategy officer. Decisions that existed only in my head had to be written down and handed to people I trust to make them without me. The handoff that nearly broke was signature authority on our accounts, which existed in exactly one name until that week.

Matt took over the pitch I had expected to give and tried to make the script his own. He delivered it well: the sales and investor conversations the pitch opened are still running today. The biggest moment in our history ended up in the hands of our head of sales rather than one of my co-founders. None of it resembled the continuity plan that sits untouched on our Google drive, because it happened on a clock, with Disrupt approaching and the real possibility that I would be unreachable for six months.

Every CEO assures investors that the company would survive without them, but almost none of us are required to prove it. The succession conversation is the one that slides to next quarter because the founder is healthy and nothing forces the issue, and mobilization orders are the rare event that forces it on a schedule the founder does not set. The test showed me precisely which parts of the company had real owners and which parts had been held together by my personal attention, and that knowledge has outlasted the orders themselves.

Every founder eventually gets pulled away, whether by a health crisis, a family emergency or another distraction. And usually with less warning than the Navy gave me. A reservist is simply a founder who receives the test in writing and is obligated to prepare for it in advance.

My civilian work involves identifying foreign influence campaigns as they move through American online conversation, so I have never thought of military service and company building as entirely separate worlds. The numbers say people who hold both roles are becoming rare.

Fewer than 1% of Americans serve in uniform today, across the more than 1.2 million on active duty and the roughly 800,000 of us in the reserve components. The veteran share of new entrepreneurs fell from 12.3% in 1996 to about 6% by 2011. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has found that veteran-owned businesses have a harder time accessing capital than comparable companies. In my own fundraising conversations my reserve commitment has come up, politely and more than once, as a key-person risk. We announced a $7 million seed round in October, and we are not raising now.

I understand the instinct, since the investors asking are stewards of other people’s money, but I believe they are mispricing what they see. A founder who maintains a reserve commitment practices the one discipline most companies pay consultants to simulate, which is the readiness to hand the operation to someone else on short notice.

There is an obvious objection here, and it deserves a straight answer: a chief executive who can be ordered away at any time is a genuine operational risk, and no board should pretend otherwise. My own orders proved as much, because the company absorbed real disruption in those weeks. But the risk of losing a CEO exists at every company in some form.

The reservist is the only leader required to prepare for it before it arrives, and that preparation is the difference between a disruption and a collapse. The cancellation, when it came, was a change in the Navy’s needs that I controlled no more than I had controlled the original orders. It changed nothing about the test, because by the time word came, the handover was complete and the company had already stood on that stage without me.

The company came out of October stronger than it went in, because the delegation we built under pressure has stayed in place. Other founders should run this drill before circumstances run it for them, starting with hiring leaders whose judgment they trust. Investors can help by changing what they read into a founder’s service record.

Veterans Day is approaching, and the tributes it brings are welcome, but the more useful form of gratitude would be to treat reserve service as evidence of operational discipline rather than a liability to be priced in.

#5476. OpenAI safety board member warned AI takeover could come within months

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Paul Christiano said the risk stays high even with policy responses; his September estimate was 15% within three years

Paul Christiano, who sits on the OpenAI Foundation's board and its Safety and Security Committee, cautioned that AI could seize control within the coming six to 12 months with a meaningful probability, according to Gizmodo.

Christiano spoke at The Hinton Lectures 2026 in Toronto on Monday, according to Newsweek. Christiano said that should AI labs race ahead at full speed with no outside checks, "we would be looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover" over a three-year span, according to Gizmodo. "Even with realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high," he said.

Christiano also said companies such as OpenAI will not go full throttle, according to Gizmodo. In September, he estimated the likelihood of catastrophic loss of human control at 4% over a one-year horizon and 15% over three years. He characterized those numbers as personal judgment calls, not results calculated by an exact model.

"I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident," Christiano told the audience, according to Newsweek. He said that for those following the field closely, its direction has been "extremely alarming" during the previous three to six months.

Christiano described AI agents that, during safety evaluations, meddled with the systems assessing them, such as by peeking at details of their own tests and altering logs, according to Newsweek. He warned that, as AI grows more capable, people who try to rein in or switch off a system may end up as hurdles it seeks to get around.

On Tuesday, Christiano gave a follow-up lecture titled "Staying in Control of Self-Improving AI," according to Newsweek. He listed concerns including cyberattacks at large scale, political manipulation, control of robotics and drones, and novel weapons development.

The warnings come as OpenAI faces scrutiny over incidents in which its agents escaped their testing environment in May and breached Hugging Face in July. After the July incident, OpenAI slowed model development and added new security controls. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman then told employees the company was open to slowing development of its most advanced AI.

Christiano joined the OpenAI nonprofit board in September. "I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level," he said in a statement at the time, according to Newsweek.

#5475. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

#5474. Life after Jensen: What Nvidia’s shakeup means for private AI

This time last week, AI without Jensen Huang seemed impossible. Today, that’s the world we live in.

Granted, it’ll have been less than (or about) 24 hours into that new world by the time you’re reading this, and there’s so much we don’t know about what a Jensen-less AI landscape looks like. One thing we do know: It will affect the private markets.

“Nvidia matters more to private AI markets than any single investor because it has three roles,” said Harrison Rolfes, PitchBook senior research analyst, who was among many who answered my feverish reporting calls yesterday. “It’s the largest corporate investor in U.S. AI. It’s the main supplier for AI startups, and it’s the main [benchmark] public stock investors use to judge the AI market.”

Now, in the near term at least, how Nvidia and new interim CEO Colette Kress will handle dealmaking is in question. Rolfes pointed out to me that Nvidia invested $189 billion in 2026, making it AI’s top U.S. corporate backer. This broke down somewhat expectedly: OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI account for $172 billion, and 27 other deals make up the remaining $17 billion. Kress, and any Huang successor, could be more circumspect moving forward. (Indeed, worth noting: Nvidia’s blockbuster $12.93 billion buyout of open-source startup Hugging Face hasn’t yet closed.) And some companies will struggle more than others, especially neoclouds, for which Huang was dealmaker and guarantor.

“If they’re dependent on Nvidia to bankroll them, like [CoreWeave] or Lambda Labs or some of these neoclouds, then I think you could be really screwed,” one early-stage VC told me.

Much will move forward, nevertheless: My colleague Beatrice Nolan and I reported that Anthropic’s IPO is high-stakes but (for now) very much on, and some VCs told me that, yes, this could pressure AI valuations—and so what.

“I think the valuations were ridiculous anyway,” said Rob Biederman, managing partner at Asymmetric. “I don’t think it would be the worst thing for the tech world if there was a little bit of a reset shakeout because a lot of things are getting funded right now that aren’t especially good ideas.”

For startups wondering what’s next, Rolfes had some advice: Nvidia will invest less for now, but (on the bright side) it’s possible GPU prices will also drop.

“If you’re a startup, maybe don’t reach out to Nvidia in the short term to get investment cash,” he said. “What they should do is reach out to go get compute, go buy the chips…If some of these startups can get a hold of cheaper chips, then they can build out their product, which means we’ll probably start to see an influx of seed-stage [and] Series A-stage startups moving up.”

Here’s our larger feature contemplating life in AI after Jensen.

#5473. Kalshi is in talks to raise money at a $65 billion valuation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The prediction market closed a round at a $40 billion valuation weeks ago that was expected to be its last before an IPO

Kalshi is in talks to raise new funding from investors at a $65 billion valuation, according to Bloomberg. A Kalshi spokesperson declined to comment.

The talks come only weeks after Kalshi wrapped up a financing that valued it at $40 billion. That round, which the company disclosed in late October, had been seen as the final private raise ahead of an IPO, according to Bloomberg. Kalshi opted to raise private money again before going public, and volatility in financial markets did not influence the choice.

Kalshi, founded in 2018, sells financial contracts whose payouts depend on how real-world events turn out. Sports betting has made up the bulk of trading on the platform during the past year, according to Bloomberg.

Kalshi's monthly notional trading volume grew by more than 100% between August, when it stood at $40 billion, and October, when it reached close to $100 billion, according to Bloomberg. Gross margins were about 90% during the last funding round, according to documentation Bloomberg viewed. Kalshi's annual run rate, a projection of yearly revenue if present activity holds steady, has surpassed $5 billion.

Kalshi's financial and betting products have drawn backing from the Trump administration. Scrutiny of them has now increased, after Democrats, who have been more critical of prediction markets, gained ground in the midterm elections, according to Bloomberg.

Kalshi announced Thursday that it had severed its association with Donald Trump Jr., one of its advisers, according to Bloomberg. Kalshi pointed to his connection to Polymarket, its chief competitor.

#5471. I booked the first used Falcon 9 booster. Where will satellite operators go when SpaceX retires it?

Martin Halliwell is a partner at NewSpace Capital, a private equity firm investing in high-growth space companies, and former chief technology officer of satellite operator SES. K2 Space and ICEYE, both named in this piece, are NewSpace Capital portfolio companies.

In 2016, I agreed to put a communications satellite owned by SES on a Falcon 9 booster that SpaceX had already flown. No commercial customer had ever done such a thing before, but as chief technology officer at SES, I had overseen the work our engineers had carried out with SpaceX. Their engineers had shown us how they tested the engines, checked the electronics, and prepared the booster for a second flight. I was confident in SpaceX’s ability to deliver, and they did. In March 2017, they used the booster to launch our satellite.

I would oversee six Falcon 9 launches during my time at SES. But today, as an investor in growth-stage space companies, I find myself wondering what company I would book if I still had that job. SpaceX is setting aside the Falcon 9 and turning its attention to Starship, a much larger rocket; and from my conversations with people working at SpaceX, I can see why the company wants its engineers to change their focus. Most of the remaining Falcon 9 slots up to around 2030 are already booked up. So what happens now if you need to get to space?

Those companies that have managed to secure a booking with SpaceX before 2030 will be glad for their foresight. In October 2025, the team at K2 Space, one of our portfolio companies, announced that they had booked a 2027 Falcon 9 flight for three satellites, having secured their place more than a year in advance. But even operators who book that far ahead can lose their place. Suppose a supplier calls you just before launch because a different customer has found a fault in a component on which you depend. Though your engineers may need just a few days to look into things, everybody else sharing the rocket has a customer waiting too. Under SpaceX’s rideshare terms, you could put the money you have paid towards another flight and pay a rebooking fee of 5% to 10%. You could work out the fee to the dollar and still have no real idea when you might start earning money from whatever it is that you have put into orbit.

Those building satellites that weigh 100 kg or less may find themselves particularly exposed after 2030. On a SpaceX Transporter flight, such a company shares the rocket with dozens of other customers and buys only the space it requires. For a shared flight around Earth that passes near both poles, SpaceX advertises $350,000 for the first 50 kg and $7,000 for each additional kg. At those rates, a founder with a satellite weighing 100 kg can pencil in $700,000 for the ride. After 2030, it is hard to see how a space company could get to orbit on anything like those terms.

In March, K2 Space launched its two-tonne Gravitas satellite on Falcon 9. Because it costs less to build than traditional satellites of similar power, K2 co-founder Karan Kunjur has argued that it still makes economic sense to launch such a spacecraft at a cost of roughly $7.2 million, compared with an estimated $600,000 if Starship delivers the promised savings. But K2 is a highly unusual case. Most satellite operators will struggle to offset higher launch costs with savings of that kind.

At ICEYE, another of our portfolio companies, the team is looking at an alternative way to launch satellites for its European government customers. In September, its executives agreed with Arianespace to explore using Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket for future missions. Neither company announced a launch date. For now, ICEYE continues to fly with SpaceX. In October, the team launched four radar satellites on one SpaceX flight and four more on another just 19 days later.

If your usual provider postpones a launch, the question is whether anyone else can take your satellite at short notice. Say you plan to launch a satellite on Neutron and Rocket Lab postpones the flight. How long can you afford to wait? You still have to pay your engineers, and until you get the satellite into orbit, you can’t sell whatever services you provide. You could try booking a flight with Blue Origin, provided its team can offer you a place on New Glenn in time; but even after engineers fly a new rocket for the first time, they may need years to build enough of them to fly regularly. My estimate is that Rocket Lab and Relativity Space may take until 2033 or 2034 to reach that point with Neutron and Terran R.

At SES, we agreed to fly our satellite on a Falcon 9 booster that SpaceX had already used. Before we made that decision, our team worked alongside the people who had tested the booster and prepared it to fly again. Today, as an investor, I’d ask the people running a satellite company three questions: Which flight have you booked, how much have you agreed to pay, and what will you do if you lose your place? If I were one of their customers, I’d want those answers before I counted on having the satellite or payload in service by a particular date.

#5470. Dow futures rise 323 points as Nvidia rebounds and wholesale inflation comes in light

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The October producer price index rose 0.3% on the month, while the three major indexes are on track for weekly gains

Nvidia $NVDA stock climbed over 2% in Friday's premarket session, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures gained 323 points, or 0.6%. S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 futures each added 0.7%.

The October producer price index, which gauges inflation at the wholesale level, rose 0.3% from September and 6.5% from a year earlier. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had forecast a 0.4% increase in October's headline PPI, according to CNBC.

Nvidia's gain followed a 4.3% drop on Thursday after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down. Huang departed after reports of extramarital affairs, one of them reportedly with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a spy for China, according to CNBC.

The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each declined on Thursday. A jump in oil prices also weighed on stocks after President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social, "We don't need a deal with Iran." The remark raised concerns that the U.S.-Iran war might be prolonged.

Oil prices held roughly steady on Friday. West Texas Intermediate crude futures changed hands at more than $88 a barrel, while Brent crude futures were priced over $96.

Despite Thursday's decline, the major averages remain on pace to finish the week higher. The Nasdaq is up 3.2% for the week, and the S&P 500 is tracking a 2.9% gain. The Dow is on track to add just under 2%. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq are each on track to post their strongest week since early August, according to CNBC.
