#5469. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5468. Ethereum Price at $2,000: Scoop the Dip, Hold, or Dump?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Ethereum price is testing investors’ patience once again. Its latest recovery attempt falls apart. After giving back its August gains, ETH has returned to the $1,900–$2,050 zone, putting a critical breakout area at risk.

The $2,000 level is the market’s battleground. Buyers need to defend this area before another wave of selling pushes Ethereum lower. On the other hand, traders are increasingly looking toward $2,200 as the threshold for a meaningful recovery. Until ETH reclaims that level, any bounce risks becoming another temporary relief rally.So, buy, hold, or time to sell?

Ethereum’s latest decline has erased much of the optimism surrounding its August recovery. The second-largest crypto has slipped back toward the price region that previously supported its breakout.

That makes the current setup particularly important. The $1,900–$2,050 range previously acted as resistance before buyers pushed ETH higher. But can this resistance become support?

The technical picture remains uncomfortable for bulls. Ethereum has continued forming lower highs, and it can be interpreted that sellers are still controlling the short-term trend. A move below $2,000 would put the lower end of the previous breakout base under pressure. The $1,900 area would then become an important downside level to watch.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Ethereum investors now face three competing strategies as ETH revisits a previous breakout area. ETH is not trading at an unfamiliar support level. If buyers defend $2,000, bargain hunters could view the correction as an opportunity to accumulate.

Long-term holders may prefer to wait. Ethereum’s underlying ecosystem continues developing, with experiments involving zETH and Activity Markets bringing fresh attention to on-chain participation.

These projects explore ways to measure and reward Ethereum activity, including trading, lending, borrowing, staking, and restaking. Reclaiming $2,200 would provide stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control. It would also help invalidate the immediate bearish structure created by successive lower highs. Until this happens, aggressive dip-buying carries the risk of catching a falling market.

The bearish scenario becomes more convincing if Ethereum loses the $2,000 price level decisively. A breakdown could expose $1,950 before bringing the $1,850 support in view.

Ethereum has two important levels to watch. $2,000 could determine whether buyers can prevent another breakdown, while $2,200 could confirm whether the recovery has enough strength to continue.

Ethereum isn’t the only crypto opportunity attracting investors. Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is counting down to its November 26 token launch, with just 14 days remaining for early participants to secure tokens through its presale.

The project has raised more than $33.2 million, with its presale price listed at just $0.0136. Its staking program also offers rewards of up to 35% APY, giving early buyers another incentive to accumulate before launch.

Bitcoin Hyper aims to bring faster transactions and smart contract functionality to Bitcoin using the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM). Its architecture combines a Bitcoin bridge, Layer 2 execution, and zero-knowledge proofs to support decentralized applications.

Developers are already working on the project’s public testnet infrastructure, including an RPC endpoint, block explorer, wallet functionality, and bridge components. The goal is to create an ecosystem where developers can build applications while leveraging Bitcoin’s underlying network.

There is a parallel with Ethereum’s early days. ETH eventually grew beyond its original payment-token narrative by attracting developers, applications, and liquidity. Bitcoin Hyper is pursuing a similar ecosystem-building strategy around Bitcoin.

HYPER isn’t competing with Ethereum’s market size today. That’s precisely where its speculative appeal lies. A smaller starting valuation could offer greater percentage-return potential if adoption accelerates, while staking rewards provide an additional attraction for early participants.

#5467. Wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago, the biggest annual rise since November 2022

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October from September, after a 1.4% gain the month before

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that producer prices for final demand rose 6.5% in the 12 months ended in October, on an unadjusted basis. That was the largest 12-month rise since a 7.4% increase in November 2022, according to the agency.

On a seasonally adjusted basis, the producer price index for final demand rose 0.3% in October. Prices advanced 1.4% in September and 0.4% in August, according to the BLS.

The index for final demand goods rose 0.5% in October after a 2.5% increase in September. Final demand food prices rose 1.3%, while energy prices edged down 0.1%. Prices for basic organic chemicals advanced 3.9%, and diesel fuel prices fell 7.9%. Over the 12 months ended in October, final demand goods prices rose 10.2%, the largest 12-month rise since a 10.5% gain in October 2022.

The index for final demand services moved up 0.2%, its fifth consecutive advance. Prices for transportation and warehousing services rose 2.0%, and truck transportation of freight rose 3.9%. Margins for final demand trade services decreased 0.2%.

The index for final demand less foods, energy and trade services rose 0.5% in October, the same as in September. That measure was up 4.9% from a year earlier.

Within intermediate demand, prices for processed goods rose 0.4% in October. They were up 14.6% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since a 17.2% jump in July 2022. Prices for unprocessed goods fell 3.1%, the largest decline since a 6.6% drop in June, as crude petroleum prices decreased 10.3%. Unprocessed goods prices were up 16.9% from a year earlier.

Prices for services for intermediate demand rose 0.6% in October and 6.8% over 12 months. That was the largest 12-month advance since a 6.9% increase in November 2022.

The BLS said figures for June through September were revised to reflect late reports and corrections by respondents. The agency scheduled the November producer price index release for Tuesday, Dec. 15, at 8:30 a.m. ET.

#5465. Current price of oil as of November 13, 2026

At 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $98.45 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s a gain of $3.87 compared with yesterday morning and around $35 higher than the price one year ago.

It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast.

Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business.

Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.”

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas.

To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks:

Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5464. Russia's October oil revenues jumped about 65% as Iran war pushed crude past $100

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Export earnings reached $21.2 billion, the highest since May, as Urals and ESPO blends topped $100 a barrel

Russian oil producers brought in nearly $21.2 billion from selling crude and refined products abroad in October, a gain of roughly 65% over the same month a year before and the best monthly tally since May, according to Bloomberg.

Crude supplied over 80% of that sum, while Ukrainian strikes on refineries weighed on the volumes of refined products produced and shipped, according to Bloomberg. Russia's Urals and ESPO blends climbed above $100 a barrel in October amid fighting in the Middle East, where tankers were being hit almost every day around the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi forces were bombarding Saudi energy facilities. Russian barrels never have to pass through Hormuz on the way to their biggest customers, China and India, which helped sustain demand.

The International Energy Agency put Russian crude production at 8.73 million barrels a day in October, up from 8.52 million in September. The agency said ongoing strikes on Russia's energy facilities are steadily squeezing the diesel the nation can send to global buyers.

Crude exports were unchanged from September, standing at 5.33 million barrels daily, which is about 4% higher than a year before, according to Bloomberg. Exports of petroleum products rose to 1.49 million barrels daily, their strongest level since June yet roughly one-third lower than 12 months before.

Russia's federal budget receives oil money through taxes on producers rather than directly from exports, according to Bloomberg. Net oil-levy income for the federal budget came to about $10 billion in October, trimmed by subsidies that underwrite fuel supplies inside Russia, according to Bloomberg calculations drawing on Finance Ministry figures.

Drone strikes launched by Ukraine during the first half of October cut into throughput at Russian refineries. The strikes eased later in the month when Kyiv paused them for two weeks, according to Bloomberg. Ukraine has gone back to hitting major refineries, among them Kirishi, which is geared toward exports, and Omsk, Russia's biggest. The renewed campaign could push waterborne crude shipments up this month, so long as the export terminals escape damage.

President Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, days after saying Moscow would supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to global markets under a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control granted a general license covering certain transactions in Russian-origin diesel, valid through April 7, 2027, according to CNBC.

#5463. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 10:44 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5462. The weaknesses that cost Binance $6.3 billion are already hitting Europe’s banks

When hackers drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, on October 29, it was tempting to treat it as a crypto problem. Less than a week later, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a French lender, disclosed that hackers had made off with roughly €100 million ($112 million).

The back-to-back attacks highlight the threat of cyber heists to traditional banks. “If a company like Binance can lose billions of dollars, the threats facing banks are overwhelming,” said Ryan Kirkley, cofounder and CEO of Global Settlement, which develops blockchain infrastructure for banks. Speaking at the Digital Asset Summit in London on November 10, he said: “It is impossible for the average bank to stay secure.”

Binance’s founder and former CEO, Changpeng Zhao, went further. “If a crypto exchange can be hacked, banks are in a worse position, in my opinion,” he told CoinDesk days after the heist.

The Binance hackers used a combination of social engineering and malicious software to take over crypto wallets and drain them of funds. This involved arranging a series of fake job interviews to persuade a Binance engineer to inadvertently download malware which allowed the hackers into the company’s systems.

The FBI has seized $1.2 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency, while Binance confirmed it had “replenished” approximately 98% of the total impacted amount.

The weaknesses hackers exploited to steal funds on Binance are not unique to crypto and the same vulnerabilities are present in traditional financial institutions, said Katerina Mitrokotsa, professor of cybersecurity at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland. “Banks are not automatically safer just because they are regulated.”

Regulators on both sides of the Atlantic have raised concerns. In the U.S., the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency began calling banks on November 2 to ask about unusual activity and service disruptions, Reuters reported.

In July, the European Central Bank wrote to the chief executives of 110 banks warning about the risks of frontier AI models, which are making it “quicker and cheaper to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IT systems.” .

Banks have some advantages over crypto platforms, according to Vivien Mura, chief technology officer of Orange Cyberdefense, the cybersecurity arm of French telecoms group Orange. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, or DORA, which has applied since January 2025, requires banks to test their defenses and report cyber incidents. “They also benefit from mechanisms crypto platforms lack, such as the ability to block or reverse payments and close cooperation with supervisors and law enforcement,” Mura said.

Yet he acknowledges that those advantages only go so far. “Banks are better placed to absorb and recover from a major attack, but they are not necessarily better at preventing one.”

Mitrokotsa highlights two weak spots: The long chain of outside suppliers banks rely on, which DORA tries to address by bringing the most critical providers under direct EU supervision, and the aging technology many banks still run.

In the Crédit Mutuel Arkéa case, hackers used the bank’s own account to carry out transactions after gaining access through an unnamed service provider. The bank told customers the incident had “no impact” on their assets.

“Compromised suppliers, staff with privileged access, fake job approaches and the misuse of internal tools have been recognized risks for years and are not unique to any one sector,” Lee Elliott, director of resilience and cyber at UK Finance, the British banking industry body, told Fortune.

Banks benefit from the sector’s practice of sharing threat intelligence through initiatives such as the Financial Sector Cyber Collaboration Centre, he adds.

Attackers are already exploiting Europe’s aging IT systems. Since October, hackers have hijacked internet-connected refrigeration systems at supermarkets in more than a dozen countries and at three French blood banks. Danfoss, which made the electronic temperature controllers, has said most affected units were older models that no longer receive security updates.

“A fridge doesn’t look like a security risk, and that’s exactly why attackers like it,” Mitrokotsa says. “Banks have the same problem. Many still run core systems that are decades old, next to old servers, building control systems and suppliers’ remote access.” Her advice is for banks to start by knowing every device connected to their networks, then make sure that the ones with no need to reach core systems are cut off from them.

Banks could even learn from crypto, Mitrokotsa added. “Some exchanges split control of a key between several parties, so no single computer can approve a transfer on its own, much like a vault that needs two keys turned at once. An attacker who compromises one laptop gets only part of what they need.”

Personal AI agents also present a new risk for financial institutions to grapple with. Increasingly, consumers are using digital assistants—such as Meta’s Muse—to make purchases or pay bills on their behalf.

Citigroup and Bank of America have restricted agents from accessing customer accounts., JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon has urged financial institutions not to allow autonomous AI agents to handle banking payments, warning of their “treacherous” risk. U.K. banks HSBC, Nationwide, NatWest, Barclays, and Lloyds have also blocked AI agents from accessing their accounts. However, some European lenders are taking a more cautious middle path. Santander and ING let agents make payments, but only within limits the customer sets in advance or after the customer approves each purchase.

With the number of cyber threats mounting, the Crédit Mutuel Arkéa hack is unlikely to be the last attack on Europe’s financial sector.

Sam Birchall is a features writer at Fortune 500 C-Suite Europe. Previously, she was a reporter at Raconteur, where she specialized in business and leadership storytelling for C-suite audiences.

#5461. Nvidia-backed Nscale warned it needs more financing ahead of its planned IPO

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The London-based data center builder said some new capital commitments cannot be deferred, reduced or cancelled

Nscale, the Nvidia $NVDA-backed data center builder, said it will have to raise more money to pay for a steep jump in the near-term spending it projects.

The London-based company filed an amended prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday for its planned U.S. initial public offering. In the filing, Nscale said it is bound to some of its newly added obligations and cannot delay them or back out of them.

"Some of the new capital commitments cannot be contractually deferred, reduced or cancelled by us," the company said. It added that it will be required "to obtain additional financing to meet our forecast obligations in 2027 and execute our business plan."

A person close to Nscale said the company believes it will be able to arrange the funding both for individual projects and for the business as a whole, according to The Wall Street Journal. The person said the money might come from a mix of sources, such as advance payments from customers and funding provided by vendors. The person also said the funding need will not derail the company's progress toward a listing, and that Nscale is still on course to go public before 2026 ends.

The filing leaves out the amount Nscale intends to raise in the offering, according to CNBC. According to Reuters, Goldman Sachs $GS, J.P. Morgan and Morgan Stanley $MS are leading the underwriting, and Nscale intends to have its shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange with the ticker "NSCL."

Nscale brought in $3.36 billion by issuing convertible notes in a September round ahead of the IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. It also brought in $2 billion earlier this year in a funding round that valued the company at $14.6 billion. Counting both equity and debt, The Wall Street Journal said, the company has brought in a total of more than $13.4 billion.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Nscale signed a $45 billion agreement in August under which Anthropic will rent capacity at its data center in West Virginia.

Doubts about the listing have grown since Nscale filed for the IPO in September. Investors had anticipated that the offering would land by year-end, but an October rout in AI shares, driven by cloud-computing names such as CoreWeave, cast doubt on the timing, according to The Wall Street Journal. Microsoft $MSFT also exited an agreement in October under which it would have leased capacity at Nscale’s facilities, pointing to worries about electricity supply in the U.K.

Nscale now has seven data centers in operation, compared with five when it first disclosed its listing plans, according to The Wall Street Journal.

#5460. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

#5459. Fresh off a $100 million raise, Paul Rabil takes pro lacrosse to the basketball courts of Venice Beach

The Premier Lacrosse League is taking a stripped-down, pick-up version of the sport to the streets of Los Angeles. On Saturday, Nov. 14, the league’s Street Lacrosse Pro Tour makes its first L.A. stop, on the basketball courts at Venice Beach, with a festival vibe and a 5-on-5 format that looks more like street basketball or hockey than the field game.

The goal is to keep growing the sport and build buzz before its long-awaited return at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, about 600 days away. Lacrosse last appeared as a medal sport in 1908. It has appeared since only as a demonstration sport, including at the 1932 L.A. Games and, most recently, in London in 1948.

Men’s and women’s pros will share the court with special guests, including streetball star The Professor and influencer Cameron Elliott Schmidt.

Paul Rabil, widely regarded as one of the best players in the sport’s history, co-founded the PLL and its sister circuit, the Women’s Lacrosse League (WLL). He is president of the parent company; his brother, Mike, is CEO. In June, the league closed a $100 million Series E led by Ares and Joe Tsai, with ESPN taking a minority equity stake.

Rabil, who has previously shared his leadership playbook with Fortune, sat down with us to discuss the Street Lacrosse Pro Tour and the sport’s state in the run-up to the Olympics.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Fortune: Lacrosse has grown quickly this century, well beyond its traditional hotbeds in New England and along the East Coast. Since 2000, the number of NCAA lacrosse programs has more than doubled to 917, while high school participation has increased by more than 353%. In 2024-25, 212,988 high schoolers played on 6,670 boys’ and girls’ teams nationwide.

Team lacrosse has surged. So how does the Street Lacrosse Pro Tour fit into the PLL portfolio?

Rabil: We’ve done a lot with our Assists program, our 501(c)(3). We donate equipment, provide coaching opportunities, and playing opportunities for kids who otherwise don’t have access.

Street Lacrosse came [in 2023] when Rich Kleiman and Kevin Durant invested in the PLL. Kevin and I grew up in the DMV [the Washington, D.C., area], and we both played hoops, so we knew you had to play pickup to get better as a player. That was always around and available for basketball, but a sport like lacrosse, that’s not always available to you.

So street lacrosse was born—basically playing a version of lacrosse on a basketball court. All you need is a stick and a tennis ball, no helmet, pads, and all that other stuff.

We felt like if we could lift off Street Lacrosse, get the pros to play it, create a ton of exciting media around it, that would start penetrating the subconscious of a young kid who wanted to try lacrosse and not worry about signing up for a rec team or club team.

Ultimately sport should be egalitarian. If anyone wants to try something, they should be allowed to try it, and if they fall in love with it, they can commit to playing it and potentially pursue a life in it.

Fortune: Both pro field leagues, which play 10 a side, just finished strong seasons. The PLL posted its most-watched season ever in its eighth year, and the WLL set women’s pro attendance records in its inaugural season. Where does the next leg of growth come from?

Rabil: We’re in a territory where professional lacrosse has never been, and that’s exciting. We’ve raised our Series E around the prospect of having growth over the last eight seasons, and now we’re pouring on growth capital to potentially take the next step into the mainstream spotlight of where the big five or six sports live.

We have a major media deal with ESPN, they’ve invested in our league [in the Series E round], and we have title sponsors across the major categories that never touched lacrosse in the past. That’s because we have real distribution of viewership [on ESPN and sister network ABC], our audience is highly sought after—families and younger generations—and we have a built-in production team that creates content that’s bespoke on behalf of our players, teams, and our partners.

We’re in the middle of producing a five-part documentary series with ESPN [releasing next spring]. I like to say we’re a league and a media company, which has been our focus since we raised our first dollar.

Fortune: All PLL and WLL teams are owned and operated by the leagues. Are you considering expanding, or bringing in individual owners like in other team sports?

Rabil: Because we own the whole thing, it makes less fiscal sense to expand in the PLL [now]… There’s room for expansion of the WLL from four teams up to eight, same as the PLL, but no plans right now that I can announce.

Lacrosse being back in the Olympics in 2028 is a very attractive time for a big shift in our operating model [to possibly selling teams to individual owners].

Fortune: What’s your biggest challenge at the moment?

Rabil: It has to be getting people to decide in today’s environment to pay for a ticket, drive to a game, pay for parking, show up in the heat of the summer for a game broadcast on ABC at one o’clock. That’s a challenge for any league, but lacrosse, in my point of view, outside of the college Final Four, has never really conditioned its fans to attend games.

This is the best lacrosse I’ve ever seen in my life, but conditioning a fan from scratch is a journey. We’re eight years into that journey and seeing a lot of success, but it takes a long time to condition human behavior.

Fortune: What’s your advice to someone starting a sports league?

Rabil: You have to understand the attention economy if you’re trying to grow an otherwise niche sport. You have to do a lot of things really well: education, storytelling around athletes, community investment of your teams, and you have to be omnipresent across mobile devices and televisions, and video boards.

You should approach your business, and find the right investors, metaphorically to think that you’re building a New York City skyscraper. That means you have to dig really deep into the ground first, which comes at an unattractive P&L, but that gives you a strong enough foundation to build upward.

People look at the skyline and say, ‘How beautiful is that!’ They don’t understand the structure that lives underneath it and the investment that went underneath it. It’s a long game.

If you’re starting a football, baseball, basketball, or hockey league, my advice is basically: don’t do it!

Fortune: The PLL and WLL are helping stage the first Lexus Global Lacrosse Games, a new international tournament set for Dec. 8-13 outside Washington, D.C., to build toward the Olympics. It will include men’s and women’s national teams from lacrosse powerhouses the U.S., Canada, Australia, and the Haudenosaunee, who originated the game centuries ago.

Rabil: The ’28 Olympics are an incredible opportunity for our sport and our players. It’s one the sport has never had.

We’re setting up a version of the 4 Nations Face-Off tournament the NHL had that built momentum around the USA and Canada through the Winter Olympics. Over the next two years we’re going to try and build as much attention and awareness around international lacrosse so that when summer 2028 comes in LA, people will be champing at the bit to see a U.S.-Canada final.

#5458. ‘I Just Cannot Get Ahead’: Why Americans Are Under Extreme Financial Pressure, According to a New Report

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

One 73-year-old borrower described owing nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards.

Why does getting ahead feel so out of reach? A new analysis from the Urban Institute offers a look at the financial strain Americans are facing.

The report, which drew from U.S. Census Bureau data, revealed that 23.5% of Americans with a credit history have debt in collections. They owe a median amount of $2,913.

As grocery bills and other essentials take a bigger toll on household budgets, some Americans are relying on credit cards to bridge the gap. However, steep interest charges can turn that short-term relief into debt that is difficult to pay off, even for borrowers who are making payments.

Susan Cannon described that cycle to Business Insider earlier this year. The 73-year-old owes nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards, with interest rates ranging from roughly 12% to 35%. She lives in a mobile home in rural Texas. Despite paying more than the minimum balance on her credit cards, she struggles to reduce her balances while continuing to charge necessities such as groceries and gas to her credit cards.

“I can’t get the balance down because I am still having to use credit cards at the end of the month to get groceries and gas,” Cannon told the publication. “I pay my bills, but because of the interest rates, it keeps going up — I feel like I’m being gouged.”

Despite Cannon’s best attempts to build a savings account, her monthly payments are all going towards interest payments on her credit cards.

“I just cannot get ahead,” Cannon told Business Insider.

Where Americans live can make a noticeable difference in how heavily overdue their bills are. For example, in rural Jim Hogg County in South Texas, more than half of residents with a credit history have debt in collections, according to the report. Nationwide, the share is 23.5%, making the county’s rate more than twice the national figure.

How quickly an unpaid bill reaches collections depends on the type of debt. Credit card accounts typically enter collections four to six months after a missed payment, while unpaid medical bills generally take three to six months. The balances also differ: The analysis put the median delinquent credit card debt at $680, compared with $1,492 for medical debt.

Student loans follow a different path, with the rules varying between federal and private lenders. Federal loans generally fall into default after 270 days without payment. Borrowers can then pursue options such as loan rehabilitation to resolve the default and restore their loans to good standing.

The New York Federal Reserve determined that Americans collectively owe $18.8 trillion in debt as of the second quarter of the year.

#5457. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5456. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5455. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO—but the succession question remains

Good morning. Nvidia is the latest Fortune 500 company to name its CFO interim CEO.

The AI giant appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, replacing Jensen Huang, the company’s co-founder and longtime leader, who resigned Thursday after admitting to an affair that raised national security concerns. Kress will continue serving as finance chief while taking the helm of Nvidia.

Kress is “very much the right interim CEO,” Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner of executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates, told me. As CFO for 13 years, she knows the company’s story “front and back” and is a highly respected spokesperson with credibility among investors, Simmons said.

Nvidia’s transformation during Kress’s tenure has been extraordinary. Since she joined in 2013, revenue has grown from $4.13 billion in fiscal 2014 to $130.5 billion in fiscal 2025, while its market capitalization has climbed from about $9 billion to nearly $4 trillion today—an increase of roughly 44,000%. Kress ranks No. 49 on the Fortune 2026 Most Powerful Women list.

When I first interviewed Kress in 2022, we discussed her previous roles at Cisco, Microsoft, and Texas Instruments, as well as how Nvidia attracted and retained employees.

“I think my career background did serve me well at Nvidia,” she told me. “When I started at Nvidia, it was the smallest company that I’d ever worked for. It’s gotten quite large, but the focus is on how do you think about the future and make sure we’re ready for it to scale?”

She also discussed her approach to leadership, emphasizing the importance of surrounding herself with “people that you can learn from; people that can help lead.”

The company had no publicly disclosed succession plan. Replacing a founder-CEO is especially challenging, said Simmons, who has worked in executive recruiting for almost 30 years. At Nvidia, whose longtime leader has achieved celebrity status, the task is even more complicated, he said.

“When you’re talking about cutting-edge technology that’s evolving at light speed, you’re trying to find someone who could pick the ball up and carry it down the field, and that’s difficult,” he said.

As interim CEO, Kress must help steer Nvidia through a leadership transition at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. The company plays a crucial role in shaping the technology’s future in the U.S. and beyond.

Whether she could eventually become the company’s permanent leader is another question. Simmons expects Nvidia’s board to look for a technologist to succeed Huang. Meanwhile, Nvidia has named Harvey Jones chair of the board. Jones has worked in technology, including semiconductors, for more than 30 years, Fortune’s Emily Forlini reported.

If the board decides to select a technologist as Huang’s successor, one potential internal contender, Simmons said, is Ian Buck. He joined Nvidia in 2004 and is now vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing and a key architect of its AI business.

For leading analysts’ picks of potential outside successors to Huang, you can read my article here.

Have a good weekend. Sheryl EstradaSheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

Murray succeeds Cody Perdue, who has served as interim CFO since Sept. 30 and will continue as SVP of treasury, investor relations and risk management. Murray joins Albertsons from Fonterra Co-operative Group, the world's largest dairy exporter, where he has been group CFO since 2024. He also oversees strategy, M&A, transformation and IT there. Before Fonterra, Murray was CFO of Simplot Australia, led global finance transformation at Toll Group, and held senior finance roles at Mondelez International.

She will succeed Kate Bueker, who will retire and remain in an advisory role through December 2027. Burgess will join HubSpot on Nov. 30 as executive vice president of finance before assuming the CFO role. She joins from Adobe, where she serves as senior vice president and CFO of its Creativity & Productivity business unit. Since joining Adobe in 2002, Burgess has helped support its business model transformation.

Dziadzio succeeds Jim Quinn, who has been CFO since 2017 and moves into the newly created role of president and chief transformation officer. Most recently, Dziadzio was interim CFO of Sterling Check during its acquisition by First Advantage.

Adrian Wood was appointed CFO of BHP Group Limited, a global resources company, effective Feb. 17. He will succeed Vandita Pant, who will step down following the release of BHP’s half-year results on Feb. 16 and remain with the company through March 29. Wood currently serves as VP of projects, minerals Australia. He joined BHP in 2015 and previously served as VP of finance, minerals Australia, and group investor relations officer.

Jacqueline Maxwell was named CFO of Prolink, a Cincinnati-based workforce solutions firm, the company announced. She succeeds Jennifer Prospero, who becomes chief administrative officer. Maxwell has been with Prolink since 2012, most recently as vice president and corporate controller. Before that, she was a controller at Mary L. Shiley, LLC. Prospero joined Prolink as interim CFO in March 2024 and was named CFO in January 2025.

Dev Ahuja was appointed CFO of QXO (NYSE: QXO), a building products distributor, effective in January. He will succeed Ihsan Essaid, who will become vice chairman, an executive role, at the same time. Ahuja brings more than two decades of experience. He joins from aluminum producer Novelis, where he has served as CFO since 2016. Previously, he held CFO roles at Novartis for Alcon North America, Alcon Japan and the company’s South Korean business.

Mike Barna was named CFO of Advantive, a provider of software for specialty manufacturing and distribution businesses. Barna brings more than two decades of finance and operating leadership across software and data businesses, most recently as CFO of Lone Wolf Technologies. He has also held leadership roles at CoreLogic, Information Services Group and The Nielsen Company.

Adrian Bartella was named CFO of Medical Solutions, a health care workforce solutions company. Bartella brings more than 20 years of finance leadership experience, including serving as CFO of Upstream Rehabilitation, The Fresh Market and Hudson Group.

#5454. What Changing College Enrollment Trends Reveal About the Future of Work

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here is what’s driving changes in student preferences and how universities can adapt academic programs and align curricula with workforce needs to help students make better career choices.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

College enrollment in the United States is growing, but the programs attracting students are changing. While some academic disciplines are experiencing renewed demand, others are seeing enrollment decline, raising important questions about how student preferences are evolving and whether universities are adapting quickly enough.

Recent findings from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center reveal that enrollment growth is not evenly distributed across academic fields. Health professions, certain STEM disciplines and career-oriented credentials are gaining momentum, while computer science enrollment has declined in some degree categories.

For university leaders, these changes present a challenge that goes beyond attracting more students. They must understand where academic demand is shifting, what these patterns suggest about the future workforce and how their institutions should respond.

Healthcare-related education is emerging as one of the stronger areas of enrollment growth. According to the National Student Clearinghouse, enrollment in health professions programs at two-year institutions increased by 7.7% in fall 2025 compared with the previous year. Biological sciences enrollment at four-year institutions also increased by 3.7%.

Interest in newer technology disciplines is another notable development. Nearly 80,000 students were enrolled in data science and data analytics programs nationwide in fall 2025, reflecting the growing presence of these specialized fields in higher education.

However, not all technology-related programs are following the same trajectory. Graduate enrollment in computer science declined by approximately 14% in fall 2025. This contrast illustrates why universities cannot treat broad categories such as technology or STEM as having uniform enrollment demand.

Community colleges are also seeing greater interest in shorter academic pathways. Between fall 2021 and fall 2025, undergraduate certificate enrollment at community colleges increased by 28.3%.

Together, these patterns suggest that students are exploring a wider range of educational options, including specialized degrees and shorter credentials that may offer more direct connections to particular occupations.

Changing enrollment patterns may reflect a broader reassessment of the relationship between education and employment.

Students making decisions about higher education must consider tuition costs, the time required to complete a program and the employment opportunities available after graduation. Programs with recognizable occupational pathways may therefore appear particularly attractive.

Healthcare offers a useful example. Many occupations require specific qualifications, certifications, or clinical training, making the connection between education and employment relatively clear. Continued demand for healthcare workers may also influence how prospective students evaluate these programs.

Technology presents a more complicated picture. Artificial intelligence is changing how some technical tasks are performed, potentially influencing perceptions of traditional computer science careers while creating interest in more specialized fields such as data analytics.

However, enrollment trends alone cannot establish why students are changing their academic choices. Demographic changes, institutional capacity, tuition costs, immigration patterns and labor market expectations can all influence enrollment.

The important lesson for universities is that student demand is not static. Understanding the factors behind changing preferences is becoming essential to academic planning.

For decades, universities have made academic planning decisions based on established program portfolios, historical enrollment, faculty resources and institutional priorities. These considerations remain important, but changing student demand requires a more responsive approach.

Institutions should regularly evaluate which programs are attracting students, how enrollment patterns compare with regional and national workforce needs, and whether graduates are finding opportunities related to their education.

This does not mean expanding every program experiencing short-term growth or discontinuing those facing temporary declines. Enrollment trends can fluctuate, and some disciplines provide substantial educational and societal value even when they do not lead directly to a specific occupation.

Instead, universities need to combine enrollment data with employment projections, graduate outcomes and employer feedback.

For example, growing interest in healthcare programs may justify additional clinical partnerships or training capacity where workforce demand supports expansion. Similarly, changing interest across technology disciplines may create opportunities to update curricula, introduce interdisciplinary programs, or integrate emerging technical skills into existing degrees.

Employer collaboration can also help institutions identify gaps between academic preparation and workplace expectations. By involving industry partners in curriculum discussions and experiential learning opportunities, universities can make their programs more responsive without sacrificing academic standards.

Ultimately, effective program planning requires institutions to anticipate change rather than respond only after enrollment patterns become difficult to ignore.

Universities also have a responsibility to help students understand the implications of their academic decisions.

A growing program is not necessarily the right choice for every student, just as declining enrollment does not automatically mean a discipline offers limited career opportunities.

Prospective students need accessible information about program requirements, potential career pathways, graduate earnings and opportunities for further education.

Academic and career advising can play a more proactive role by helping students connect their interests and abilities with realistic educational and professional goals.

Technology can support this process by making program information easier to access and helping advisors provide more personalized guidance. However, meaningful advising must consider individual aspirations rather than relying solely on enrollment trends or projected salaries.

For institutions, providing this transparency can help students make informed choices while strengthening the connection between academic offerings and long-term outcomes.

The current enrollment shifts should serve as a reminder that academic demand will continue to evolve alongside technology, industry requirements and student expectations.

Universities that rely exclusively on historical enrollment patterns risk overlooking emerging opportunities and changing student needs. Yet reacting to every short-term trend can be equally problematic.

The institutions best positioned for the future will be those that consistently evaluate their programs, strengthen relationships with employers and use evidence to guide academic decisions.

The goal is not simply to offer the most popular degrees. It is to build an academic portfolio that remains relevant, adaptable and capable of preparing students for a workforce that will look different from the one universities serve today.
